Ch. 7 — Neurons — The Matter of the Mind

Week 9 · study page · 39 multiple choice · 5 short answer · 42 flashcards · Uncertain. Listed here and on Unit 2. It belongs to whichever exam Whalen says; delete it from the other.

1Ch. 77.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

A thermal receptor in a fingertip and the nerve running up the arm to the spinal cord belong to which division of the nervous system?

Answer: c

The CNS is the brain and spinal cord only, and the PNS is everything else — "everything, and when I mean everything, outside of the brain and the spinal cord." Whalen asked the room for both halves twice. A nerve that plugs into the cord is still outside it, so it is peripheral. Options a and d make the same mistake: they assume that anything carrying information to the CNS is part of it. Option b splits the pair on the same faulty logic.

2Ch. 77.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

A neuron receives a signal from a sensory neuron, compares it with past input, and passes a decision to a motor neuron. Where must this neuron be?

Answer: b

That is an interneuron, and interneurons are found only in the CNS — "You will not find an interneuron anywhere except the central nervous system." They are also more than 99% of the body's neurons. The ganglion is the tempting wrong answer because it sits right beside the cord. But a ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies in the PNS. The receptor and effector ends are where the sensory and motor neurons reach, not where the decision is made.

3Ch. 77.1 · L1.9
  • lecture
  • textbook

You touch a hot pan and drop it before you feel the heat. Which order does the signal take?

Answer: d

This is Whalen's worked reflex arc. The afferent (sensory) neuron carries the signal toward the CNS. An interneuron there integrates it and decides. The efferent (motor) neuron carries the decision out to the effector, a skeletal muscle. Option a swaps afferent and efferent, which is the easiest error under time pressure. Options b and c misplace the interneuron: it sits between the two, because it is in the CNS that the afferent reaches and the efferent leaves. "You dropped it long before you ever thought hot."

4Ch. 7L1.9
  • lecture

Every neuron sends the same kind of signal — an action potential. According to lecture, what gives one particular signal its meaning?

Answer: b

"All neurons say exactly the same thing… Depending on who says it, and who they say it to, gives it meaning." The interneuron knows where the signal came from, and that is the content. Size cannot carry meaning, because the action potential is all-or-nothing and the same size every time. The ion cannot either: every action potential is Na⁺ in and K⁺ out. Speed depends on myelin and diameter, and carries no message.

5Ch. 77.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

A student lists the jobs of neuroglial cells. Which item on the list is wrong?

Answer: d

Sending action potentials is the neuron's job. Neurons are the excitable cells; glia support them. The other three are all glial roles: structural support, nerve growth factors (without which neurons die), and the myelin sheath (Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes). Glia outnumber neurons by about 10 to 1, the figure in the chapter and the deck. Whalen added "in Anatomy I talk more on a scale of 20 to 1" without choosing between them. 10:1 is the course figure.

6Ch. 77.2 · L1.10
  • lecture

According to lecture, at which part of the neuron does a nerve impulse originate?

Answer: c

The axon hillock is the area of the soma where the axon leaves it, and impulses start there. Whalen took this from the animation he played and used it again on Wednesday: a synapse near the hillock counts for more "because right here is where the action potential technically starts." The chapter never names the hillock, so this is a lecture term. Dendrites receive and carry signals toward the soma. A node of Ranvier regenerates an impulse that is already moving. The terminal is where neurotransmitter is released.

7Ch. 77.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

A lab partner calls the sciatic nerve "one very long neuron." What is the correction?

Answer: b

A neuron is one cell; a nerve is a bundle of parallel axons, dendrites or both, from many neurons, wrapped in tough connective tissue. Nerves are classed as sensory, motor or mixed. Whalen asked for this distinction directly. Option c describes a ganglion, a cluster of cell bodies in the PNS. Options a and d each shrink the nerve back to a single cell, which is the original mistake.

8Ch. 77.2 · L1.10
  • lecture
detail

Whalen gave several names for the swelling at the end of an axon branch. Which is not one of them?

Answer: a

Axon terminal, synaptic terminal, synaptic bouton and synaptic knob are four names for one structure: the swelling at the end of the axon that holds synaptic vesicles of neurotransmitter. Expect any of them on the exam. The axon hillock is at the other end of the axon, where it leaves the soma and where the impulse begins.

9Ch. 77.2 · L1.11
  • lecture

Under the microscope, one glial cell sends out several arms, each wrapping a section of a different axon. Which cell is it, and where?

Answer: d

"Yes, you need to know the difference." One oligodendrocyte myelinates sections of many different axons, in the CNS. One Schwann cell wraps one section of one axon, about 1 mm, in the PNS. Option a is the right cell for the PNS but the wrong wrapping pattern. Options b and c put each cell in the wrong division. The chapter names only Schwann cells; oligodendrocytes and the one-to-many difference come from the deck and lecture.

10Ch. 77.2 · L1.11
  • lecture
  • textbook

Multiple sclerosis destroys myelin in the brain and spinal cord. Which statement about it is correct?

Answer: a

MS is the progressive destruction of myelin in the CNS. CNS myelin is made by oligodendrocytes, so that is the cell whose work is lost. The chapter never names it; put Whalen's two facts together. Sclerosis means scars. The scars interfere with impulses along the axon and cause loss of sensation, paralysis and loss of vision. Option c is myasthenia gravis. Whalen himself drifted toward "myelin" on the way to it before landing on receptors. Option d is botulism. Option b puts MS in the wrong division.

11Ch. 77.2 · L1.12
  • lecture
  • textbook

The textbook says the impulse "jumps" from node to node. What did Whalen say is physically happening?

Answer: b

The two sources disagree on the picture, not on the facts. The textbook, the chapter summary and the Pearson animation all say the impulse "jumps" — and if a question asks for the name, it is saltatory conduction. Whalen rejected the picture of a spark arcing over the sheath ("That's not how it happens"), which is option a. The conductor is the axolemma, the neuron's plasma membrane. Myelin is insulation, like the plastic on a wire, so option c is wrong. The signal is boosted at each bare node and nowhere else. Neurotransmitter works only at synapses, so option d is wrong. The "jump" is a metaphor for the speed, not the path.

12Ch. 77.2 · L1.12
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why can the travelling signal be boosted back up only at a node of Ranvier, and nowhere under the myelin?

Answer: a

Whalen made the room work this out. Only at a bare node can the membrane reach the extracellular fluid, because that is where the ions are. There, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, sodium floods in, and the fading signal is boosted again, like slapping a gym rope partway down. This is why myelinated conduction is up to 100 times faster than unmyelinated conduction on an axon of the same diameter. Diameter (b) does not change at a node. Schwann cells supply insulation, not sodium (c). The pump restores gradients after an impulse and does not boost it (d).

13Ch. 77.2 · 7.4
  • textbook
  • lecture

The chapter has two gaps, drawn a page apart. Which description of them is correct?

Answer: b

A node of Ranvier is the bare stretch between two Schwann cells on one axon, and it is what makes saltatory conduction possible. A synaptic cleft is the gap between two cells, the presynaptic and the postsynaptic, and neurotransmitter crosses it. Every wrong option swaps the two. This is end-of-chapter Q5, rewritten so all the options are the same shape. The book's own distractors also include "a chemical that lets neurons communicate", which is a neurotransmitter and not a gap.

14Ch. 77.3 · L1.13
  • textbook
  • lecture

Choose the incorrect statement about ion channels.

Answer: c

Option c describes the sodium-potassium pump, not a channel. Channels move ions for free, down their concentration gradient. The pump spends ATP to move them against it. Whalen drew that line hard: "Why? It's free. The steeper the hill, the faster they move." The other three statements are true. Channels are pores. They are selective ("molecular sieves": sodium channels pass only sodium). Their gates opening and closing is the action potential. This is end-of-chapter Q8, kept.

15Ch. 77.3 · L1.13
  • lecture

A channel on a dendrite opens only when a neurotransmitter binds to it. Which kind of channel is it?

Answer: a

Whalen gives three kinds of channel. Leak channels are permanently open. Ligand-gated channels need a chemical key, such as a neurotransmitter. Voltage-gated channels are opened by an arriving electrical signal (his garage door: no power, no door). A channel that waits for a neurotransmitter is ligand-gated. The chapter only distinguishes "permanently open" from "gated"; the three-way split is his. The pump is not a channel at all, and it costs ATP.

16Ch. 77.3 · L1.14
  • lecture
  • textbook

One cycle of the sodium-potassium pump runs. What has it done?

Answer: d

3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, one ATP per cycle, against both gradients, so it is active transport. Whalen added the arithmetic: three positive charges go out and two come back, so the inside ends up one positive charge more negative per cycle. Option b swaps the ions, a slip he made twice in the Wednesday recap and corrected both times. Option a reverses the ratio. Option c loses the 3:2 that makes the pump build an electrical gradient.

17Ch. 77.3 · L1.14
  • lecture
  • textbook

Probes inside and outside a resting neuron read −70 mV. What does that number describe?

Answer: a

The resting membrane potential is a potential difference, read with one probe inside the membrane and one outside. The inside is more negative: more Na⁺ is outside, more K⁺ is inside, and large negatively charged proteins are stuck inside. Option b inverts it. Option c is wrong because a resting neuron is not firing at all ("just chilling", about 99% of the time). Option d is the threshold, which is −55 mV.

18Ch. 77.3 · L1.15
  • lecture
  • textbook

A little sodium enters a resting neuron and nudges it from −70 mV up to −55 mV. On Whalen's account, what happens next?

Answer: b

−55 mV is threshold, and from there it is "like pulling the trigger on a loaded gun." The action potential cannot be stopped. The number comes only from lecture: the chapter and deck never give threshold a value. Sources differ on how many gates open. The deck says threshold opens all voltage-gated sodium channels; the textbook says more sodium gates open. Answer "all" for the lecture exam. Option a describes a stimulus that falls short of threshold. Option c happens later (repolarization, then hyperpolarization). The pumps (d) come at the end.

19Ch. 77.3 · L1.15
  • lecture

At a synapse on a dendrite, what opens the first sodium gates that carry the cell from −70 mV toward threshold?

Answer: d

Whalen put this to the room twice. Not voltage, because there is not enough voltage yet. A ligand: a neurotransmitter opens ligand-gated channels and lets "just a little sodium" in. Enough of it reaches −55 mV, and only then do the voltage-gated channels take over. Option a is the mistake he was guarding against. The pump never reverses (b). Potassium leaving makes the inside more negative, so it moves the cell away from threshold (c).

20Ch. 77.3 · L1.15
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which pairing of each phase with its ion movement is correct?

Answer: c

Up means sodium in; down means potassium out. Whalen asked for direction and ion at every phase. Both ions are positive, so the charge moves with the ion. Sodium entering raises the inside from −55 to about +30 mV. At the peak the sodium channels close and potassium channels open, and potassium leaving brings the inside back down. Every other option gets an ion or a direction backwards. Potassium never moves in during the impulse; the pump brings it back in afterwards.

21Ch. 77.3 · L1.15
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen drew the action potential with lines marked on the voltage axis. Which set of values is right?

Answer: a

He drew four lines: −70 (rest), −55 (threshold), 0 and +30 (peak). Every wrong option uses the same numbers in the wrong places. Option b swaps rest and threshold. Option c swaps threshold and peak. Option d inflates the peak. The chapter's Figure 7.5 prints only +30, 0 and −70 and draws the threshold line with no number. The −55 comes from lecture.

22Ch. 77.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

A classmate says the sodium-potassium pump drives repolarization by moving potassium out. What is wrong with that?

Answer: c

Repolarization is K⁺ leaving through gated potassium channels. The book says outright that the pump is slow and does not contribute directly to the events of the action potential. Whalen puts the pumps at the end, switching on during hyperpolarization to rebuild the gradients. Options a and b get the pump's direction backwards: it moves Na⁺ out and K⁺ in. Option d puts the pump in the wrong phase. This is the trap in end-of-chapter Q10's last option.

23Ch. 77.3 · L2.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

A second strong stimulus reaches a patch of axon while sodium is still flooding in. According to lecture, what happens?

Answer: b

Whalen splits the refractory period in two; the textbook has one. During the Na⁺-driven depolarization is the absolute period: "you cannot start another action potential." The sodium channel is plugged by a blocking segment, like a time-lock safe. Option a is the relative period, which starts after the Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ is leaving: a second impulse is possible but unlikely. The textbook's single period ("cannot be stimulated again") matches his absolute period. Options c and d break all-or-nothing: impulses never get bigger or longer.

24Ch. 77.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

You touch a warm mug, then a hot pan. How do the impulses in the same sensory neuron differ?

Answer: c

The impulse is all-or-nothing: its size does not depend on the strength of the stimulus. The book's analogy is that the bullet's force does not depend on how hard you pull the trigger. The refractory period breaks a strong, lasting stimulus into a series of separate impulses, so a stronger stimulus raises their frequency, up to a point. The book uses exactly this heat example. Option a is the classic trap (size instead of frequency). Option d is what the refractory period prevents. Speed is set by myelin and diameter, not by the stimulus (b).

25Ch. 77.4 · L2.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

An action potential arrives at an axon terminal. Which ion's entry makes the synaptic vesicles release their contents?

Answer: c

Ca²⁺, through voltage-gated calcium channels (deck slide 7.42). It floods in down its gradient ("It's always the answer"), and the vesicles fuse and release. Whalen said "sodium" first and corrected himself, which makes option a the tempting slip. Each of the chapter's ions has its own job: Na⁺ depolarizes, K⁺ repolarizes, Ca²⁺ triggers release. Chloride belongs to the inhibitory synapse, on the other side of the cleft.

26Ch. 77.4 · L2.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Put these synaptic events in order: (1) neurotransmitter binds receptors, (2) Ca²⁺ enters the knob, (3) vesicles fuse by exocytosis, (4) the action potential arrives.

Answer: d

The action potential arrives, which opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels. Calcium entering makes the vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and empty into the cleft by exocytosis. They can fuse because they are made of the same phospholipid as the membrane. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors coupled to ion channels. Option a puts fusion before the calcium that triggers it. Option b starts with calcium before anything has opened its channels. Option c has binding before any release.

27Ch. 77.4
  • textbook
  • lecture

Acetylcholine makes skeletal muscle contract, yet it inhibits certain other cells. What explains the difference?

Answer: a

The chapter's central claim for §7.4 is that the receptor decides, not the transmitter. The receptor determines which ion channel opens, and so whether the effect is excitatory or inhibitory. Acetylcholine and norepinephrine are the book's own proof: each excites in some places and inhibits in others. Whalen's version is that the neurotransmitter is the key, the receptor the lock and the channel the door. Amount (b) and shape (c) are not what changes. The sending neuron (d) releases the same chemical whatever the target.

28Ch. 77.4 · L2.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

A neurotransmitter opens chloride channels on a postsynaptic neuron. What is the effect?

Answer: b

This is an inhibitory synapse. Cl⁻ is an anion, so its entry makes the inside more negative than usual, moving the cell further from threshold. Opening K⁺ channels does the same thing, because K⁺ leaves. The deck names K⁺ or Cl⁻; the chapter says only "different ion channels". Whalen calls the result an IPSP. Inhibition raises the bar; it does not block firing, so option c is wrong. Option a is an excitatory synapse (EPSP). Option d is the "presynaptic" swap that makes end-of-chapter Q6's option false.

29Ch. 77.4 · L2.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Two identical excitatory synapses fire on one neuron — one at a dendrite tip, one beside the axon hillock. Which has more influence on whether the neuron fires?

Answer: b

Summation adds up all the excitatory and inhibitory input at a given moment. A neuron can have up to 10,000 synapses at once. Where a synapse sits matters: one by the axon hillock counts for more "because right here is where the action potential technically starts." That is how synapses give fine control. Option c ignores location, which was Whalen's point. Option d ignores summation altogether. Dendrites do receive (a), but a tip is the farthest point from where firing begins.

30Ch. 77.4 · L2.9
  • lecture
  • textbook

On the lecture exam, which list gives every way a neurotransmitter is cleared from the synaptic cleft?

Answer: d

The sources disagree on the count. Whalen's deck (slide 7.49) and his lecture give three routes: diffusion away, reuptake into the presynaptic knob, and enzymatic breakdown (e.g. AChE splitting ACh into an acetyl group and choline). The textbook gives two, and option a is its version. The study guide asks for this list by name, and lecture outranks the book, so give all three. Exocytosis is how the transmitter gets into the cleft, not out of it, so b and c are wrong.

31Ch. 77.4 · L2.9
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

A patient starts an SSRI. What does the drug do at a serotonin synapse?

Answer: a

SSRI stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. It shuts down reuptake, so serotonin stays in the cleft, binds more, and has a longer effect. Whalen explained why the drug does not just give serotonin (b): "Anything you put into your body that your body already makes, your body will stop making it." That is also why SSRIs are tapered slowly under a physician. Option c and option d would both reduce the serotonin signal. The book describes Prozac, Zoloft and Paxil the same way: they raise serotonin by slowing its removal.

32Ch. 77.4 · L2.10
  • lecture
  • textbook

A patient's muscles weaken quickly with repeated movement, and tests find antibodies against her own acetylcholine receptors. Which statement fits?

Answer: b

Myasthenia gravis is autoimmune: it attacks the acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. "If there is no receptors, it doesn't matter how much ACh you have." With few receptors, the normal drop in ACh after repeated firing is enough to fail, so repeated movements quickly become feeble. Whalen also named general malaise, weakness and fatigue. Treatment is drugs that inhibit acetylcholinesterase. MS (a) is myelin, not receptors. Whalen drifted toward myelin before landing on receptors, so do not carry his slip into the exam. Options c and d are other diseases with no antibody against receptors.

33Ch. 77.4 · L2.10
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which disease is correctly paired with the neurotransmitter that falls in it?

Answer: d

Parkinson's — ↓dopamine, from the death of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain's movement control centre. Alzheimer's — ↓acetylcholine, which can fall by as much as 90%. Clinical depression — ↓serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine. Options a and b swap the two diseases' transmitters. Option c borrows depression's transmitter.

34Ch. 77.4
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

A Parkinson's patient is given L-dopa with carbidopa rather than dopamine itself. Why?

Answer: a

Swallowed dopamine is kept out of the brain by the blood–brain barrier. L-dopa can cross, and the brain converts it to dopamine. Carbidopa stops dopamine forming outside the brain, where it causes side effects. The treatment does not stop the neurons dying, which is why it loses effect over time. Whalen called levodopa "just a band-aid." Acetylcholinesterase acts only on acetylcholine (b). Option c misapplies his point that the body stops making what you supply, which is about the same chemical, not another one. Nothing in the sources says dopamine fails to fit its own receptor (d).

35Ch. 77.4 · L2.10
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which neurotransmitter is tied to emotions and to complex, finely controlled movement?

Answer: c

Dopamine regulates emotions and is used in the pathways for complex movements. Whalen added very fine motor skills. That is why losing it in Parkinson's shows up as movement problems. Serotonin is a general feeling of well-being ("everything is okay"). Norepinephrine covers mood, arousal, hunger, thirst and sex drive. Acetylcholine triggers skeletal muscle contraction at the NMJ but is not the transmitter linked to complex movement.

36Ch. 7Ch. 6 · L1.2
  • lecture

You pick up a pin, then a heavy suitcase with the same arm. How does the nervous system scale up the contraction?

Answer: a

This is recruitment: increasing the number of motor units stimulated, smallest first. Large units cost more ATP, in Whalen's analogy of construction crews that cost "exponentially more… every hour." Option c is wrong because all fibres in a motor unit contract together on the same signal; nothing in a unit fires partially. Option d is wrong because fibre number is fixed. Option b reverses the size order. This muscle material was taught on 10/05, after the Unit 2 Exam.

37Ch. 7Ch. 6 · L1.5
  • lecture

Whalen refused "it makes ATP" as the reason working muscle needs oxygen. Which answer did he want?

Answer: c

"I want you to know this phrase." Oxygen is the final (terminal) electron acceptor at the inner mitochondrial membrane. Without it the electron transport chain stops. He refused "it's passing the hydrogen", which is option d. Myoglobin does release oxygen, but to the mitochondria, not to creatine phosphate (b). Clearing lactic acid is part of repaying the oxygen debt after exercise, not oxygen's role in making ATP (a).

38Ch. 7Ch. 6 · L1.6
  • lecture

A muscle biopsy shows dark red fibres packed with mitochondria and myoglobin, with a rich blood supply. Which description fits them?

Answer: b

Dark red means packed with myoglobin, which means oxygen-dependent: these are slow-twitch, endurance fibres. Whalen's example is chicken dark meat. Fast-twitch fibres contract quickly and powerfully, tire fast, and use glycolysis and lactic acid fermentation (a, c). Option d is the trap he named: every muscle has both types, and training shifts the ratio.

39Ch. 7Ch. 6 · L1.7
  • lecture
detail

After months of lifting above 75% of maximum force, a muscle's cross-section has grown. What has increased?

Answer: d

The number of muscle fibres is fixed. Hypertrophy adds myofilaments, actin and myosin, which make larger myofibrils inside the fibres you already have: "more ropes to pull upon." Option a is the misconception Whalen built the section to rule out. More mitochondria (b) is an effect of aerobic training, which does not make muscles bigger. Nothing in the lecture adds motor units (c).

1Ch. 7short answer7.3 · L1.15
  • lecture
  • textbook

List the steps of an action potential from rest back to rest. Give the voltage at each point and the ion and channel responsible.

Model answer

Rest, −70 mV. The inside is more negative than the outside. The sodium-potassium pump keeps Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside. Reaching threshold. A neurotransmitter opens ligand-gated Na⁺ channels, and a little sodium enters. If enough enters, the cell reaches threshold, −55 mV. Depolarization. At threshold the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, sodium floods in down its gradient, and the inside rises to about +30 mV. Repolarization. At the peak the Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open. Potassium leaves, and the inside becomes negative again. Hyperpolarization. So much K⁺ leaves that the membrane dips below −70 mV. Restoration. The K⁺ channels close and the pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, using ATP) rebuilds both gradients, returning the cell to −70 mV. During depolarization a second impulse cannot start (the absolute refractory period). During repolarization one is possible but unlikely (the relative period).

Marks are for the four voltages (−70, −55, +30, below −70) with the right ion and direction at each phase: Na⁺ in going up, K⁺ out going down. Extra marks for ligand-gated versus voltage-gated channels and for placing the pump after the impulse. The −55 threshold is from lecture only; the chapter gives no number. The two refractory periods are also lecture; the book has one.

2Ch. 7short answer7.4 · L2.6 · L2.9
  • lecture
  • textbook

Describe how a signal passes from one neuron to the next across a synapse, and list how the neurotransmitter is then removed.

Model answer

The action potential reaches the synaptic knob (axon terminal) of the presynaptic neuron. It opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, and calcium flows in down its gradient. Calcium makes the synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. The receptors are coupled to ion channels, so binding opens them. At an excitatory synapse Na⁺ enters and the cell moves toward threshold. At an inhibitory synapse K⁺ leaves or Cl⁻ enters, and the cell moves away from threshold. The neurotransmitter must then be removed, or the channel stays open. There are three ways: it diffuses away from the cleft; it is taken back up into the presynaptic knob and repackaged (reuptake); or it is broken down by an enzyme, as acetylcholinesterase splits acetylcholine into acetyl and choline.

Marks are for the sequence: AP, then Ca²⁺, then fusion and exocytosis, then diffusion, then receptor binding, then channel opening. Calcium is the mark most answers lose. Saying the receptor decides the effect, and naming both outcomes, earns more. For removal, give all three routes, the lecture and deck answer. The textbook gives only reuptake and enzymatic breakdown.

3Ch. 7short answer7.2 · L1.11 · L1.12
  • lecture
  • textbook

Explain what the myelin sheath is, which cells make it, and why it speeds conduction. Then explain what goes wrong in multiple sclerosis.

Model answer

The myelin sheath is an insulating wrapping of glial-cell plasma membrane around an axon. In the PNS it is made by Schwann cells: each wraps one section of one axon, about 1 mm, over and over. In the CNS it is made by oligodendrocytes: each sends out many arms and wraps sections of many different axons. The bare gaps between the wrappings are the nodes of Ranvier. The impulse travels along the axolemma and fades as it goes. At each node, the only place the membrane touches the extracellular fluid, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and the signal is regenerated. The impulse is boosted only at the nodes rather than continuously, so this saltatory conduction is up to 100 times faster than conduction on an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter. In multiple sclerosis, myelin in the brain and spinal cord (oligodendrocyte myelin) is progressively destroyed and replaced by hardened scars, scleroses. These slow or block impulses and short-circuit them between paths, causing loss of sensation, paralysis and loss of vision.

Marks are for: what myelin is made of; Schwann = PNS, oligodendrocyte = CNS, with the one-to-one versus one-to-many difference (Whalen: "you need to know the difference"); nodes; the 100× figure with its diameter condition; and MS as a CNS disease with its symptoms. The best answers name saltatory conduction and say that the signal is regenerated at the nodes rather than arcing over the sheath.

4Ch. 7short answer7.3 · L1.14
  • lecture
  • textbook

How is the resting potential set up and maintained? Name both gradients, and explain why the neuron spends ATP on it.

Model answer

At rest the inside of a neuron is about 70 mV more negative than the outside (−70 mV). The sodium-potassium pump maintains this. It is active transport: one ATP per cycle moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, against their gradients. The result is two gradients. One is a concentration gradient: Na⁺ is high outside and K⁺ is high inside. The other is an electrical gradient: the outside is more positive and the inside more negative. Each cycle removes three positive charges and returns two, and large negatively charged proteins stay trapped inside. Potassium leak channels are always open and let K⁺ trickle out, and some Na⁺ leaks in, so the pump has to keep running. The ATP is worth it because steep gradients mean that when the gates open, ions move as fast as possible. The neuron can respond at once, like a car battery kept charged.

Marks are for −70 mV with its meaning (inside against outside), the pump's 3:2 ratio and ATP cost, and both gradients by name. Whalen asks for the pair, and the chapter never names it. Leak channels, and the reason for spending ATP, earn the rest. Do not swap the ions; Whalen did twice and corrected himself.

5Ch. 7short answer7.4 · L2.10
  • textbook
  • lecture

For myasthenia gravis, Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease, name the neurotransmitter involved, say what goes wrong, and give the symptoms.

Model answer

Myasthenia gravis — acetylcholine. An autoimmune disease that attacks the acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. With few receptors, the normal fall in ACh during repeated firing is enough to fail, so there is little muscle strength and repeated movements quickly become feeble, with weakness, fatigue and malaise. It is treated with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which keep more ACh in the junction. Parkinson's — dopamine. Dopamine-producing neurons die in the brain's movement control centre; up to 80% may be gone before diagnosis. Symptoms are slow movement, a shuffling gait and hunched posture, tremors, and rigidity that can cause sudden "freezing" mid-movement. Whalen also described a cogwheeling motion when reaching. It is treated with L-dopa plus carbidopa, because dopamine cannot cross the blood–brain barrier. This does not stop the neurons dying. Alzheimer's — acetylcholine, which can fall by up to 90%. It causes progressive loss of memory, especially for recent events, followed by personality changes. The hippocampus and cerebral cortex lose neurons. The brain also shows amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.

One mark each for disease plus transmitter, mechanism, and two symptoms. The symptoms are in the reading, not the deck, which names only the transmitter, so this answer comes from the Health Issue essay. MG is receptors, not myelin. Write "tremor" or "cogwheeling" for Parkinson's, not Whalen's "essential tremor", which is a different condition.

1Ch. 7flashcard7.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neurons

Back

Nerve cells: excitable cells that generate and transmit messages (action potentials). Their job is communication.

2Ch. 7flashcard7.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neuroglia cells

Back

Support cells of the nervous system. They are not excitable. They give structural support, supply nerve growth factors and form myelin. They outnumber neurons by about 10 to 1.

3Ch. 7flashcard7.1
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Nerve growth factors

Back

Chemicals supplied by glial cells that stimulate nerve growth. Without them, neurons die.

4Ch. 7flashcard7.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Function of the nervous system, and its two primary divisions

Back

To integrate and coordinate body activities. CNS = brain and spinal cord only. PNS = everything else.

5Ch. 7flashcard7.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sensory neuron

Back

Afferent: carries information from sensory receptors toward the CNS.

6Ch. 7flashcard7.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Interneuron

Back

The association neuron between sensory and motor neurons. It integrates, interprets and decides. Found only in the CNS, and makes up more than 99% of the body's neurons.

7Ch. 7flashcard7.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Motor neuron

Back

Efferent: carries the decision away from the CNS to an effector, a muscle (which contracts) or a gland (which secretes).

8Ch. 7flashcard7.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Dendrite

Back

Short, branching projections with a huge surface for receiving signals, which they carry toward the soma.

9Ch. 7flashcard7.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Axon

Back

A single long extension that conducts the impulse away from the soma to another neuron or an effector. It can be over a metre long.

10Ch. 7flashcard7.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Soma (cell body)

Back

The fattest part of the neuron. It holds the nucleus and organelles and keeps the cell functioning ("like management").

11Ch. 7flashcardL1.10
  • lecture

Axon hillock

Back

The area of the soma where the axon leaves it, and where the nerve impulse originates. A lecture term; the chapter never names it.

12Ch. 7flashcard7.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Nerve

Back

A bundle of parallel axons, dendrites or both from many neurons, covered in tough connective tissue. Classed as sensory, motor or mixed. Not a neuron.

13Ch. 7flashcard7.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Myelin sheath

Back

An insulating wrap of glial plasma membrane around an axon. It speeds conduction. Found on most axons outside the CNS and some inside.

14Ch. 7flashcard7.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Schwann cells

Back

Make myelin in the PNS. One Schwann cell wraps one section of one axon, about 1 mm.

15Ch. 7flashcardL1.11
  • lecture

Oligodendrocyte

Back

Makes myelin in the CNS. One cell sends out many arms and wraps many different axons.

16Ch. 7flashcard7.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Node of Ranvier

Back

The bare gap of axon between adjacent Schwann cells, where the membrane touches the extracellular fluid and the impulse is regenerated.

17Ch. 7flashcard7.2 · L1.12
  • lecture
  • textbook

Saltatory conduction

Back

Node-to-node conduction along a myelinated axon, up to 100× faster than an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter. The signal is regenerated at each node; it does not arc over the sheath.

18Ch. 7flashcardL1.12
  • lecture
detail

Axolemma

Back

The plasma membrane of a neuron, its conductive part. It is the neuron's equivalent of the muscle fibre's sarcolemma.

19Ch. 7flashcard7.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Multiple sclerosis

Back

Progressive destruction of myelin in the CNS (so oligodendrocyte myelin), leaving scars called scleroses. Causes loss of sensation, paralysis and loss of vision.

20Ch. 7flashcardL1.13
  • lecture

The three kinds of ion channel

Back

Leak (always open) · ligand-gated (opened by a chemical key such as a neurotransmitter) · voltage-gated (opened by an electrical signal). Channels cost no energy.

21Ch. 7flashcardL1.13
  • lecture

Why ions need channels to cross the membrane

Back

Because they are charged, not because they are large.

22Ch. 7flashcardL1.3
  • lecture

Why does an ion move when its channel opens?

Back

Down its concentration gradient. "That's always the answer."

23Ch. 7flashcard7.3 · L1.14
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sodium-potassium pump

Back

Active transport: one ATP moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, against their gradients. It builds a concentration gradient and an electrical gradient.

24Ch. 7flashcard7.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Resting potential

Back

−70 mV: the inside is 70 mV more negative than the outside in a neuron that is not transmitting. Na⁺ is high outside, K⁺ high inside, and the pump maintains it.

25Ch. 7flashcardL1.15
  • lecture

Threshold

Back

−55 mV, the level at which voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and the action potential becomes unstoppable. The number is from lecture only.

26Ch. 7flashcard7.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Action potential

Back

An electrochemical signal: Na⁺ in (depolarization to +30 mV), then K⁺ out (repolarization). The charge difference is reversed and then restored. All-or-nothing.

27Ch. 7flashcardL1.15
  • lecture

Hyperpolarization

Back

The dip below −70 mV after repolarization, because so much K⁺ has left. The pumps switch on here to restore the gradients.

28Ch. 7flashcard7.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Refractory period

Back

The brief interval after an impulse when the Na⁺ channels cannot reopen. It makes the impulse one-way and makes stimulus strength show as frequency.

29Ch. 7flashcardL2.4
  • lecture
detail

Absolute vs relative refractory period

Back

Absolute: during Na⁺-driven depolarization, no new action potential is possible. Relative: after the Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ is leaving, a new one is possible but unlikely. This split is from lecture; the book gives one period.

30Ch. 7flashcard7.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neurotransmitter

Back

The chemical stored in synaptic vesicles and released into the cleft. It binds receptors on the next cell and opens ion channels.

31Ch. 7flashcard7.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Pre-synaptic membrane

Back

The membrane of the sending neuron's synaptic knob, where vesicles fuse and release neurotransmitter.

32Ch. 7flashcard7.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Post-synaptic membrane

Back

The membrane of the receiving cell, carrying the receptors coupled to ion channels.

33Ch. 7flashcard7.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Excitatory synapse

Back

Neurotransmitter opens Na⁺ channels. The cell moves toward threshold (an EPSP), so an action potential is more likely.

34Ch. 7flashcard7.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Inhibitory synapse

Back

Neurotransmitter opens K⁺ or Cl⁻ channels. The inside becomes more negative (an IPSP), so more excitation is needed to reach threshold.

35Ch. 7flashcardL1.4 · L2.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

"Summation" — its two meanings in this course

Back

Muscle: a second stimulus before relaxation gives a stronger twitch. Synapse: the combined effect of all excitatory and inhibitory input at one moment decides whether the neuron fires.

36Ch. 7flashcard7.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Acetylcholine and acetylcholinesterase

Back

ACh is released at every neuromuscular junction and triggers skeletal muscle contraction. AChE splits it into an acetyl group and choline, ending its action.

37Ch. 7flashcard7.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Functions of dopamine and serotonin

Back

Dopamine: emotions, complex movements, fine motor skills. Serotonin: a general feeling of well-being.

38Ch. 7flashcard7.4 · L2.13
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Epinephrine — what the sources give

Back

The study guide asks for its function, but Ch. 7 never gives one. The only lecture link is the 10/07 start of Ch. 8: epinephrine (adrenaline) from the adrenal glands drives fight-or-flight. Do not mix it up with norepinephrine (mood, hunger, thirst, sex drive).

39Ch. 7flashcardCh. 6 · L1.2
  • lecture

Motor unit, and why small ones are recruited first

Back

One motor neuron plus every fibre it innervates, all contracting together. Precise movement uses few fibres per unit. Small units go first because large ones cost more ATP.

40Ch. 7flashcardCh. 6 · L1.4
  • lecture

Twitch → summation → tetanus → fatigue

Back

Twitch: one stimulus. Summation: a second before relaxation, which is stronger. Tetanus: very frequent stimuli lock the muscle. Fatigue: failure from lack of ATP or run-down ion gradients.

41Ch. 7flashcardCh. 6 · L1.5
  • lecture
detail

Muscle fuel timeline

Back

Stored ATP 6 s → creatine phosphate 10 s → muscle glycogen ~30–40 s → aerobic metabolism.

42Ch. 7flashcardCh. 6 · L1.5
  • lecture
detail

Oxygen debt — the four things restored

Back

Lactic acid washed away · creatine phosphate rebuilt · oxygen restored to myoglobin · glycogen reserves restored.

Ch. 8 — The Nervous System

Week 10 · study page · 48 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 52 flashcards

1Ch. 88.1
  • lecture

A receptor in your fingertip detects heat, and the signal travels to the spinal cord. What kind of neuron carries it there?

Answer: b

Whalen's sequence is afferent (sensory) in → integrating centre → efferent (motor) out. Anything travelling from a receptor toward the CNS is afferent, and the neuron doing it is sensory. Efferent is the trap — it is the outbound leg, from the CNS to an effector such as a muscle or gland. The two mixed options pair a direction with the wrong neuron type: motor neurons only ever carry commands out.

2Ch. 88.1
  • lecture

With your eyes closed you touch your nose, then your left ear, and never miss. Which division of the nervous system is reporting where your hand is?

Answer: c

That is Whalen's own test of proprioception — "where my body is in space" — and he filed it under somatic sensory, alongside sight and hearing. Somatic motor is the tempting answer because the hand is moving voluntarily, but the question asks what reports position, which is input, not output. Visceral sensory is information from the internal environment (the guts, plus smell and taste); autonomic motor is involuntary output to organs.

3Ch. 88.1
  • lecture
detail

In lecture, which two senses did Whalen give as the visceral sensory inputs we are consciously aware of?

Answer: d

Visceral sensory is "think about your guts" — information from the internal environment — and the conscious examples are olfaction and gustation: molecules dissolve in "snot or saliva" and bind receptors on olfactory hairs and taste buds. Sight and hearing are the trap: they are somatic sensory, scanning the outside world "first and foremost for danger." Proprioception is also somatic. Balance and pain were not given as visceral examples.

4Ch. 88.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which statement correctly describes the autonomic nervous system?

Answer: a

This is the book's definition (end-of-chapter Q2). Whalen: "you should be thinking automatic. It takes care of itself" — heart, diaphragm, the gut's segmentation and peristalsis. Conscious skeletal movement is the somatic system. The autonomic system is a division of the peripheral system, so it is not contained in the CNS. And emotion drives it all the time — fear switches on the sympathetic branch, and the hypothalamus takes input from the cortex.

5Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Put the coverings of the brain in order from the skull inward, including the two named spaces.

Answer: c

Dura mater ("tough mother") is outermost, then the subdural space, the arachnoid, the subarachnoid space — "a big, long gap filled with cerebrospinal fluid" — and the pia mater ("tender mother") molded onto the brain. Each space is named for the layer it sits under: subdural under the dura, subarachnoid under the arachnoid. Option a swaps the two spaces; b is the correct list read backward; d puts the arachnoid outside the dura. The book names only the three layers; the two spaces are from lecture.

6Ch. 88.2
  • lecture

Which space around the brain and spinal cord is filled with cerebrospinal fluid?

Answer: d

The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and the pia, holds the CSF — Whalen said so on Monday and repeated it for the cord on Wednesday. The subdural space is the near-miss: it is the gap one layer further out. "Dural sinus" is what he guessed on Wednesday when he blanked on that outer gap and said he wasn't sure — don't write it. There is no space under the pia: it is attached directly to the brain and cord.

7Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

The blood–brain barrier works because the cells of CNS capillary walls are joined by which kind of junction?

Answer: b

Tight junctions — Whalen's "duct tape" — seal the cells together so nothing passes between them. Anything leaving the blood must go through a cell, and the cell membranes filter what gets in. He sent you back to Ch. 3's four adhesive junctions for this, which is why the other three are here: gap junctions are channels that let things pass, and desmosomes and hemidesmosomes resist mechanical stress without sealing anything.

8Ch. 88.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Caffeine and alcohol reach the brain within minutes, yet many infection-fighting drugs never get in. What explains the difference?

Answer: c

The barrier forces everything through cell membranes, and membranes are largely lipid, so lipid-soluble substances — oxygen, carbon dioxide, caffeine, alcohol — cross easily. Many lifesaving drugs are not lipid-soluble, which is the barrier's cost (Ch. 7's L-dopa problem is the same thing). Slipping between cells is exactly what the tight junctions prevent, so a is backward. Nothing in the sources has red cells ferrying drugs across, and the ependymal cells line the choroid plexus where CSF is made — they are not a drug pump.

9Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where is cerebrospinal fluid made?

Answer: d

The choroid plexus is a bed of specialised capillaries in each ventricle, lined by a neuroglial cell, the ependymal cell ("with an E"): "we take stuff from the blood and we modify it." Arachnoid granulations are the opposite end of the trip — where CSF drains back into the blood. Oligodendrocytes make myelin, not fluid, and the pia is a covering.

10Ch. 88.2
  • lecture

Trace CSF from the ventricles where it is made to the fourth ventricle.

Answer: b

The two lateral ventricles drain through the interventricular foramen ("foramen equals hole") into the third ventricle, which empties down the cerebral aqueduct — "a waterslide" — into the fourth. From there it leaves by one median and two lateral apertures and continues down the central canal. Option a swaps the two connectors; c starts in the third; d is the right path run backward. He put the ventricle model out in lab for this and nobody picked it up — "I pulled it out for a reason."

11Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
detail

Which pairing of structure and description at the lower end of the spinal cord is correct?

Answer: c

The filum terminale is an extension of the pia mater running to the coccygeal ligament, anchoring the cord. The conus medullaris is the cord's tapered end (around L2 in an adult), and the cauda equina — "horse's tail" — is the bundle of nerves hanging below it. Options a and b swap conus and cauda; d gives the cauda equina the filum's job. All three are lecture terms the book never uses.

12Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

A tissue sample from the brain turns out to be almost entirely myelinated axons. Which structure is it most likely from?

Answer: a

Myelinated axons make white matter, and the corpus callosum is the band of white matter joining the two hemispheres. The cortex is gray matter — neuroglia, cell bodies and unmyelinated axons — and both gyri named here are strips of that cortex (primary somatosensory and primary motor). Whalen: "somas are never myelinated," so any region full of cell bodies is gray.

13Ch. 88.2
  • lecture

Which cell lays down the myelin in the white matter of the brain?

Answer: d

In the CNS myelin comes from oligodendrocytes — "long word, starts with an O." The Schwann cell is the trap: it is the PNS's myelinating cell, the one the endoneurium wraps around in a peripheral nerve. Ependymal cells line the choroid plexus and make CSF. The CNS-level payoff of myelin is his line: "further, faster, and for cheaper."

14Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

A stroke in the left cerebral hemisphere takes away feeling and movement in the right arm. What is this pattern called, and where do the fibres cross?

Answer: b

Each hemisphere runs the opposite side — contralateral — because fibres cross at the pyramids of decussation in the medulla oblongata. Whalen asked for contralateral and ipsilateral two lectures running: "I want you to remember it." The corpus callosum is the trap — it connects the two hemispheres to each other, but it is not where body pathways change sides. Ipsilateral means same side.

15Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

A surgeon stimulates the gyrus immediately in front of the central sulcus and the patient's thumb twitches. Which area was stimulated?

Answer: d

The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal. In front of it is the precentral gyrus = primary motor area (voluntary movement); behind it, the postcentral gyrus = primary somatosensory area. The somatosensory option is the mirror-image trap — one gyrus back. The premotor cortex lies further forward still and coordinates learned skills; the prefrontal cortex is the most anterior frontal lobe, for reasoning and planning.

16Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

On the somatosensory body map, the face and mouth get far more cortex than the whole leg. Why?

Answer: b

Cortex goes to sensitivity, not size or distance — "the greater the sensitivity, the greater the area of cortex." Whalen's splinter: you "hella feel it with your tongue" but not with your cheek. Distance from the brain is a distractor the book itself offered (end-of-chapter Q4) and is wrong. On the motor map the rule is the same idea applied to fine control, which is why the two maps are similar but not identical.

17Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Where are the complex movement sequences of a learned skill, such as dancing, stored? Lecture and textbook disagree — which pairing is right?

Answer: c

This is a recorded conflict. Whalen said the premotor cortex coordinates learned skills but "you actually store them in another area called the cerebellum" — matching the cerebellum box of Figure 8.3. The textbook's text (the guitarist) stores the pattern in the premotor cortex, and his own deck sides with the text. On his exam, the lecture answer is cerebellum; on a book-worded question, premotor cortex. Option a is the conflict reversed.

18Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

After a car accident, an intracranial bleed pushed on Whalen's prefrontal cortex. Which abilities did he describe losing for a long time?

Answer: b

The prefrontal cortex predicts the consequences of possible responses and picks the best one — reasoning, long-term planning, abstract thought, personality. Whalen: reason, planning and consequences "went bye-bye for a really long time." Balance and timing are the cerebellum; touch, pain and temperature are the primary somatosensory area in the parietal lobe; hearing and smell are temporal-lobe sensory areas.

19Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Which sensory signal reaches the cerebrum without first being relayed through the thalamus?

Answer: d

The thalamus is "the relay station for the brain" — every sense passes through it except smell, which goes from the olfactory bulb straight to the limbic system. That is also why smell is so tied to memory and emotion. Vision (to the occipital lobe), hearing (temporal) and taste (parietal) all go to the thalamus first.

20Ch. 88.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which of the following is NOT a function of the hypothalamus?

Answer: c

Sensory–motor coordination is the cerebellum. The hypothalamus — Whalen's "baller, a boss" — keeps homeostasis: blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate, digestion, body temperature, hunger and thirst. Heart rate and blood pressure tempt because the medulla also has them: the medulla holds the reflex centres, and the hypothalamus influences them from above (book end-of-chapter Q7).

21Ch. 88.2
  • lecture

How does the hypothalamus control the pituitary gland (hypophysis)?

Answer: a

The hypothalamus makes releasing and inhibiting hormones that travel down the infundibulum through the hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system to the hypophysis, telling it to release or hold its own hormones. This is where Whalen's wired nervous system meets the wireless endocrine system, and the hypothalamus coordinates both. The vagus goes to the heart and gut, the sympathetic chain to the organs, and the corpus callosum joins the hemispheres.

22Ch. 88.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Reaching to scratch an itch, your hand stops at your cheek instead of slapping your face. Which cerebellar process made that happen?

Answer: a

Prediction calculates a body part's future position during a movement and stops it at the intended point — the book's itch example. Comparison is the close partner and the trap: it checks where a part is against where it should be, and corrects (Whalen standing on his own shoelace while rock-hopping). Decussation is the crossing of fibres in the medulla; adaptation is receptors going quiet under constant stimulation.

23Ch. 88.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why would a tumour destroying the medulla kill sooner than a tumour of the same size in the cerebral cortex?

Answer: c

The medulla holds the reflex centres for the rhythm of breathing, the force and rate of the heartbeat and blood pressure (vasomotor tone) — things that cannot pause — and all traffic between brain and body passes through it. A cortical lesion costs a function; a medullary one stops breathing. Most neurons everywhere cannot divide, so a is not special to the medulla; nothing says it lacks the barrier; long-term memory needs the hippocampus.

24Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Tires screech behind you and you turn your head and eyes toward the sound before you think. Which structures run that reflex?

Answer: a

The four bumps on the back of the midbrain — the corpora quadrigemina or tectum — are two superior colliculi (sight) and two inferior colliculi (hearing), and their reflex ties visual tracking to an auditory stimulus. "This has kept your ancestors alive long enough to give rise to you." The gray horns are cord reflex centres for limbs; the limbic structures handle memory and emotion; the gyri are the primary motor and somatosensory strips.

25Ch. 88.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

In the textbook's text, which structure connects the spinal cord and cerebellum with the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus?

Answer: a

Pons means "bridge", and the text, the deck and the lecture all give it this connecting role (it also helps the medulla with breathing). The midbrain is the trap from a recorded conflict: Figure 8.3's midbrain box says it "relays information between the cerebellum or spinal cord and the cerebrum," but the text and deck give the midbrain sights, sounds and simple reflexes. The medulla is the lowest link, joining the cord to the brain; the thalamus relays sensory input.

26Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which two structures does Whalen's deck name as parts of the limbic system?

Answer: d

The hippocampus (essential for consolidating short-term into long-term memory) and the amygdala (ties memories to emotional states) are the deck's limbic structures; the book adds the hypothalamus. Putamen and lentiform are the trap — he said them in passing, but they are basal nuclei, not limbic, and neither the chapter nor the deck uses them. The limbic system is defined by function — memory stored together with emotion — not by one anatomical region.

27Ch. 88.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

After a car accident, Jorge remembers his childhood clearly but forgets a conversation within minutes of it ending. Which structure was most likely damaged?

Answer: c

Old memories intact and new ones not sticking is a failure to move short-term memory into long-term storage — and for that the hippocampus is essential (book end-of-chapter Q19). The amygdala is the limbic near-miss: it attaches emotion to memories, it does not consolidate them. The cerebellum coordinates movement, and prefrontal damage costs reasoning and planning rather than new memories.

28Ch. 88.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

While studying, you stop noticing the pressure of your clothes and the rustle of pages turning. Which system screens these stimuli out, according to the textbook?

Answer: a

The RAS filters repetitive, familiar stimuli and passes the important ones on — rustling paper and clothing pressure are the book's own examples (end-of-chapter Q14). Whalen gave the RAS this job on Wednesday. On Monday he called the same effect a "thalamic block," putting it in the thalamus — a recorded conflict; if he asks for "thalamic block" by name, give him that. The medulla tempts because the RAS runs through it, but filtering is the network's job, not the reflex centres'.

29Ch. 88.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

A boxer takes a twisting blow to the jaw and is knocked out, though his cerebral cortex is undamaged. Why does he lose consciousness?

Answer: b

"Consciousness occurs only while the RAS stimulates the cerebral cortex." The twisting blow whips the brain stem, where the RAS runs, and with nothing driving it the cortex shuts off — a very brief coma (book Stop and Think). The other three are real structures with the wrong job: the cerebellum handles balance and coordination, the corpus callosum joins the hemispheres, and the hypothalamus regulates temperature without controlling consciousness.

30Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

According to Whalen, what moves information from short-term memory into long-term memory?

Answer: d

Repetition and rehearsal: "Recall leads to reinforcement. The more often you use something, the stronger that pathway gets." Option b is the one he ruled out by name — "labeling a model one time doesn't teach you shit." Emotion does not block memory; the limbic system stores memory with emotion. Short-term memory holds a small amount for seconds to minutes; long-term holds it for hours to forever.

31Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

How are gray and white matter arranged in a cross-section of the spinal cord?

Answer: a

The cord is the inside-out of the brain: white matter outside (myelinated axons in ascending and descending tracts), gray matter inside in a butterfly of horns — posterior, anterior and to some extent lateral — around the CSF-filled central canal. Option b is the cerebrum's arrangement, which is exactly why it tempts. The gray matter holds the interneurons and motor-neuron cell bodies, which is what lets the cord act as a reflex centre.

32Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Whalen said the reflex arc "will probably be on an upcoming exam, three." Which lists its parts in the correct order?

Answer: d

In at the receptor, along the sensory (afferent) neuron to the cord, through an interneuron, out on the motor (efferent) neuron, act at the effector — Figure 8.8's order and the one he flagged as on Exam 3. Option a puts integration after the command has already gone out; b and c start at the effector, which is the end of the arc.

In lecture: "That will probably be on an upcoming exam, three, that I've already looked at." — the reflex arc, Wed 10/14

33Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Which part of a reflex arc can be missing, with the sensory neuron synapsing directly on the motor neuron?

Answer: b

There is usually at least one interneuron, but Whalen said it "may or may not" be there — the sensory neuron can synapse straight onto the motor neuron. Without a receptor nothing is detected; without the sensory neuron nothing reaches the cord; without an effector nothing happens. Know the five parts in order and that this one is optional.

34Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

You let go of a hot pan before you consciously think "hot." Why?

Answer: c

"Your brain wasn't involved in that decision. Your spinal cord made that decision." The withdrawal is a spinal reflex. The pain still travels up the ascending tracts, but that route is longer in distance and in synapses, so you feel it after the hand has moved — and can learn from it. The thalamus does not block it; you do feel the burn. The cerebellum and motor cortex are not involved in the reflex decision.

35Ch. 88.2
  • lecture
detail

You step on a nail. As the injured leg withdraws, what does the other leg do, and what lets the two sides of the cord coordinate it?

Answer: d

This is the crossed extensor reflex: the stepping leg withdraws while the contralateral leg contracts to hold you up — "or else I just fall over, probably into that glass." The gray commissures, bands of gray matter in front of and behind the central canal, let axons cross the cord so the two halves talk without going up to the brain. Withdrawing or relaxing the other leg drops you; the corpus callosum and thalamus are in the brain, which is not in the loop.

36Ch. 88.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

A spinal nerve's dorsal root is cut, but its ventral root is intact. What is lost in the region that nerve serves?

Answer: a

Sensory in the back, motor out the front — Whalen said it four times. The dorsal root carries sensory neurons only; the ventral root carries motor neurons only. Cut the dorsal root and sensation goes while movement stays. Option b is the ventral-root injury; the ventral root cannot take over because it carries no sensory fibres at all.

37Ch. 88.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

A spinal nerve is cut just outside the intervertebral foramen, after its two roots have joined. What is lost?

Answer: c

The dorsal and ventral roots join to form the spinal nerve, and all 31 pairs are mixed — sensory and motor together. Cut beyond the junction and both are lost in that region. The dorsal-root ganglion holds the sensory cell bodies; it reroutes nothing. Compare the previous item, where cutting only one root costs only one function.

38Ch. 88.3
  • lecture
detail

Which cranial nerve entry is correct for number, name and function?

Answer: b

V is the trigeminal and is both sensory and motor. III is the oculomotor (IV is trochlear), and Whalen himself muddled IV and V while pointing, so watch those two. VIII, vestibulocochlear, is sensory only. XI is the accessory; the hypoglossal is XII, to the tongue. The book and deck never name the cranial nerves — he requires the names, so this is lecture material and on the exam.

39Ch. 88.3
  • lecture
detail

Which cranial nerve carries roughly 75% of all parasympathetic outflow, including fibres to the heart?

Answer: d

The vagus nerve, cranial nerve X, carries about 75% of parasympathetic outflow — a lecture-only figure Whalen said twice, the second time "for those of you recording." The book's note that cranial nerves serve the heart and diaphragm is the vagus too. The other three are real cranial nerves, but the lecture gives the 75% share to the vagus alone; the parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral, leaving the brain stem mostly through cranial nerve X.

40Ch. 88.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where do sympathetic fibres leave the CNS, and where do parasympathetic fibres leave it? (Sympathetic · parasympathetic)

Answer: c

Sympathetic = thoracolumbar — "pretty much in the middle." Parasympathetic = craniosacral — "top and bottom," mostly via cranial nerve X and the sacral cord. Option d is a recorded conflict: Whalen said "cervical and sacral" once and slide 8.37 prints it, but his own word craniosacral, slide 8.39, Figure 8.10 and the animation all say cranial. Write cranial. Option a is the correct pair swapped.

41Ch. 88.3
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Whalen called this "an A question right there." Which transmitters do autonomic neurons release? (Preganglionic · postganglionic)

Answer: b

Every preganglionic neuron releases acetylcholine. At the postganglionic neuron the sympathetic switches to norepinephrine and the parasympathetic stays with acetylcholine — "it never makes that switch." Option c swaps the two divisions; a and d wrongly start with NE. The opposite chemicals are what make dual innervation work: one organ, receptors for both, opposite messages.

In lecture: "That's an A question right there." — postganglionic transmitters, Wed 10/14

42Ch. 88.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why does the sympathetic system act all at once while the parasympathetic system acts organ by organ?

Answer: d

Sympathetic ganglia are linked in a chain just outside the spinal column, so the system fires as a unit — "exactly what is needed in an emergency." Parasympathetic ganglia sit near their target organs, so each organ returns to rest at its own pace. Option a is the trap: the transmitters are true but the book says the difference in behaviour comes from ganglion position, not the neurotransmitters. Both divisions are autonomic, and c gets the outflow backward.

43Ch. 88.3
  • lecture

Once a threat has passed, which body systems does the parasympathetic division switch back on?

Answer: c

Rest and digest: after the threat the parasympathetic turns back on the digestive, salivary, reproductive and urinary systems — the vegetative functions. Option a is the trap: those are the systems the body needs at their peak during the threat, under the sympathetic. The heightened state cannot last because it is expensive in ATP, which "cannot be stored."

44Ch. 88.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which pairing correctly matches Whalen's two kinds of stroke to their causes?

Answer: b

A stroke (cerebrovascular accident) is an interruption of blood flow that kills nerve cells. Hemorrhagic: a vessel bursts, usually from high blood pressure. Occlusive: a clot or fatty deposit blocks a vessel, and everything distal gets less blood. Option a is the pair swapped. Whalen's timeline: permanent damage in about 4 to 5 minutes; the book says only "within minutes."

45Ch. 88.4
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

After a stroke in the right rear of her brain, a woman combs only the right side of her hair and eats only from the right side of her plate. What is this?

Answer: a

Damage to the right rear of the brain can cause the neglect syndrome: the person acts as if the left side of things, even of her own body, does not exist. Bell's palsy is the trap — Whalen said facial drooping from it is not a stroke. Quadriplegia is paralysis of all four limbs from a neck-level cord injury; an aura is the visual or sensory warning before a migraine.

46Ch. 88.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

A coma patient does not respond to a sternal rub or anything else. Damage where most commonly causes a coma?

Answer: d

Coma comes from trauma to the neurons that stimulate the cerebrum — chiefly the reticular activating system (the book adds the thalamus). The cortex is the trap: it is most directly responsible for consciousness, yet cerebral damage is rarely the cause. A medically induced coma is different — Whalen: it chemically turns the neurons off and does not damage them.

47Ch. 88.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Which pairing of headache type and cause is correct?

Answer: c

Tension headaches come from contracting the muscles of the head, face and neck ("honestly, you need a massage"). Migraines come from an imbalance in brain chemistry, perhaps low serotonin. Options a and d are both impossible: the brain has no pain receptors — "thinking too much cannot cause a headache." Option b gives the migraine the tension headache's cause.

48Ch. 88.4
  • textbook
  • lecture

Joe's spinal cord is injured in the lower back and Henry's in the neck, to a similar degree. Whose problems are more severe?

Answer: b

Function is lost below — distal to — the site of injury, so a neck injury takes everything a lower-back injury takes and more: arms, most of the trunk, and possibly independent breathing, since the nerves to the diaphragm leave high in the neck. Paralysis of all four limbs is quadriplegia. "Equal degree" is the trap — where the damage is decides the loss. CNS damage does not heal; today the best is "an electric wheelchair."

1Ch. 8short answer8.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Name the five components of a reflex arc in order, say what each does, and explain why the withdrawal reflex is handled by the spinal cord rather than the brain.

Model answer

(1) Receptor — detects the stimulus. (2) Sensory (afferent) neuron — carries the impulse into the spinal cord through the dorsal root. (3) Interneuron in the gray matter — usually at least one, though the sensory neuron can synapse directly on the motor neuron. (4) Motor (efferent) neuron — carries the command out through the ventral root. (5) Effector — the muscle or gland that responds. A reflex is an automatic response, used when damage is being done and speed is everything; routing through the cord is shorter in distance and synapses than going up to the brain, so the hand leaves the hot pan before you feel "hot." The pain message still travels up the ascending tracts so the brain learns what happened.

Whalen said this "will probably be on an upcoming exam, three." One mark per component in the right order, one for noting the interneuron is optional, one for the speed argument, one for the message still reaching the brain.

In lecture: "That will probably be on an upcoming exam, three, that I've already looked at." — the reflex arc, Wed 10/14

2Ch. 8short answer8.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Compare the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions on arrangement of ganglia, function, speed of response, where they leave the CNS, and transmitters. Give one example action for each.

Model answer

Sympathetic — fight or flight; leaves the thoracic and lumbar cord; fast; ganglia in a chain just outside the spinal column, so it fires as a unit; preganglionic ACh, postganglionic norepinephrine. Examples: raises heart rate, breathing rate and blood pressure, dilates the pupils, inhibits digestion, has the adrenals release epinephrine. Parasympathetic — rest and digest, conserving energy; craniosacral, about 75% of it through the vagus nerve (X); slow; ganglia near the target organs, so effects are organ by organ; preganglionic ACh, postganglionic acetylcholine. Examples: slows the heart, switches digestion, salivation and urinary function back on. Both are two-neuron (pre- and postganglionic) pathways and reach most but not all organs; where both reach one organ they are antagonistic — dual innervation.

This is the study guide's compare-and-contrast objective, item by item: ganglia, function, speed and examples. Marks for each row on both sides. Writing "cervical" for the parasympathetic outflow loses the mark — his own word is craniosacral.

3Ch. 8short answer8.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

List the four ways the CNS is protected and describe each one, including the three meninges in order.

Model answer

(1) Bone — the eight cranial bones around the brain and the vertebral column around the cord. (2) Meninges, outer to inner: dura mater (tough, leathery), the arachnoid (cobweb-like) and the pia mater (molded to the brain and cord); the subdural space lies under the dura and the subarachnoid space, filled with CSF, under the arachnoid. (3) Cerebrospinal fluid — cushions the CNS like an air bag, floats the brain so it is not crushed by its own weight, and nourishes the cells and removes wastes. (4) Blood–brain barrier — tight junctions between CNS capillary cells force substances to pass through the cells, so only what the membranes allow — lipid-soluble substances such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, caffeine and alcohol — gets into the CNS.

One mark for each defence; the meninges in the right order; at least two jobs of CSF; tight junctions as the mechanism of the barrier. Naming the two spaces is the lecture's extra.

4Ch. 8short answer8.2
  • lecture

Describe where cerebrospinal fluid is made, the path it takes through the ventricles, and where it returns to the blood. Why can it drain into the blood but blood must not get into it?

Model answer

CSF is made by the choroid plexus — specialised capillaries lined by ependymal cells — in each ventricle, by taking material from the blood and modifying it. It flows from the two lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramen to the third ventricle, down the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, then out through the median and two lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space and down the central canal of the cord. It drains into the blood through arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus. CSF draining out is fine; blood getting in would carry contaminants that inflame the neurons and glia, which is why the blood–brain barrier lets in only what is "deemed worthy."

Marks for the choroid plexus and ependymal cells, the ventricle sequence with both connectors, the drainage site, and the one-way logic. All of this is lecture material — he taught the ventricles early because he wants them known.

5Ch. 8short answer8.3
  • lecture

List the twelve cranial nerves by Roman numeral and name, and say whether each is sensory, motor or both.

Model answer

I olfactory — S; II optic — S; III oculomotor — M; IV trochlear — M; V trigeminal — B; VI abducens — M; VII facial — B; VIII vestibulocochlear — S; IX glossopharyngeal — B; X vagus — B; XI accessory — M; XII hypoglossal — M. (Function mnemonic: "Some say marry money, but my brother says big brains matter more.")

A student asked whether the names are required and Whalen said "Yes" — number, name and function. The book and deck give only numerals and functions, so the names are lecture-sourced. Half a mark per correct entry.

6Ch. 8short answer8.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Describe a cross-section of the spinal cord and how a spinal nerve attaches to it. Include the arrangement of gray and white matter, the two roots, and how many pairs of spinal nerves there are.

Model answer

The cord is the reverse of the cerebrum: white matter outside, made of myelinated axons in ascending (sensory) and descending (motor) tracts, and gray matter inside in posterior, anterior and lateral horns around the CSF-filled central canal, joined across the midline by the gray commissures. The anterior median fissure marks the front and the posterior median sulcus the back. Each spinal nerve has a dorsal root, carrying sensory fibres in, with their cell bodies in the dorsal-root ganglion outside the cord, and a ventral root, carrying motor fibres out from cell bodies in the gray matter. The roots join into one mixed spinal nerve that leaves through the intervertebral foramen. There are 31 pairs, each serving a specific region.

Marks for white-outside/gray-inside, tracts vs horns, dorsal = sensory and ventral = motor, the ganglion's location, mixed nerve, and 31 pairs. "Sensory in the back, motor out the front" — he said it four times.

1Ch. 8flashcard8.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

CNS — Central Nervous System

Back

The brain and spinal cord. Integrates incoming information — "gives it meaning" — and coordinates voluntary and involuntary function.

2Ch. 8flashcard8.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

PNS — Peripheral Nervous System

Back

Everything outside the brain and spinal cord — nerves and ganglia that carry information in and commands out to effectors.

3Ch. 8flashcard8.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Ganglia

Back

Clusters of nerve cell bodies outside the CNS — enlargements in a nerve that fit the somas, often on the sensory side (the dorsal-root ganglion).

4Ch. 8flashcard8.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Somatic nervous system

Back

The PNS division for conscious sensation and voluntary movement — "you told it to happen."

5Ch. 8flashcard8.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Autonomic nervous system (ANS)

Back

The PNS division that automatically adjusts internal organs — heart, gut, glands — without conscious control. Two halves: sympathetic and parasympathetic.

6Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Sympathetic nervous system

Back

Fight or flight. Thoracolumbar outflow, fast, ganglia in a chain so it fires as a unit; postganglionic transmitter norepinephrine.

7Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Parasympathetic nervous system

Back

Rest and digest. Craniosacral outflow, slow, ganglia near the organs so it acts organ by organ; postganglionic transmitter acetylcholine.

8Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Meninges

Back

The three connective-tissue coverings of the brain and cord: dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater (outer to inner).

9Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Dura mater

Back

The outermost, tough, leathery meninx — "tough mother." The subdural space lies beneath it.

10Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Arachnoid layer

Back

The middle, cobweb-like meninx, anchored to the pia by thin threads. The CSF-filled subarachnoid space lies beneath it.

11Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Pia mater

Back

The innermost meninx, molded to the brain and cord "like a leotard" — "tender mother." Its extension, the filum terminale, anchors the cord.

12Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Cerebrum

Back

The largest part of the brain, about 83% of its mass — "the seat of your conscious thinking." Two hemispheres split by the longitudinal fissure.

13Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Cerebral cortex

Back

The thin outer layer of gray matter on the cerebrum (cortex = bark), about 2.5 mm thick and folded to triple its area.

14Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

White matter

Back

Mostly myelinated axons, which make it white; lets regions talk to each other. Inside the cerebrum, outside in the cord.

15Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Gray matter

Back

Neuroglia, cell bodies (somas) and unmyelinated axons. Outside in the cerebrum (cortex), inside in the cord (horns).

16Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Thalamus

Back

The relay station — every sense except smell passes through it to the cortex. Also motor activity, cortical arousal and memory.

17Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Hypothalamus

Back

Below the thalamus; keeps homeostasis (blood pressure, heart rate, breathing, digestion, temperature, hunger, thirst) and controls the pituitary. Part of the limbic system.

18Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Pons

Back

"Bridge" — connects the cord and cerebellum with the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus; helps the medulla regulate breathing.

19Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Medulla oblongata

Back

Reflex centres for breathing rhythm, heart force and rate, and blood pressure; every message between cord and brain passes through it, and it is where they cross.

20Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Cerebellum

Back

Smooth, well-timed movement, balance and posture, by comparison and prediction. Two hemispheres joined by the vermis.

21Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Midbrain (mesencephalon)

Back

Processes sight and sound and runs simple reflexes to them — the turn-toward-the-sound reflex — through the colliculi.

22Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Limbic system

Back
