Defined by function, not anatomy: stores memory together with emotion. Includes the hippocampus, amygdala and hypothalamus; smell feeds straight into it.

23Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Reticular activating system (RAS)

Back

Neurons from the medulla up to the cortex that filter repetitive sensory input and keep the cortex awake; consciousness needs it.

24Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Amygdala

Back

Limbic structure that ties memories from different senses to emotional states.

25Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Hippocampus

Back

Limbic structure essential for consolidating short-term memory into long-term memory.

26Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Short-term memory

Back

A small amount of information held for seconds to minutes — a phone number. "Here and gone."

27Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Long-term memory

Back

Information held for hours, days, years — built from short-term memory by repetition and rehearsal.

28Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Number of spinal and cranial nerve pairs

Back

31 pairs of spinal nerves (all mixed) and 12 pairs of cranial nerves. "I want you to know that."

29Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

Where the adult spinal cord ends

Back

Around L2, tapering to the conus medullaris; below it hangs the cauda equina ("horse's tail").

30Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

The bones of the cranial cavity

Back

Eight: frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, ethmoid and sphenoid.

31Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture

The four ventricles

Back

Left and right lateral, third, fourth — the cavities where CSF is made.

32Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture

Arachnoid granulations

Back

Where CSF drains into the blood, into the superior sagittal sinus. One way only.

33Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture

Contralateral vs ipsilateral

Back

Contralateral = opposite side; ipsilateral = same side. Each hemisphere runs the contralateral side of the body.

34Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

Pyramids of decussation

Back

Where motor and sensory fibres cross to the opposite side, in the medulla oblongata.

35Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Corpus callosum

Back

The band of white matter joining the two cerebral hemispheres.

36Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

Coronal plane

Back

The name used for the frontal plane in the head — a side-to-side cut separating front from back.

37Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Central sulcus, precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus

Back

The central sulcus divides frontal from parietal; precentral gyrus = primary motor area, postcentral gyrus = primary somatosensory area.

38Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

Lateral sulcus and insula

Back

The lateral sulcus separates frontal from temporal lobe; spread it open and the insula is folded inside.

39Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture

Diencephalon

Back

"Di means two, yet it's formed of three" — thalamus, hypothalamus and epithalamus.

40Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

Superior vs inferior colliculi

Back

The four bumps on the midbrain (corpora quadrigemina, tectum): superior = sight, inferior = hearing.

41Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

Normal resting breathing rate

Back

12 to 20 respirations per minute, its rhythm set by the medulla.

42Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

The three connective-tissue wraps of a nerve, inner to outer

Back

Endoneurium (each axon) → perineurium (each fascicle) → epineurium (whole nerve). The muscle wraps with -neurium for -mysium.

43Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

Gray commissures

Back

Bands of gray matter in front of and behind the central canal that let axons cross the cord without going up to the brain.

44Ch. 8flashcard8.2
  • lecture
detail

Crossed extensor reflex

Back

One leg withdraws from the nail while the contralateral leg contracts to bear your weight.

45Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Dorsal root vs ventral root

Back

Dorsal = sensory in (cell bodies in the dorsal-root ganglion). Ventral = motor out. They join into the mixed spinal nerve.

46Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • lecture
detail

Dermatome

Back

The region of skin served by one spinal nerve; the dermatome map is clinically significant.

47Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • lecture
detail

Cranial nerve names, in order

Back

Olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal.

48Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • lecture
detail

Cranial nerve functions, I to XII

Back

S S M M B M B S B B M M — "Some say marry money, but my brother says big brains matter more."

49Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • lecture
detail

Abducens nerve (VI)

Back

Goes to one muscle only, the lateral rectus, which pulls the eye away from the midline — abduction.

50Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • lecture
detail

Vagus nerve (X)

Back

Carries about 75% of all parasympathetic outflow; reaches the heart and other organs.

51Ch. 8flashcard8.3
  • lecture

Dual innervation

Back

One organ supplied by both autonomic divisions, with opposite messages in different chemicals so it doesn't go too far either way.

52Ch. 8flashcard8.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

How long before stroke damage becomes permanent

Back

About 4 to 5 minutes without blood flow, by Whalen's lecture. The book says neurons begin to die "within minutes."

Ch. 9 — Sensory Systems

Week 11 · study page · 47 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 43 flashcards

1Ch. 99.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

You press gently on your closed eyelids and see faint flashes of light. What explains this?

Answer: c

Which sensation you experience depends on which part of the brain receives the impulse, not on the stimulus. Photoreceptors respond best to light but also to pressure, and either way their impulses go to the visual cortex — so you see it. Whalen: "All action potentials are exactly the same… Where they come from and where they go is the only thing that gives it meaning." Touch receptors (b) do not feed the optic nerve, nothing stores light (a), and no pain is involved (d).

2Ch. 99.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Your phone rings in another room and you know at once it is your ringtone. Which part of that is perception?

Answer: d

Sensation is awareness of a stimulus (c); perception is the conscious understanding of it, after the cerebral cortex integrates the input against past experience — memory, "which, as you recall, not exactly reliable." Options a and b are reception and transduction, which come before either.

3Ch. 99.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Ten minutes into a shift at Starbucks you no longer smell the coffee, yet you still know exactly where your legs are. Why the difference?

Answer: a

Sensory adaptation — most receptors stop responding to a continuous stimulus and you become less aware of it (his coffee smell, "gone in about two seconds"). The muscle and joint receptors that report body position never adapt, because continuous input is essential for coordinated movement and balance. Option b is true of smell receptors but is not why the smell fades.

4Ch. 99.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which list contains only special senses?

Answer: a

Special senses: vision, hearing, balance (equilibrium), smell, taste — receptors in the head, mostly inside specific organs. Touch, pain and temperature are general senses, from receptors scattered through skin, muscle, joints and viscera — one of them sinks each wrong option.

5Ch. 99.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen's pin-prick example named a Pacinian corpuscle. Going by the chapter, what reports the sharp pain of a pin?

Answer: b

Pain receptors are free nerve endings in almost every tissue. The chapter makes the Pacinian corpuscle a strong-pressure and vibration receptor, so his example used the wrong corpuscle — for a sharp prick, say pain receptor. Ruffini is continuous pressure and Meissner's is touch location; neither is pain.

6Ch. 99.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Which pairing of skin receptor and stimulus is correct, according to the chapter?

Answer: d

Pacinian corpuscles respond when pressure is first applied and adapt quickly, so they sense vibration (Figure 9.2: "strong pressure; vibration"). Ruffini = continuous pressure — option b swaps the two. Meissner's = light touch, telling you exactly where you were touched. The lab adds that Ruffini endings sense stretch for proprioception.

7Ch. 99.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

A weightlifter's contracting biceps pulls hard on its tendon. Which receptor reports that tension?

Answer: c

Tendon organs measure muscle tension and fire when a contracting muscle pulls on the tendon. Muscle spindles (a) measure length and fire when the muscle is stretched — the classic swap. Both are position receptors that never adapt.

8Ch. 99.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

To read fine print, your eyes move so the image lands on which part of the retina?

Answer: d

The fovea, the centre of the macula — densely packed cones, the area of highest acuity. It is pinhead-sized, so the eye keeps moving to bring detail onto it. The optic disc (a) is the blind spot; the choroid and ciliary body are not retina at all.

9Ch. 99.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

An image that falls on the optic disc is not seen. Why?

Answer: c

Where the optic nerve leaves the retina there are no photoreceptors, so nothing there sends a signal to the cortex — the blind spot. You don't notice it because involuntary eye movements shift the image and the brain fills the gap. Option a is backward and describes no blind region.

10Ch. 99.4
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Light entering the eye reaches which retinal cells last?

Answer: d

Light passes through several layers of neurons — ganglion, then bipolar — before it reaches the photoreceptors, which sit at the back of the retina with their light-sensitive ends pointing away from the light. The signal then travels back up the same chain and out the optic nerve.

11Ch. 99.4
  • lecture
detail

In a rod's photopigment, which molecule actually absorbs the light?

Answer: d

Retinal is the light-sensitive part. Light changes retinal's shape → opsin changes shape → a cascade activates the cell. Rhodopsin is not a third molecule — it is the name of the opsin-plus-retinal complex in rods (b). Melanin is in the choroid and absorbs stray light.

12Ch. 99.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Walking under moonlight, you can make out shapes and movement but no colours. Why?

Answer: a

Rods are far more light-sensitive and work in low light, but give black-and-white vision; cones need bright light and give colour. Option c has the pupil backwards — it dilates in dim light.

13Ch. 99.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

There are only three cone types. How do they let you tell many hues apart?

Answer: b

The blue, green and red cones each have a different opsin, absorbing a range of wavelengths, and the ranges overlap — so any colour stimulates each type to a different degree, and the brain reads colour from the mix (a banana fires red and green cones). Each cone has one opsin (a), and rods give no colour (c).

14Ch. 99.4
  • lecture
detail

Which statement about visible light is correct?

Answer: c

Visible light is a sliver of the electromagnetic spectrum, about 400–760 nm, and red is the long-wavelength end (~700 nm). Whalen said it backwards in lecture and corrected himself — "I have it backwards" — so option a is his slip. Ultraviolet and infrared lie just outside what our receptors detect.

15Ch. 99.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

When light strikes a rod, what happens to its release of neurotransmitter?

Answer: b

Light splits the photopigment and reduces the photoreceptor's release of inhibitory neurotransmitter — the lab calls the step hyperpolarization. That transmitter normally inhibits the processing cells, so less of it means more activity in the bipolar and ganglion cells. The counter-intuitive part is the whole point: light turns the photoreceptor's output down.

16Ch. 99.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

What does the brown pigment in the choroid do?

Answer: a

The choroid carries blood vessels and melanin, which absorbs light reflected from the retina and sharpens vision by preventing reflection inside the eye — the lab's "absorbs light, stops scatter". The rod pigment is rhodopsin (b); feeding the lens and cornea is the aqueous humor (d).

17Ch. 99.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

You walk out into bright sunlight. Which structure contracts to shrink the pupil?

Answer: b

The iris's smooth muscle constricts the pupil in bright light and dilates it in dim. The pupil is only the hole, so this asks for the structure that does the regulating — the chapter text's answer. End-of-chapter Q9 answers "pupil" to "what determines the amount of light that enters", because its options omit the iris; both are right in their own frame (CONFLICT, §9.4). The ciliary body (a) changes the lens's shape, not the pupil's.

18Ch. 99.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

You look up from your phone to a distant mountain. What happens to the ciliary muscle and lens?

Answer: d

Far: muscle relaxes → its ring widens → ligaments tighten → lens flattens. Near: muscle contracts → ring narrows (pursed lips) → ligaments slacken → lens rounds — option a, the phone-reading state you just left. Changing the lens's shape is accommodation.

19Ch. 99.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which structure does most of the bending of light but cannot adjust for distance?

Answer: c

Most bending happens at the curved cornea, but its shape is fixed. The lens (a) bends less but is elastic, so it does the adjusting. The lab words it as the eye's curve refracting light toward the fovea, then the lens refracting it more.

20Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The same note is played twice on a piano, the second time much louder. What changed?

Answer: c

Loudness = amplitude, the height of the waves. Pitch = frequency in hertz — options a, b and d are all the same property under different names, and the note didn't change. (End-of-chapter Q6.)

21Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

By roughly how much does the middle ear amplify the vibration that reaches it?

Answer: c

About 22 times — "You should probably know that number." The reason, from the chapter: the eardrum is larger than the oval window, so the force is concentrated. The inner ear needs it, because moving fluid takes more force than moving air.

22Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Put the auditory ossicles in order, from the eardrum inward.

Answer: a

Malleus (hammer/mallet) → incus (anvil) → stapes (stirrup). The malleus is fixed to the eardrum; the stapes sits on the oval window and pushes it in and out like a speaker cone. Option c is the right order read backwards.

23Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Driving up to Shaver Lake, your ears feel full and sounds are muffled until you yawn. What did the yawn do?

Answer: a

Outside pressure falls as you climb, so the middle-ear air expands and pushes the eardrum out (his chip bag puffing up). Yawning, swallowing or chewing gum opens the auditory (Eustachian) tube to the throat and lets the pressure equalise. The eardrum vibrates properly only when pressure is nearly equal on both sides.

24Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Noah, age four, has a middle ear infection. What is the most likely route the bacteria took?

Answer: b

Middle ear infection spreads from the nose and throat up the auditory tube — easily in children, whose tubes are more horizontal until about age six ("it rolls across a flat table"). Trapped water (a) causes swimmer's ear, an outer-ear infection. (End-of-chapter Q4.)

25Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
detail

Why does a middle ear infection need oral antibiotics rather than ear drops?

Answer: c

An intact tympanic membrane stands between the drops and the infection, so the treatment has to be systemic — oral antibiotics. Drops do work for an outer-ear infection (swimmer's ear), because that is on the near side of the eardrum. He flagged this as the kind of "why" he asks.

26Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • lab manual

When the stapes pushes the oval window, which chamber of the cochlea experiences the pressure wave first?

Answer: c

The vestibular canal (scala vestibuli) is attached to the oval window, so the wave hits it first — "Be specific." It runs to the tip, U-turns, and returns along the tympanic canal to the round window; they are one tube. The cochlear duct sits between them.

27Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is the round window for?

Answer: d

Liquid is incompressible, so when the oval window pushes in, the round window bulges out — it relieves the pressure. Passing sound in (a) is the oval window; equalising air pressure (c) is the auditory tube.

28Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In the organ of Corti, what lies directly below and directly above the hair cells?

Answer: b

Hair cells sit on the basilar membrane; their stereocilia touch the tectorial membrane above. He asked both in class. The vestibular membrane roofs the cochlear duct — "never gonna have to do that one." Option a is the classic flip.

29Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • lab manual

Put these steps of hearing in order: (1) basilar membrane pushed up, (2) hair cells bend against the tectorial membrane, (3) stapes pushes oval window, (4) neuron reaches −55 mV, (5) wave runs through the canals.

Answer: a

Stapes → oval window → wave in the vestibular canal and back along the tympanic → basilar membrane pushed up → hair cells bend against the tectorial membrane → permeability and membrane potential change → at threshold, −55 mV, the neuron fires along the cochlear branch of CN VIII. Option d bends the hair cells before the membrane has lifted them.

30Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A high whistle and a low bass drum stimulate hair cells in different places. Where does each register?

Answer: b

Pitch is coded by place. Near the oval window (the base) the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff and answers high frequencies; at the tip it is wider and more flexible and answers low ones. The brain reads location as pitch. Options a and c each swap one end.

31Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

How does the brain know one sound is louder than another?

Answer: d

Higher amplitude bends the basilar membrane more, so more hair cells are stimulated, each bending further, sending more impulses — and the brain reads more impulses as louder. Every action potential is the same size (a); a higher frequency (b) would be a higher pitch.

32Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Hardened earwax blocks a patient's ear canal. What kind of hearing loss is this?

Answer: b

Conductive loss = something in the way on the route to the inner ear — wax, a thickened or perforated eardrum, fluid in the middle ear. The easier one to treat. Sensorineural loss is damage to the hair cells or the neurons of the inner ear (a, c); option d attaches the wrong cause to the right name.

33Ch. 99.5
  • lecture
  • lab manual
detail

You hear a balloon pop behind you and turn to look before you have thought about it. Which structures link the sound to that visual tracking?

Answer: c

The cochlear branch of CN VIII reaches the midbrain, where the inferior colliculi of the corpora quadrigemina tie sound to visual tracking — you hear a pop and turn to look. Whalen's lecture names the inferior pair; the lab carries the signal on to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

34Ch. 99.6
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

"Vestibule — static equilibrium; semicircular canals — dynamic equilibrium." Which situation relies mainly on the semicircular canals?

Answer: b

Semicircular canals = dynamic equilibrium — balance while moving, monitoring rotation. Vestibule (utricle and saccule) = static equilibrium — head position relative to gravity while still (a, c, d). He called it outright: "Test question."

In lecture: "Vestibule responsible for static equilibrium… Semicircular canals, dynamic equilibrium, test question." — Wed 10/21

35Ch. 99.6
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

You shake your head "no". Which semicircular canal is chiefly stimulated, in Whalen's scheme?

Answer: c

Anterior → pitch (nodding yes); posterior → roll (shoulder to shoulder); lateral → yaw (shaking no). That naming is his — the chapter says only that the three canals sit at right angles and that "no" swirls the canals parallel to the horizon. The utricle is not a canal; it is in the vestibule.

36Ch. 99.6
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

You turn your head quickly to the right. What happens inside the semicircular canal?

Answer: a

The canal turns with the head but the fluid lags and moves the opposite way, pushing the cupula — the gel cap in the ampulla — and bending the stereocilia; the neuron reaches −55 mV and fires. Otoliths (b) belong to the vestibule, not the canals.

37Ch. 99.6
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What are otoliths, and where are they?

Answer: b

Calcium carbonate crystals on the gel over the hair cells of the utricle and saccule. They add weight, so when the head tilts gravity drags the gel further than it would move alone — "You literally got rocks in your head." Not in the ampulla: the ampulla has the cupula (d). Option c is the ossicles.

38Ch. 99.6
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

An elevator suddenly drops a floor. Which receptor organ chiefly registers this?

Answer: c

Saccule — vertical movement: falling, jumping, rolling hills on a country road. Utricle (a) — forward tilt of the head and forward motion. The canals report rotation, and the cochlea is hearing.

39Ch. 99.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Reading in a moving car makes you nauseous. What is the cause?

Answer: a

Motion sickness is a disconnect between what the eyes see and what the vestibular apparatus feels. Treated with Dramamine (which inhibits vestibular messages) or a transdermal patch behind the ear. Loose crystals (b) came up for vertigo in class and he was not convinced.

40Ch. 99.7
  • lecture
detail

Bipolar neurons are found in only two places. Which two?

Answer: b

Retina and olfactory epithelium — only these two, he said in both lectures. Taste cells are not neurons at all (c, d) — they signal an attached sensory neuron — and the cochlea's receptors are hair cells.

41Ch. 99.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

A whiff of a cologne brings back a vivid memory of an ex. Why is smell such a strong memory trigger?

Answer: d

The olfactory bulbs pass the signal to the cortex through the limbic system — the seat of emotion and memory. "The closest thing we have to time travel" — Anton Ego's ratatouille. Olfactory neurons are among the few replaced through life (c is backward).

42Ch. 99.7
  • lecture

Where does an olfactory signal first become electrical?

Answer: a

Odorants dissolved in the mucus bind receptors on the olfactory hairs, and the bipolar neuron reaches threshold there — chemical becomes electrical. It goes back to chemical at the synapse with a multipolar neuron in the olfactory bulb (b), then electrical again on the way to the association area. Dissolving (d) is still chemistry.

43Ch. 99.7
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Olfactory axons pass up through which bone to reach the olfactory bulb?

Answer: b

The olfactory bulb sits just above the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone — the start of cranial nerve I. The petrous temporal bone (c) encases the middle and inner ear.

44Ch. 99.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

You have a heavy head cold and your dinner tastes bland. Why?

Answer: d

Flavour = taste + smell, including retronasal olfaction — odorants rising up the back of the nose. The chapter puts about 80% of a food's flavour down to smell. Losing smell with COVID left only taste — the taste cells were fine; the smell was gone.

45Ch. 99.7
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Which pairing of taste and trigger is correct?

Answer: d

Sweet — glucose and similar sugars · salty — metal ions, sodium first · sour — H⁺ (protons from acids) · bitter — alkaloids · umami — glutamate. He listed all five: "You potentially want to know them." Each wrong option takes a real trigger and pins it on the wrong taste.

46Ch. 99.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about taste cells is correct?

Answer: b

Taste cells are not neurons (unlike the bipolar olfactory receptors). Their microvilli — taste hairs — project through the taste pore into saliva; chemicals bind there and the taste cell signals an attached sensory neuron. "The hairs in the senses are not hairs": stereocilia in the ear, microvilli in taste.

47Ch. 99.7
  • lecture
detail

An artificial sweetener tastes far sweeter than sugar but supplies no calories. Why?

Answer: a

Artificial sweeteners hit the same receptors as sugar and are up to 10,000 times sweeter than glucose, but you lack the enzymes to break their bonds, so they supply no energy. Option d gets the energy out and then loses it; the point is that it is never released.

1Ch. 9short answer9.5
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Trace a sound from the air outside your head to the brain, naming each structure it passes and what each one does.

Model answer

The pinna gathers sound and funnels it down the auditory canal (external acoustic meatus) to the tympanic membrane, which vibrates at the sound's frequency. In the air-filled middle ear the malleus → incus → stapes carry the vibration and amplify it about 22 times, because the eardrum is larger than the oval window. The stapes pushes the oval window, making a pressure wave in the fluid of the vestibular canal first; it runs to the tip of the cochlea and back along the tympanic canal, and the round window bulges out to relieve the pressure. The wave pushes up the basilar membrane, so the hair cells of the organ of Corti bend against the tectorial membrane; that changes their permeability and membrane potential, and their neuron fires at −55 mV. The signal travels along the cochlear branch of CN VIII to the midbrain (inferior colliculi) and on to the auditory cortex.

One mark per structure with its job, in order. The marks he flagged: 22×, vestibular canal first, basilar below / tectorial above, −55 mV, CN VIII. The auditory tube is not on the path — it equalises pressure.

2Ch. 9short answer9.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Explain how the cochlea codes pitch and how it codes loudness.

Model answer

Pitch is place. The basilar membrane varies along its length — narrow and stiff near the oval window (the base), wider and more flexible at the tip (the apex). High frequencies vibrate the base most and low frequencies the apex, so different pitches stimulate hair cells in different places, and the brain reads the location as pitch. Loudness is number. A bigger amplitude pushes the membrane further, so more hair cells are stimulated and each bends further, sending more impulses; the brain reads more impulses as louder. Every action potential is identical, so neither is coded by the size of the impulse.

Two mechanisms, kept apart: place for pitch, number of impulses for loudness. Getting base = high and apex = low the right way round is the mark most often lost.

3Ch. 9short answer9.6
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

Compare dynamic and static equilibrium: which organ handles each, what it detects, and how its hair cells are bent.

Model answer

Dynamic equilibrium — the semicircular canals. Balance while moving: rotation of the head, in three planes (anterior → pitch, posterior → roll, lateral → yaw). Each canal's ampulla holds hair cells embedded in a gel cupula. When the head turns, the fluid lags and moves the opposite way, bending the cupula and the hair cells. Static equilibrium — the vestibule (utricle and saccule). Head position relative to gravity, plus linear acceleration; the utricle senses forward tilt and the saccule vertical movement. Their hair cells are under a gel weighted with otoliths (calcium carbonate), so when the head tilts gravity drags the gel and bends the hair cells. In both, bending changes the membrane potential and the neuron fires at −55 mV along the vestibular branch of CN VIII.

He called the canal/vestibule split a test question. Marks: the right organ for each, cupula vs otoliths, fluid lag vs gravity, and otoliths in the vestibule, not the ampulla.

In lecture: "Vestibule responsible for static equilibrium… Semicircular canals, dynamic equilibrium, test question." — Wed 10/21

4Ch. 9short answer9.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Describe how the eye focuses on a near object and then on a distant one.

Model answer

Light is bent mostly by the cornea, whose shape is fixed, and then by the lens, which is elastic and can change shape — accommodation. The ciliary muscle is a ring attached to the lens by ligaments. Near: the ciliary muscle contracts, its ring narrows, the ligaments slacken, and the lens rounds to bend the light more. Far: the ciliary muscle relaxes, its ring widens, the ligaments tighten, and the lens flattens. With age the lens loses elasticity and rounds less easily, which is why people hold reading farther away.

The chain in both directions, with contract → slack → round for near. Most errors reverse the ligaments. End-of-chapter Q14 (the baseball game) is this question with a scenario on it.

5Ch. 9short answer9.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Compare rods and cones.

Model answer

Rods — far more numerous; very light-sensitive, so they work in dim light; black-and-white vision and movement; pigment rhodopsin (opsin plus retinal) in stacked discs in a long, columnar outer segment; many rods converge on one bipolar cell, which adds sensitivity but loses sharpness. Cones — respond to bright light; give colour and sharp detail; three types (blue, green, red), each with its own opsin and overlapping ranges; short, tapered outer segment; concentrated in the fovea; each foveal cone feeds one bipolar cell, which gives acuity. In both, light changes retinal's shape, the cell hyperpolarizes and releases less inhibitory neurotransmitter, so the bipolar cells fire.

Light level, colour, acuity, pigment and location for each. The shared mechanism — light reduces the transmitter — earns the last mark.

6Ch. 9short answer9.7
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Trace the sense of smell from an odour in the air to the brain, and say why smells call up memories.

Model answer

Odorant molecules are carried in on the air and dissolve in the mucus coating the olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity. They bind receptors on the olfactory hairs of bipolar neurons — one of the few neuron types replaced through life. At threshold the neuron fires (chemical → electrical) and its axon passes up through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid to the olfactory bulb, the start of cranial nerve I, where it synapses (electrical → chemical → electrical). The signal runs along the olfactory tract and reaches the cortex through the limbic system, the seat of emotion and memory — which is why a smell can bring back an old memory.

He named "the mechanisms of taste and smell" as a Ch. 9 objective. Marks: mucus, bipolar neuron, cribriform plate, olfactory bulb / CN I, limbic system.

1Ch. 9flashcard9.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sensation vs perception

Back

Sensation — awareness of a stimulus; which one depends on where in the brain the impulse arrives. Perception — the cortex's interpretation of it against past experience.

2Ch. 9flashcard9.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Sensory adaptation

Back

Receptors stop responding to a continuous stimulus, so you become less aware of it. Touch and pressure adapt fastest; muscle and joint position receptors never adapt.

3Ch. 9flashcard9.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

The five classes of receptor

Back

Mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors, photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, pain receptors (nociceptors). Classified by the stimulus each detects.

4Ch. 9flashcard9.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual

General senses vs special senses

Back

General — touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, body position, pain; receptors throughout the body. Special — vision, hearing, balance, smell, taste; receptors in the head.

5Ch. 9flashcard9.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Free vs encapsulated nerve endings

Back

Free — bare dendrite tips (pain, temperature, hair movement). Encapsulated — dendrite tips wrapped in a connective-tissue capsule (Meissner's, Pacinian, Ruffini).

6Ch. 9flashcard9.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Merkel disk

Back

A free nerve ending plus the Merkel cell it ends on; light touch.

7Ch. 9flashcard9.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Meissner's corpuscle

Back

Encapsulated; light touch — exactly where you were touched. Hairless sensitive skin: lips, fingertips.

8Ch. 9flashcard9.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Pacinian corpuscle

Back

Onion-like layered capsule, deep; strong pressure and vibration — adapts quickly.

9Ch. 9flashcard9.3
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Ruffini corpuscle

Back

Encapsulated; continuous pressure (book) — the lab adds stretch, for proprioception.

10Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

The eye's three layers

Back

Outer — sclera, cornea. Middle — choroid, ciliary body, iris. Inner — retina.

11Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Sclera

Back

The white of the eye — protects and shapes the eyeball and anchors the muscles that move it.

12Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Cornea

Back

The clear front window; does most of the bending of light but cannot change shape.

13Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Iris and pupil

Back

Iris — the coloured smooth muscle that sets the pupil's size. Pupil — the hole that lets light in.

14Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Ciliary body

Back

Ring of mostly muscle around the lens; holds the lens and changes its shape for near and far.

15Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Fovea

Back

Centre of the macula; densely packed cones; the point of sharpest vision.

16Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Blind spot (optic disc)

Back

Where the optic nerve leaves the retina — no photoreceptors, so nothing there is seen.

17Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Aqueous vs vitreous humor

Back

Aqueous — front of the lens; feeds cornea and lens; replaced every ~90 min. Vitreous — behind the lens; jelly; holds the retina in place; never replaced.

18Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Rhodopsin

Back

The rod pigment — opsin (protein) plus retinal (the light-sensitive part).

19Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

The three cone types

Back

Blue, green, red — named for the wavelength each absorbs best; each has its own opsin.

20Ch. 9flashcard9.4
  • lecture
detail

The visible spectrum

Back

About 400–760 nm; red is the long-wavelength end. Ultraviolet and infrared lie just outside it.

21Ch. 9flashcard9.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Pitch and loudness

Back

Pitch = frequency (hertz). Loudness = amplitude (wave height).

22Ch. 9flashcard9.5
  • lecture

The earbones, collectively

Back

The auditory ossicles — malleus, incus, stapes. He asked twice and wants the full term.

23Ch. 9flashcard9.5

Middle-ear amplification

Back

About 22 times — the eardrum is larger than the oval window.

Tympanic membrane

Back

The eardrum; vibrates at the frequency of the incoming sound; outer/middle ear boundary.

Auditory (Eustachian) tube

Back

Middle ear ↔ throat; equalises pressure across the eardrum. More horizontal in children under ~6.

  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Oval window vs round window

Back

Oval — the stapes pushes it; starts the fluid wave. Round — bulges out to relieve the pressure.

  • lecture
  • lab manual

Vestibular canal, tympanic canal, cochlear duct

Back

Vestibular — upper, from the oval window; hit first. Tympanic — lower, to the round window; same tube. Cochlear duct — between them, holding the organ of Corti.

28Ch. 9flashcard9.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Organ of Corti (spiral organ)

Back

The organ of hearing — hair cells on the basilar membrane, their stereocilia touching the tectorial membrane.

29Ch. 9flashcard9.5

  • textbook
detail

Conductive vs sensorineural hearing loss

Back

Conductive — an obstruction on the way in. Sensorineural — damaged hair cells or neurons.

30Ch. 9flashcard9.5

detail

Outer- vs middle-ear infection — treatment

Back

Outer (swimmer's ear) — ear drops. Middle — oral antibiotics; the eardrum blocks drops.

  • lecture

Threshold for the hair cell's neuron

Back

−55 mV — the same threshold he asked for in the cochlea and the vestibular apparatus.

said it’s on the exam

Dynamic vs static equilibrium

Back

Dynamic — semicircular canals; rotation, balance while moving. Static — vestibule (utricle, saccule); head position, balance at rest.

Anterior → pitch (yes) · posterior → roll (shoulder to shoulder) · lateral → yaw (no).

Ampulla — the enlarged base of a canal. Cupula — the gel cap in it holding the hair cells.

Olfactory bulb

Above the cribriform plate of the ethmoid; the start of cranial nerve I; relays via the limbic system.
