Ch. 10 — The Endocrine System

Week 12 · study page · 66 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 63 flashcards

1Ch. 10L1.5 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

A salivary gland's product reaches the mouth; a thyroid's product reaches the bloodstream. What structural difference explains this?

Answer: b

Exocrine glands secrete into ducts leading to a body surface, a cavity or a space within an organ — salivary and sebaceous (oil) glands are his examples, and they stay local. Endocrine glands are ductless: hormones go into the extracellular fluid, then diffuse into capillaries and reach anywhere blood flows. Option c is the same pair reversed; option a invents a tissue difference — both are glandular epithelium.

2Ch. 10L1.5 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where does a hormone go immediately after an endocrine cell releases it?

Answer: c

Endocrine cells release hormones into the extracellular fluid just outside the cells; the hormones diffuse into the bloodstream from there. That is why he calls the system "wireless" — slower than the nervous system, but its effects last longer. A duct (option a) is the exocrine route. Acting on an adjacent cell (option b) describes a local signaling molecule, not a hormone.

3Ch. 10L1.6 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

LH circulates past every cell in the body, yet only the interstitial cells of the testes respond with testosterone. Why?

Answer: a

Hormones contact virtually every cell, but only target cells respond — a target cell has a receptor, a protein that recognises and binds that hormone. Receptor = lock, hormone = key. Cells without it are unaffected, "almost like they don't even see the hormone." Option c confuses distance with specificity: hormones work anywhere blood flows.

4Ch. 10L1.7 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

He asked it twice in lecture. Where is the receptor for a lipid-soluble hormone?

Answer: b

"Where's the receptor for a lipid-soluble hormone? Always — inside the cell." Lipid-soluble hormones pass straight through the membrane ("like a curtain of beads") and bind a receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus. A surface receptor (option a) belongs to water-soluble hormones. The carrier protein (option c) is only the hormone's "Uber driver" in the plasma, not its receptor.

5Ch. 10L1.7 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

A steroid hormone has reached its target cell. Which outcome is guaranteed?

Answer: c

"Lipid-soluble hormones always result in production of brand new protein. Write that shit down." The hormone–receptor complex enters the nucleus, attaches to DNA, activates genes → transcription of mRNA → translation into new proteins, including enzymes. Options a and b are the water-soluble route, which activates proteins the cell already has. Option d is far too fast — new protein takes time.

6Ch. 10L1.7 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which pairing correctly describes lipid-soluble hormones?

Answer: d

All lipid-soluble hormones share cholesterol's four-ring backbone and include the steroid hormones; the main source glands are the gonads (ovaries, testes) and the adrenal (suprarenal) glands. Amino acids (option a) build the water-soluble hormones. Option c pairs the right raw material with the wrong gland — the lab does class T3/T4 as lipid soluble, but calls them amines, and neither lecture nor book names the thyroid as a steroid source.

7Ch. 10L1.8 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

In a water-soluble hormone's mechanism, which molecule is the "first messenger"?

Answer: a

A water-soluble hormone can't cross the hydrophobic lipid tails, so it binds a receptor on the outside of the membrane — the hormone is the first messenger. That binding makes cAMP, the second messenger (option b), which starts an enzyme cascade switching on proteins already in the cell. mRNA (option d) belongs to the lipid-soluble route.

8Ch. 10L1.8 · Fig 10.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Epinephrine binds a liver cell. Put the events in order.

Answer: b

Epinephrine binds a surface receptor → an enzyme converts ATP to cAMP → cAMP activates enzyme 1 → 2 → 3 ("Is it always 3? No… That's just this story") → glycogen is broken down to glucose. Option c is the steroid route. Option d has the hormone entering the cell, and runs glycogen the wrong way. Glycogen is stored in the liver and skeletal muscle.

9Ch. 10L1.9
  • lecture

Plasma is mostly water. Which hormone class therefore needs a transport protein to travel in the blood?

Answer: b

His "Uber driver": lipid-soluble hormones ride bound to transport proteins in the watery plasma, are dropped at the cell, and pass straight in. Water-soluble hormones travel freely. Options a and c give the carrier to the wrong class.

10Ch. 10L2.10 · L2.9
  • lecture
  • textbook

Oxytocin contracts the uterus during labour and ejects milk during nursing. What lets one hormone produce such different effects?

Answer: a

A hormone's effect depends on the target cell, not just the hormone. OT's targets are the uterus, the mammary glands and the brain — smooth muscle and muscle-like cells that contract in response. ADH is the same story: kidney tubules reabsorb water and vessel smooth muscle constricts. Option c is the PRL/OT mix-up he corrected twice: PRL makes milk; OT ejects it.

11Ch. 10L1.10 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Blood glucose rises after lunch, insulin is released, glucose falls, and insulin release stops. This is an example of…

Answer: d

Negative feedback: the outcome shuts the process off and pulls back to baseline — "I wasn't hungry after that first sandwich." It regulates most hormones and was his worked example. Positive feedback (option a) pushes away from baseline. Insulin and glucagon are antagonistic, not synergistic or permissive.

12Ch. 10L1.10 · Fig 10.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

During labour, what finally breaks the oxytocin positive-feedback loop?

Answer: c

The baby stretches the cervix → signals reach the hypothalamus → the posterior pituitary releases OT → the myometrium contracts harder → more stretch → more OT. Positive feedback pushes away from baseline until something ends it: delivery of the baby and placenta. Option a would make it negative feedback. His other positive example is fever; the lab adds the LH surge.

13Ch. 10L1.11 · 10.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which pair of hormones is antagonistic?

Answer: a

Antagonistic: one hormone opposes another — calcitonin lowers blood calcium and PTH raises it; insulin lowers glucose and glucagon raises it. Option b is the book's synergistic example; option c is its permissive example. FSH and LH work together on the ovary rather than opposing.

14Ch. 10L1.11 · 10.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Epinephrine and glucagon together make the liver release far more glucose than the sum of each alone. This interaction is…

Answer: d

Synergistic: the response to both together is much greater than to either alone. Antagonistic hormones oppose each other; permissive means one must be present for the other to act at all. Tropic is not an interaction — it names a hormone that acts on another gland. He gave no examples in lecture; this one is the textbook's.

15Ch. 10L1.11 · 10.1
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Aldosterone cannot stimulate sodium reabsorption in the kidney unless thyroid hormone is present. This interaction is…

Answer: b

Permissive: one hormone must be present for another to have its effect — "a really nice safeguard." It is not synergistic, because aldosterone has no effect without TH, rather than a smaller one. The book's Stop and Think uses the same idea for TH and the reproductive hormones.

16Ch. 10L1.12 · L2.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

How do hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary?

Answer: c

The anterior lobe has a circulatory connection — the hypothalamic–hypophyseal portal system: a primary capillary plexus in the hypothalamus, through the infundibulum, to a secondary capillary plexus in the anterior lobe. Axons down into the lobe (option a) are the posterior lobe's neural connection.

17Ch. 10L2.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

Which hormones are made in the posterior pituitary?

Answer: c

His trap: "Which hormones are made in the posterior pituitary? Mark all that apply." — none. ADH and OT are made by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus, travel down their axons, and are stored and released in the posterior lobe. The posterior lobe releases both, which is why option a looks right.

In lecture: "Don't fall for a question that says, which of the following hormones are made in the posterior pituitary? Mark all that apply. Because none of them were made there." — Wed 10/28

18Ch. 1010.2 · EOC 3select all that apply
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which statements about the posterior pituitary are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c

The book's end-of-chapter Q3, reworked as select-all. The posterior lobe stores and releases ADH and OT. GH is anterior. Its link to the hypothalamus is neural, not circulatory — the portal system serves the anterior lobe.

19Ch. 10L2.3
  • lecture
  • lab manual

The class was asked four times where TRH comes from. What is the answer?

Answer: b

"Where does TRH come from?" took the class four tries. Every releasing and inhibiting hormone comes from the hypothalamus. TRH travels through the portal system and tells the anterior pituitary's thyrotropic cells to release TSH (option a is where TSH comes from). The thyroid makes T3/T4 in response.

20Ch. 10L2.2
  • lecture
detail

On a pituitary slide, one lobe is deep burgundy and the other pale pink to greyish. Which is which, and why?

Answer: a

The adenohypophysis (anterior) is deep burgundy because of its blood supply — it is fed by the portal system. The neurohypophysis (posterior) is light pink to greyish from short unmyelinated neurosecretory axons. He misspoke once, calling the neural lobe burgundy; his own reasons (few vessels versus many) settle it.

21Ch. 10L2.4 · CONFLICT
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

According to the lecture, deck and lab, how many main hormones does the anterior pituitary make?

Answer: a

Seven: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and MSH — MSH is the one "that wasn't on that chart." The deck says "7 main hormones" and the lab says the anterior pituitary releases 7. The textbook says six and never mentions MSH, so six is the textbook-exam answer. Four is the number of tropic hormones; the posterior lobe releases two.

22Ch. 10L2.4
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which hormone is NOT made by the anterior pituitary?

Answer: b

ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior lobe. PRL, MSH and ACTH are all anterior-lobe hormones — MSH is anterior on the lecture's and lab's count of seven, though the textbook leaves it out.

23Ch. 10L2.4 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which hormone is NOT a tropic hormone?

Answer: d

Tropic = "to nourish, grow, activate, turn on" — a hormone that influences another endocrine gland's secretion. His four: TSH (thyroid), ACTH (adrenal cortex), FSH and LH (gonads — the gonadotropic hormones). GH acts directly on body cells — bone, muscle, cartilage — not on another gland.

24Ch. 10L2.5 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Which tissues respond most strongly to growth hormone?

Answer: a

GH increases the rate of cell division and cell size in all cells, but bone, muscle and cartilage respond most. A surge at puberty is the growth spurt. GH is controlled by two hypothalamic hormones, GHRH and GHIH. The book adds that GH conserves glucose by making fats more available as fuel.

25Ch. 10L2.5 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

A 40-year-old's hands, feet and jaw have grown thicker over ten years, but he is no taller. His GH is high. What is the diagnosis?

Answer: c

The distinguishing word is the growth plate. Gigantism is excess GH in childhood, while the epiphyseal plate is still open and bones can lengthen. Acromegaly ("enlarged extremities") is excess GH in adulthood, after the plate has closed — bones get thicker but not longer. Pituitary dwarfism is too little GH in childhood. The usual cause of excess is an anterior-pituitary tumour.

26Ch. 10L2.5 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

A child is diagnosed with pituitary dwarfism. What is the cause, and the treatment?

Answer: d

Pituitary dwarfism is too little GH in childhood — about 4 feet at most in the book. GH in childhood treats it (his friend's son caught up on GH shots), though not other dwarfisms. Option c describes cretinism, a thyroid disorder that also causes dwarfism.

27Ch. 10L2.6 · L2.10
  • lecture
  • textbook

A new mother is making plenty of milk, but it will not let down when the baby nurses. Which hormone's action is lacking?

Answer: a

Prolactin produces milk; oxytocin ejects it — he stopped the class to correct this, twice. OT causes let-down and ejection by contracting the muscle-like cells around the milk ducts, and its stimulus is suckling. Milk is already being made here, so PRL is working.

28Ch. 10L2.6 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

A woman who has never been pregnant is producing milk and cannot conceive. Which hormone is most likely being oversecreted?

Answer: c

Excess prolactin in females causes infertility and lactation when no birth has occurred — "get the pituitary checked"; the book names a pituitary tumour. PRL interferes with female sex hormones. Oxytocin ejects milk but does not make it, and does not explain the infertility.

29Ch. 10L2.6
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

What is prolactin's role in males, and the effect of too much?

Answer: c

In males PRL is involved in producing mature sperm; too much → sterility (the book adds impotence). Testosterone release is LH's job (option a). Contracting the vas deferens is oxytocin's male role (option b).

30Ch. 10L2.3 · board 3
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which sequence is the thyroid's negative-feedback loop?

Answer: b

The loop he ran as a class quiz: hypothalamus → TRH → through the portal system → thyrotropic cells release TSH → follicular cells release T3 and T4 → basal metabolic rate rises. High T3/T4 feed back to both the pituitary (stop TSH) and the hypothalamus (stop TRH). The lab calls it 3-tier negative feedback.

31Ch. 10L2.7 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

ACTH from the anterior pituitary acts mainly on which target, and causes the release of what?

Answer: b

ACTH (corticotropin) is the tropic hormone for the adrenal cortex and controls glucocorticoid (cortisol) secretion. The medulla (option a) is driven by nerves from the hypothalamus, not by ACTH. The lab and deck also have ACTH stimulating aldosterone; the textbook says mineralocorticoids are released independently — see the stress question.

32Ch. 10L2.7 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of FSH's function by sex is correct?

Answer: d

FSH promotes development of the egg in its follicle (and, in the book, estrogen secretion by the ovary); in males it supports sperm production (the book: sperm maturation; the lab: via Sertoli cells). Option a is LH's pair. Milk production (option b) is prolactin.

33Ch. 10L2.7 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of LH's function by sex is correct?

Answer: a

LH surge → ovulation — the landlord telling the egg to leave — and the leftover follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which makes estrogen and progesterone. In males LH tells the interstitial (Leydig) cells to make testosterone. Option b is FSH; option c is oxytocin.

34Ch. 10L2.9
  • lecture
  • lab manual

What stimulates the release of ADH?

Answer: b

Increased osmolality — more solute dissolved in the plasma — triggers ADH. ADH adds water back from the renal tubules and dilutes the solutes (his too-sweet Gatorade). The lab adds low blood volume or pressure via RAAS. Cervical stretch (option d) releases oxytocin.

35Ch. 10L2.9 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which pair of effects belongs to ADH?

Answer: c

ADH increases water reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct (the lab: by inserting aquaporins) and causes vasoconstriction — hence its other name, vasopressin. Both raise blood pressure; blood volume and pressure always move together. Option b is aldosterone; option d is PTH.

36Ch. 10L2.9 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why does a night of heavy drinking leave you dehydrated with a dry mouth and headache?

Answer: b

Alcohol (ethanol) inhibits ADH secretion → less water reabsorbed → more urine → dehydration — the book's hangover headache and dry mouth. The study guide asks for this explicitly. Option a has the direction backwards; retaining water would not dehydrate you.

37Ch. 10L2.9 · 10.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

A patient produces huge volumes of dilute urine, is constantly thirsty and dehydrated, and has normal blood glucose. What is the likely diagnosis and treatment?

Answer: c

Diabetes insipidus is too little ADH — excessive urine production, constant thirst, dehydration — treated with ADH by nasal spray. Normal glucose rules out diabetes mellitus, which also raises urine output but from glucose lost in urine (insipidus, tasteless; mel, honey). The book: damage to the posterior pituitary or hypothalamus.

38Ch. 10L2.10
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

What are oxytocin's functions in males?

Answer: c

In males OT facilitates sexual behaviour and transport of sperm — peristalsis of the vas deferens from the epididymis at ejaculation; stimulus, sexual excitation. The book says only that men secrete OT and it may aid sperm transport. Option b is ADH; sperm maturation (option d) is PRL and FSH territory.

39Ch. 10L2.2 · CONFLICT
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

The lab's Activity 1 figure labels two hypothalamic nuclei. Which pairing does the lab give?

Answer: a

Lab: paraventricular → OT, supraoptic → ADH. Lecture: he called the supraoptic nucleus "home to the production and secretion of oxytocin" and did not say what the paraventricular makes. The textbook names neither. Lecture outranks lab under the course rules, but the lab's pairing is the standard one — know both, and ask Whalen which he wants.

40Ch. 10L2.11 · 10.3
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Within the thyroid, where are thyroid hormone and calcitonin made?

Answer: c

Follicular cells → T3 and T4, stored in colloid inside the follicles. Parafollicular (C) cells → calcitonin. The parathyroids (option d) make PTH, calcitonin's antagonist. The thyroid sits in the anterior neck, just in front of the trachea, below the larynx.

41Ch. 10L2.11 · 10.3
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which set of effects belongs to thyroid hormone?

Answer: a

TH regulates metabolic rate and heat production, maintains blood pressure, and promotes normal function of several organ systems — nearly every cell is a target. The lab: the calorigenic effect, raising basal metabolic rate and body temperature. Option b is calcitonin; c is cortisol; d is ADH.

42Ch. 10L2.11 · 10.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why does an iodine-deficient diet make the thyroid swell into a simple goiter?

Answer: b

Without iodine the follicles can't make enough T3 (three iodines) and T4 (four). With no negative feedback, the hypothalamus keeps releasing TRH and the pituitary keeps releasing TSH, and constant stimulation enlarges the gland — "if you work out something enough, it gets bigger." Option a is Graves' disease. The book's end-of-chapter Q7 has the same answer: iodine lack → goiter.

43Ch. 10L2.11 · 10.3
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

An adult has a puffy face, low alertness, a slow heart rate and a low body temperature. Which disorder fits?

Answer: d

Myxedema is too little TH in adults (hypothyroid): fluid in the facial tissues, and decreased alertness, body temperature and heart rate; treated with synthetic T3/T4. Cretinism is the same deficit in the fetus or infant. Body temperature falls — the transcript's "increase" was a misread; the deck and book both say decrease. Cushing's also puffs the face, but from cortisol, with high blood pressure and glucose.

44Ch. 10L2.11 · 10.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

An infant shows dwarfism with delayed mental and sexual development. Which deficiency is responsible?

Answer: a

Cretinism — too little TH in the fetus or infant — causes delayed mental and sexual development and dwarfism. Pituitary dwarfism (option b) is short stature without the mental delay. The book: newborns in industrialised nations are tested, and oral TH prevents it.

45Ch. 10L2.11 · 10.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

What causes Graves' disease?

Answer: c

Graves' disease is autoimmune: antibodies mimic TSH, so the thyroid is stimulated without end and oversecretes TH (hyperthyroid). Signs: raised metabolic rate and heart rate, sweating, nervousness, weight loss, and exophthalmos. Option a is simple goiter. Option d would lower TH.

46Ch. 10L2.12 · 10.3
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Blood calcium rises above normal. How does calcitonin bring it back down?

Answer: d

Calcitonin from the parafollicular cells responds to high blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts (osteoblasts keep building bone from blood calcium) and inhibiting calcium reabsorption in the kidneys, so calcium leaves in urine. Options a and b are PTH's levers. Option c is backwards — calcitonin spares the osteoblasts.

47Ch. 10L2.12 · 10.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Blood calcium falls. Which response does parathyroid hormone NOT produce?

Answer: d

PTH raises blood calcium three ways: stimulating osteoclasts (bone resorption), increasing kidney calcium reabsorption, and activating vitamin D → calcitriol for more GI absorption. Inhibiting osteoclasts is calcitonin. "Calcitonin, not calcitriol" — calcitriol is the activated vitamin D that PTH switches on.

48Ch. 10L2.12 · CONFLICT
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

According to the lecture, deck and textbook, how many parathyroid glands are there, and where?

Answer: b

Four small round masses on the back of the thyroid — "these four buffs", deck slide 71 and the textbook agree. The lab says 3–5 separate nodules embedded in the posterior thyroid. Expect four on the lecture exam and know the lab's range for the lab portion. On top of the kidneys are the adrenals; the center of the brain is the pineal.

49Ch. 10L2.12 · 10.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

A parathyroid tumour oversecretes PTH. Which set of effects follows?

Answer: a

Too much PTH pulls calcium from bone → weakened bones; elevated blood calcium → kidney stones, calcium deposits in soft tissue, and decreased nervous-system activity. Option b is too little PTH — low calcium makes neurons hyperexcitable. Option d is Addison's disease.

50Ch. 10L2.7 · board 2
  • lecture
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

He confirmed it would be tested. From outside to inside, which order of adrenal-cortex zones and products is right?

Answer: c

"Wait, are you gonna test us on this?" "Yeah." Glomerulosa → mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); fasciculata → glucocorticoids (cortisol); reticularis → androgens and estrogen. Option b is the right pairs listed inside-out. He once said "fasciculata… mineralocorticoids" (option a's error) and then corrected himself; the deck and lab agree with option c.

In lecture: Asked "Are you gonna test us on this?" about the three adrenal-cortex zones, he said "Yeah." — Wed 10/28

51Ch. 10L2.13 · 10.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Aldosterone acts on the kidney's principal cells. What is the result?

Answer: b

"I'll give up some potassium if I can get more sodium." Aldosterone, the main mineralocorticoid, increases Na⁺ reabsorption and gives up K⁺; water follows sodium, so blood volume and pressure rise. Option a is what goes wrong in Addison's disease — too little aldosterone leaves Na⁺ low and K⁺ high.

52Ch. 10L2.13 · 10.5
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Velma tells Carlos that he produces estrogen. Is she right?

Answer: d

The book's Applying the Concepts Q16. The adrenal cortex (zona reticularis) secretes gonadocorticoids — androgens and estrogens — in both sexes. He added that men also make estrogen from testosterone via aromatase. In adult males testicular androgen far outweighs adrenal; after menopause, adrenal gonadocorticoids may ease the loss of ovarian estrogen.

53Ch. 1010.5 · EOC 13
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Mary has an itchy poison-ivy rash; Rick has cut his finger on glass. Who should use a cortisone cream?

Answer: c

The book's Applying the Concepts Q13. Glucocorticoids affect glucose — the liver makes glucose from fat and protein — and inhibit inflammation, slowing white blood cells to the injury. That also slows wound healing, so steroid creams are for superficial rashes, never open wounds. Option d forgets the anti-inflammatory role; the lab adds that cortisol suppresses inflammation and immunity.

54Ch. 1010.5
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

A patient has bronzed skin, weight loss, fatigue, poor appetite and an electrolyte imbalance, and copes badly with stress. Which disorder fits?

Answer: d

Addison's disease — undersecretion of cortisol and aldosterone, apparently from autoimmune destruction of adrenal-cortex cells (the deck adds: or inadequate ACTH). Signs: bronzing of the skin, weight loss, fatigue, electrolyte imbalance, poor appetite, poor stress resistance. John F. Kennedy had it. Lecture did not reach these slides; this is deck and book.

55Ch. 1010.5 · case
  • textbook
  • lecture

Linda took high-dose prednisone for rheumatoid arthritis for years. Now her face is puffy, she tires easily and her blood glucose is high. What does she have?

Answer: b

Cushing's syndrome is prolonged exposure to high cortisol: fat redistributed, fluid in the face, fatigue, high blood pressure, high glucose. Causes: a tumour of the adrenal cortex or the anterior pituitary (ACTH), or glucocorticoid treatment — Linda's case, from the book. Addison's is the opposite — too little.

56Ch. 1010.5 · Fig 10.16
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A stranger steps out at night and your heart races within seconds. How did the signal reach the adrenal medulla?

Answer: b

Acute (short-term) stress reaches the medulla by neurons — sympathetic fibres — and it releases epinephrine and norepinephrine: heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose rise; vessels to muscle and heart dilate; gut vessels constrict. The CRH → ACTH → cortex route (option a) is long-term stress, which is slower to start and longer lasting.

57Ch. 1010.5 · CONFLICT
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which description of the long-term stress response matches the lab and the deck?

Answer: b

Long-term stress travels by hormones: hypothalamus CRH → anterior pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortex. The lab and deck slide 90 have ACTH driving cortisol and aldosterone. The textbook says ACTH controls the glucocorticoids and the cortex releases mineralocorticoids "independent of the hypothalamus." Use the lab's version on the lab exam; on a book-based question, ACTH → glucocorticoids. Option a is short-term stress.

58Ch. 1010.6 · board 4
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which statement about the endocrine pancreas is correct?

Answer: d

The pancreas is both exocrine and endocrine, lying behind the stomach. Acinar cells send digestive enzymes down the duct to the duodenum; the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans) are the endocrine part — beta cells → insulin, alpha cells → glucagon (the lab's pairing). Options a and c swap the cell types.

59Ch. 1010.6
  • textbook
  • lab manual

It has been six hours since you ate, and your blood glucose is falling. What does glucagon do?

Answer: c

Glucagon is released between meals as glucose falls; the liver converts glycogen to glucose and makes glucose from lactic acid and amino acids, then releases it — blood glucose rises. Options a, b and d are all insulin's actions. Insulin and glucagon are the textbook's antagonistic pair.

60Ch. 1010.6 · EOC 9
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which does NOT happen in a healthy person after a meal?

Answer: c

The book's end-of-chapter Q9. Glucagon is secreted between meals. After a meal, insulin moves glucose into muscle, white blood cells and connective tissue cells, inhibits glycogen breakdown, and blocks conversion of amino and fatty acids to glucose — net protein synthesis, fat storage, and glucose burned for energy.

61Ch. 1010.7 · L1.5
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Where is the thymus, and what do its hormones do?

Answer: d

The thymus lies behind the breastbone, on top of the heart; it is prominent in children and shrinks with age. Thymosin and thymopoietin promote maturation of T lymphocytes from bone-marrow precursors — his "T-cell university", where about 5% graduate. Option a is the pineal; b the parathyroids; c the pancreas.

62Ch. 1010.8 · EOC 15
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Every winter Theresa feels low and lethargic, oversleeps and craves carbohydrates. Which gland and hormone are implicated?

Answer: a

Seasonal affective disorder — too much melatonin as short winter days cut light exposure. The pineal gland, at the center of the brain, makes melatonin from serotonin; light inhibits it, so levels are higher at night. Treatment is about an hour a day of very bright light, which inhibits melatonin. Option b has the direction wrong.

63Ch. 1010.9 · EOC 5select all that apply
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Which statements about prostaglandins are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b

The book's end-of-chapter Q5, reworked as select-all. Prostaglandins are local signaling molecules — lipids continually released by the plasma membranes of most cells (about 16 kinds) — acting on adjacent cells in seconds. They influence reproduction (menstrual cramps), inflammation, blood clotting and body temperature; aspirin and ibuprofen block their synthesis. Growth factors are a separate group of peptides and proteins.

64Ch. 1010.9
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Endothelial cells lining an artery release a gas, and the smooth muscle around the vessel relaxes. Which messenger is this?

Answer: b

Nitric oxide (NO) is a gas and a local messenger: released by endothelial cells, it relaxes vessel smooth muscle, dilating the vessel. It may also aid peristalsis and act as a neurotransmitter. Prostaglandins are lipids; growth factors are peptides or proteins; epinephrine is a blood-borne hormone.

65Ch. 1010.9
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

A signal makes bone-marrow precursor cells develop into particular white blood cells. Which kind of local messenger fits?

Answer: d

Growth factors are peptides or proteins that make target cells grow, develop and multiply — one turns marrow precursors into particular white blood cells; another organises endothelial cells into new blood vessels. Like all local signaling molecules, they act on nearby cells far faster than a hormone carried to a distant site.

66Ch. 1010.2 · EOC 6
  • textbook
  • lecture

Choose the incorrect statement.

Answer: a

The book's end-of-chapter Q6. Calcitonin comes from the thyroid's parafollicular cells. Statements b–d are all true of the anterior lobe: the portal system, the four tropic hormones, and GH and PRL.

1Ch. 10short answerL1.7–L1.9
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Compare how a lipid-soluble hormone and a water-soluble hormone act on a target cell. Include what each is made from, where its receptor is, and what the cell ends up doing.

Model answer

Lipid-soluble (steroid) hormones are made from cholesterol and ride a transport protein in the blood. They pass through the membrane and bind a receptor inside the cell (cytoplasm or nucleus); the complex enters the nucleus, binds DNA and switches on genes, so the cell makes new proteins — always. Slower, longer-lasting. Water-soluble hormones are made of amino acids and travel freely. They cannot cross the membrane, so they bind a surface receptor as the first messenger; this makes a second messenger (cAMP) inside, which starts a kinase/enzyme cascade that activates proteins already in the cell — e.g. epinephrine makes a liver cell break glycogen to glucose. Faster.

Marks for: raw material for each; receptor location for each (inside vs surface — he asked the lipid one twice); new protein vs existing protein ("always result in production of brand new protein"); first and second messenger named, cAMP as the example.

2Ch. 10short answerL1.12 · L2.2
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Describe the structural relationship between the hypothalamus and each lobe of the pituitary, and name the hormones each lobe releases.

Model answer

Anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) — a circulatory link, the hypothalamic–hypophyseal portal system: hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones enter a primary capillary plexus in the hypothalamus, travel through the infundibulum and reach a secondary capillary plexus in the anterior lobe, turning its secretion on or off. The anterior lobe makes its own hormones: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and MSH (seven per lecture and lab; the book lists six, without MSH). Posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) — a neural link: neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus make ADH and oxytocin, send them down their axons, and the posterior lobe stores and releases them. It makes no hormones of its own.

Marks for: blood (portal system) vs nerves; releasing/inhibiting hormones named; the anterior list; ADH and OT made in the hypothalamus, not the posterior lobe — his "none of them" trap.

3Ch. 10short answerL2.3 · L2.11
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Trace the hypothalamus–pituitary–thyroid loop, show where negative feedback acts, and use it to explain why an iodine-deficient diet causes a simple goiter.

Model answer

Hypothalamus releases TRH → portal system → anterior pituitary thyrotropic cells release TSH → thyroid follicular cells release T3 and T4 → basal metabolic rate and heat production rise. High T3/T4 inhibit both the pituitary (TSH) and the hypothalamus (TRH) — negative feedback. T3/T4 need iodine (three and four atoms). Without it, T3/T4 stay low, so the feedback never arrives; TRH and TSH keep coming, and the constantly stimulated thyroid enlarges — a simple goiter.

Marks for: the three tiers in order with the right source of each hormone (TRH is from the hypothalamus — it took the class four tries); feedback to both levels; the goiter explained by the missing feedback, which is what his warning asks for.

4Ch. 10short answerL2.12 · 10.4
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Explain how calcitonin and parathyroid hormone together keep blood calcium in range. Name the source of each and at least two actions of each.

Model answer

They are antagonists — the calcium seesaw. Calcitonin, from the thyroid's parafollicular cells, responds to high blood calcium and lowers it: it inhibits osteoclasts so bone takes up calcium, and inhibits kidney calcium reabsorption so calcium leaves in urine. PTH, from the parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid (four per lecture and book; 3–5 nodules per lab), responds to low calcium and raises it: it stimulates osteoclasts (bone resorption), increases kidney reabsorption, and activates vitamin D (calcitriol) so the gut absorbs more calcium.

Marks for: each hormone's source and stimulus; opposite actions on osteoclasts and kidney; PTH's vitamin D route; the word antagonistic. "Calcitonin, not calcitriol."

5Ch. 10short answer10.5 · Fig 10.16
  • textbook
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Compare the body's response to acute (short-term) stress and long-term stress: the pathway from the hypothalamus, the part of the adrenal gland involved, the hormones, and their effects.

Model answer

Acute stress — the hypothalamus sends nerve impulses (sympathetic fibres) to the adrenal medulla, which releases epinephrine and norepinephrine: fight-or-flight — heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose rise, vessels to skeletal and heart muscle dilate, gut vessels constrict, alertness rises. Fast to start, short. Long-term stress — the hypothalamus releases CRH → anterior pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex releases glucocorticoids (cortisol), which raise blood glucose by making glucose from fat and protein, and suppress inflammation. Slower to start, longer lasting. The cortex also releases mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) — driven by ACTH per the lab and deck, independent of the hypothalamus per the textbook.

Marks for: nerves vs hormones; medulla vs cortex; the CRH → ACTH step; one effect each. Naming the aldosterone conflict shows you know both sources.

6Ch. 10short answerL1.10 · L2.10
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Describe oxytocin's functions in females and in males, and explain why its role in childbirth is positive feedback.

Model answer

Females: OT contracts the myometrium in labour and causes milk let-down and ejection by contracting the cells around the milk ducts (stimulus: suckling); suckling after birth also keeps the uterus contracting to deliver the placenta. Males: it facilitates sexual behaviour and sperm transport by contracting the vas deferens. Positive feedback: the baby presses on the cervix → stretch signals the hypothalamus → the posterior pituitary releases more OT → stronger contractions → more stretch → more OT. The outcome amplifies the process, pushing away from baseline, until delivery ends it.

Marks for: both sexes (the study guide asks); prolactin makes milk, OT ejects it; the loop drawn as a loop with the stopping event. Fever is his other positive-feedback example.

1Ch. 10flashcardL1.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Endocrine gland

Back

A ductless gland: secretes hormones into the extracellular fluid, which diffuse into the blood and reach anywhere blood flows.

2Ch. 10flashcardL1.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Exocrine gland

Back

A gland that secretes into ducts leading to a body surface, cavity or organ space — sebaceous, salivary, pancreatic acinar cells.

3Ch. 10flashcardL1.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Hormone

Back

A chemical messenger secreted into the blood that acts on target cells with matching receptors — slower than a nerve signal, but longer lasting.

4Ch. 10flashcardL1.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Target cells

Back

The cells with a receptor for a given hormone — the only ones that respond. Receptor = lock, hormone = key.

5Ch. 10flashcardL1.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Lipid-soluble hormone

Back

Made from cholesterol (steroids); crosses the membrane, binds a receptor inside the cell, binds DNA — always new protein.

6Ch. 10flashcardL1.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Water-soluble hormone

Back

Made of amino acids; can't cross the membrane; binds a surface receptor and works through a second messenger to activate existing proteins.

7Ch. 10flashcardL1.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

First messenger

Back

The water-soluble hormone itself, bound to its receptor on the cell surface.

8Ch. 10flashcardL1.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Second messenger

Back

The molecule inside the cell that carries out the hormone's effect — cAMP, made from ATP, which starts an enzyme (kinase) cascade.

9Ch. 10flashcardL1.11
  • lecture
  • textbook

Antagonistic hormones — define and give an example

Back

One hormone opposes another: insulin vs glucagon (glucose), calcitonin vs PTH (calcium).

10Ch. 10flashcardL1.11
  • textbook
  • lecture

Synergistic hormones — define and give an example

Back

Together, a response far greater than either alone: epinephrine + glucagon on liver glucose release.

11Ch. 10flashcardL1.10
  • lecture
  • textbook

Negative feedback — define and give an example

Back

The outcome shuts the process off, restoring baseline: high glucose → insulin → glucose falls → insulin stops. Regulates most hormones.

12Ch. 10flashcardL1.10
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Positive feedback — define and give an example

Back

The outcome amplifies the process until something ends it: oxytocin in childbirth; also fever, and the lab's LH surge.

13Ch. 10flashcardL2.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Pituitary

Back

The pea-sized hypophysis at the base of the brain: anterior lobe (adenohypophysis, makes hormones) and posterior lobe (neurohypophysis, stores ADH and OT).

14Ch. 10flashcardL1.12
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Hypothalamus

Back

Brain region (diencephalon) that controls the pituitary — the anterior lobe by blood, the posterior lobe by nerves; makes every releasing and inhibiting hormone.

15Ch. 10flashcardL1.12
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neurosecretory cell

Back

A hypothalamic neuron that secretes a hormone instead of a neurotransmitter — e.g. ADH and OT, or releasing hormones.

16Ch. 10flashcardL1.12
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Releasing hormone

Back

A hypothalamic hormone that starts anterior-pituitary secretion — e.g. TRH → TSH, GHRH → GH, CRH → ACTH.

17Ch. 10flashcardL1.12
  • lecture
  • textbook

Inhibiting hormone

Back

A hypothalamic hormone that stops anterior-pituitary secretion — e.g. GHIH stops GH.

18Ch. 10flashcardL2.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Growth hormone (GH)

Back

Anterior pituitary; increases cell division and cell size, most in bone, muscle and cartilage. Excess: gigantism (child) or acromegaly (adult); deficit: pituitary dwarfism.

19Ch. 10flashcardL2.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Prolactin (PRL)

Back

Anterior pituitary; makes the mammary glands produce milk; aids sperm maturation in males. Excess: infertility and milk without birth; sterility in males.

20Ch. 10flashcardL2.7
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)

Back

Anterior-pituitary tropic hormone, released on TRH; stimulates thyroid follicular cells to release T3/T4.

21Ch. 10flashcardL2.7
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

Back

Anterior-pituitary tropic hormone, released on CRH; stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol (and aldosterone, per lab and deck).

22Ch. 10flashcardL2.7
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)

Back

Gonadotropin. Females: egg and follicle development (and estrogen). Males: sperm production.

23Ch. 10flashcardL2.7
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Luteinizing hormone (LH)

Back

Gonadotropin. Females: ovulation and the corpus luteum. Males: testosterone from Leydig (interstitial) cells.

24Ch. 10flashcardL2.9
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)

Back

Vasopressin; made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary on high osmolality. More water reabsorbed (DCT, collecting duct) and vasoconstriction. Too little: diabetes insipidus. Alcohol inhibits it.

25Ch. 10flashcardL2.10
  • lecture
  • textbook

Oxytocin (OT)

Back

Made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary. Females: uterine contraction (positive feedback) and milk ejection. Males: sexual behaviour, sperm transport.

26Ch. 10flashcardL2.11
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Thyroid gland

Back

Butterfly/shield-shaped gland in the anterior neck, in front of the trachea, below the larynx. Follicular cells → T3/T4; parafollicular cells → calcitonin.

27Ch. 10flashcardL2.11
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Thyroid hormone (T3/T4)

Back

Triiodothyronine (3 iodines) and thyroxine (4); sets metabolic rate and heat production, maintains blood pressure. Needs iodine.

28Ch. 10flashcardL2.11
  • lecture
  • textbook

Cretinism

Back

Too little thyroid hormone in the fetus or infant: dwarfism with delayed mental and sexual development.

29Ch. 10flashcardL2.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Gigantism

Back

Too much GH in childhood, while the epiphyseal plates are open — bones lengthen; 8–9 feet in the book.

30Ch. 10flashcardL2.11
  • lecture
  • textbook

Graves' disease

Back

Autoimmune hyperthyroidism: antibodies mimic TSH. Fast metabolism and heart rate, sweating, nervousness, weight loss, exophthalmos.

31Ch. 10flashcardL2.12
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Calcitonin

Back

From thyroid parafollicular cells on high blood calcium; lowers it — inhibits osteoclasts and kidney calcium reabsorption.

32Ch. 10flashcardL2.11
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Parafollicular cells

Back

The thyroid's C cells, between the follicles; make calcitonin.

33Ch. 10flashcardL2.11
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Follicular cells

Back

Cells lining the thyroid follicles; make T3 and T4, stored in the colloid.

34Ch. 10flashcardL2.12
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Parathyroid hormone (PTH)

Back

Parathormone, from the parathyroids on low calcium; raises it — stimulates osteoclasts, kidney reabsorption, vitamin D activation (gut absorption).

35Ch. 10flashcardL2.7 · L2.13
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Adrenal cortex

Back

The outer adrenal region; steroid hormones from three zones — glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens).

In lecture: Asked "Are you gonna test us on this?" about the three adrenal-cortex zones, he said "Yeah." — Wed 10/28

36Ch. 10flashcardL2.13 · 10.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Adrenal medulla

Back

The inner adrenal region; releases epinephrine and norepinephrine for fight-or-flight when stimulated by nerves.

37Ch. 10flashcardL2.13
  • lecture
  • textbook

Gonadocorticoids

Back

Androgens and estrogens from the adrenal cortex (zona reticularis), in both sexes.

38Ch. 10flashcardL2.13
  • lecture
  • textbook

Mineralocorticoids

Back

Adrenal-cortex hormones (zona glomerulosa) for mineral and water balance — chiefly aldosterone.

39Ch. 10flashcardL2.13 · 10.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Glucocorticoids

Back

Adrenal-cortex hormones (zona fasciculata) — cortisol — that raise blood glucose from fat and protein and suppress inflammation.

40Ch. 10flashcardL2.7 · L2.13
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Androgens

Back

Masculinising hormones such as testosterone — from the testes (Leydig cells) and the adrenal cortex in both sexes.

41Ch. 10flashcardL2.7
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Estrogens

Back

Female sex hormones from ovarian follicles (and the adrenal cortex, both sexes). Build the endometrium, maintain bone density; men make them from testosterone via aromatase.

42Ch. 10flashcardL2.13
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Aldosterone

Back

The main mineralocorticoid: kidney reabsorbs Na⁺ and gives up K⁺; water follows → blood volume and pressure rise.

43Ch. 10flashcardL1.8 · 10.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Epinephrine

Back

Adrenaline, from the adrenal medulla; fight-or-flight. A water-soluble hormone — on liver cells it works through cAMP to break glycogen to glucose.

44Ch. 10flashcard10.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Norepinephrine

Back

Noradrenaline, from the adrenal medulla alongside epinephrine — the short-term stress response.

45Ch. 10flashcard10.5
  • textbook
  • lecture

Addison's disease

Back

Too little cortisol and aldosterone, usually autoimmune: bronzed skin, weight loss, fatigue, electrolyte imbalance (Na⁺ low, K⁺ high), poor stress resistance.

46Ch. 10flashcard10.5
  • textbook
  • lecture

Cushing's syndrome

Back

Prolonged high cortisol — tumour (adrenal cortex or pituitary) or glucocorticoid drugs: redistributed fat, puffy face, high blood pressure and glucose.

47Ch. 10flashcard10.6
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Pancreatic islets

Back

The islets of Langerhans — the pancreas's endocrine clusters: beta cells → insulin, alpha cells → glucagon.

48Ch. 10flashcard10.6
  • textbook
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Insulin

Back

From beta cells on high glucose; moves glucose into cells, stops glycogen breakdown — blood glucose falls.

49Ch. 10flashcard10.6
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Glucagon

Back

From alpha cells on low glucose (between meals); the liver turns glycogen into glucose — blood glucose rises.

50Ch. 10flashcard10.7
  • textbook
  • lecture

Thymus

Back

Gland on top of the heart, behind the breastbone; large in children, shrinks with age. "T-cell university."

51Ch. 10flashcard10.7
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Thymosin / thymopoietin

Back

Thymus hormones that promote maturation of T lymphocytes.

52Ch. 10flashcard10.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

Pineal gland

Back

Tiny gland at the center of the brain; makes melatonin; its input comes from the visual pathways.

53Ch. 10flashcard10.8
  • textbook
  • lecture

Melatonin

Back

Pineal hormone made from serotonin; higher at night because light inhibits it; promotes sleep. Too much: seasonal affective disorder.

54Ch. 10flashcard10.9
  • textbook
  • lecture

Local signaling molecules

Back

Messengers that act on adjacent cells within seconds or milliseconds — neurotransmitters, prostaglandins, growth factors, nitric oxide.

55Ch. 10flashcard10.9
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Prostaglandins

Back

Lipids released by most cells' membranes (~16 kinds); affect menstrual cramps, inflammation, blood clotting, body temperature.

56Ch. 10flashcard10.9
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Nitric oxide (NO)

Back

A gas from endothelial cells that dilates blood vessels; may aid peristalsis; acts as a neurotransmitter.

57Ch. 10flashcard10.9
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Growth factors

Back

Peptides or proteins that make nearby cells grow, develop and multiply — e.g. marrow precursors into white blood cells.

58Ch. 10flashcardL2.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Tropic hormone

Back

A hormone that turns on another endocrine gland — TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH. FSH and LH are the gonadotropins.

59Ch. 10flashcardL2.4
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The anterior pituitary's hormones — how many, and which?

Back

Seven (lecture, deck, lab): GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, MSH. The textbook says six — no MSH.

60Ch. 10flashcardL2.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Acromegaly

Back

Too much GH in adulthood, after the growth plates close — bones thicken, not lengthen (hands, feet, face).

61Ch. 10flashcardL2.11
  • lecture
  • textbook

Myxedema

Back

Too little thyroid hormone in adults: puffy face, ↓ alertness, ↓ body temperature, ↓ heart rate.

62Ch. 10flashcardL2.11
  • lecture
  • textbook

Simple goiter

Back

Thyroid enlargement from iodine deficiency — low T3/T4 means no negative feedback, so TSH never stops.

63Ch. 10flashcardL2.9
  • lecture
  • textbook

Diabetes insipidus

Back

Too little ADH: excessive urine, constant thirst, dehydration. Treated with ADH nasal spray.

Ch. 10a — Special Topic — Diabetes Mellitus

Week 12 · study page · 16 multiple choice · 2 short answer · 16 flashcards

1Ch. 10a10a.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Every form of diabetes mellitus comes down to the same defect. Which?

Answer: d

Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders with abnormally high blood glucose from problems in insulin production or insulin function: not enough insulin, or target cells that do not respond adequately. Either way glucose cannot leave the blood. Too little ADH (option b) is diabetes insipidus — a different disease that shares only the high urine output.

2Ch. 10a10a.1 · Fig 10a.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

How does insulin actually move glucose into a target cell?

Answer: b

Insulin increases the number of glucose transport proteins (the deck: GLUT) in the target-cell membrane, and they carry glucose in by facilitated diffusion. Insulin does not carry glucose itself (option a); it changes the membrane so glucose can cross. In type 1 the failure is at insulin secretion; in type 2, adequate GLUT transporters are not placed.

3Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

What causes type 1 diabetes?

Answer: a

Type 1 is autoimmune: the immune system attacks the beta cells, which make insulin, leaving little or none — so insulin must be given by injection or pump. A virus may trigger it in someone genetically predisposed. Option b is type 2; option c is gestational diabetes.

4Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which form of diabetes accounts for 90–95% of diagnosed cases, and what is its defect?

Answer: c

Type 2 is 90–95% of cases and is insulin resistance — cells fail to respond adequately, and over time the pancreas may secrete less. Type 1 is about 5% in the book (the deck says 5–10%). Gestational is about 7% of pregnancies; "other specific types" are 1–5% of cases.

5Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Why was "non-insulin-dependent" dropped as a name for type 2 diabetes?

Answer: d

About 40% of type 2 diabetics need insulin, so the old name misled — the deck: type 2 "may or may not require insulin." "Adult-onset" was dropped too, as type 2 now appears in overweight, sedentary young people. Type 1 is the autoimmune form (option a).

6Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

A diabetic injects too much insulin and becomes anxious, sweaty, weak and disoriented. What is happening?

Answer: c

Too much insulin causes hypoglycemia: anxiety, sweating, hunger, weakness, disorientation, then convulsions and unconsciousness as brain cells starve — together called insulin shock, fatal unless glucose is raised (a glucagon emergency kit, or juice or glucose tablets for milder lows). Hyperglycemia is treated with insulin.

7Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

In diabetic ketoacidosis, where do the ketones come from?

Answer: d

Without insulin, glucose can't enter cells, so energy-starved cells break down lipids; the liver metabolises the fatty acids and produces ketones. Ketones are acids that release H⁺; in excess they overwhelm the buffers and blood pH drops → coma, abnormal heart rhythms, death. Treated in hospital with IV insulin, fluids and electrolytes.

8Ch. 10a10a.2 · case
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

During finals week, Cathy, a diabetic, has nausea, extreme thirst and confusion, with glucose near 300 mg/dl that home insulin won't bring down. What is the complication, and which type does she most likely have?

Answer: a

The book's Consider This Case. Stress is a DKA trigger; the symptoms fit; and home insulin fails because the liver keeps making glucose from amino acids. DKA is much more common in type 1 and rare in type 2. Glucose of 300 rules out hypoglycemia. The book's threshold for seeking care: above 300 mg/dl with ketones and symptoms.

9Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why do the long-term complications of diabetes land on so many different organs?

Answer: a

Years of high glucose damage blood vessels, and through them almost every organ: high blood pressure and atherosclerosis (heart attack, stroke), kidney failure (damaged glomeruli; dialysis), poor sensation and lower-leg amputation, blindness from retinal vessels, plus skin and gum infections and depression. Ketoacidosis (option b) is an acute complication.

10Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

A clinician wants to know a patient's average blood glucose over the past few months. Which test, and why does it work?

Answer: d

The glycated hemoglobin A1c test measures the percentage of hemoglobin carrying glucose; once glycated it stays so for the red cell's ~120-day life, giving the average over 2–3 months. Diabetes is 6.5% or higher on two tests; prediabetes 5.7–6.4%. Fasting and random tests read glucose now.

11Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

A patient's fasting blood glucose is 112 mg/dl, and a repeat test agrees. How does the chapter classify this?

Answer: b

Fasting glucose (American Diabetes Association guidelines): normal below 100 mg/dl; prediabetes 100–125; diabetes 126 or higher on two tests. 112 is in the prediabetes range. Note that 112 is above the lab's 70–110 mg/dL homeostatic range — the lab gives a single normal range, not a fasting cutoff.

12Ch. 10aboard 4 · CONFLICT
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

According to the Lab 11 board work, what is the normal homeostatic range for blood glucose?

Answer: b

Lab: 70–110 mg/dL, held by negative feedback between insulin and glucagon. Textbook (Ch. 10a): 70–150 mg/dl over the course of a day, with a fasting value under 100 normal. The two are different measurements, but they read as a conflict — use 70–110 on the lab exam and 70–150 on a textbook question. 100–125 is the fasting prediabetes band.

13Ch. 10a10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

Which treatment plan fits type 2 diabetes and prediabetes best?

Answer: c

Diet (nutritious, low in fat and calories) and exercise (which lowers glucose and makes cells more sensitive to insulin) come first, with monitoring by glucometer and A1c; oral antidiabetic medications or insulin follow if needed. Type 2 can be prevented or delayed by weight loss and exercise; type 1 cannot. Glucagon is for an emergency low, not after meals.

14Ch. 10a10a.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

What causes gestational diabetes?

Answer: b

Placental hormones make the mother's cells progressively insulin resistant; normally her pancreas compensates, and when it can't, gestational diabetes appears — worse as the placenta grows. It usually resolves after delivery. Option c is wrong twice: maternal insulin does not cross the placenta.

15Ch. 10a10a.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why are babies of mothers with gestational diabetes often very large?

Answer: b

Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, but maternal insulin does not. From about three months of gestation the fetal pancreas responds by overproducing insulin, driving glucose into fetal cells → excessive growth (the deck: macrosomia, birth weight over 9 pounds), difficult delivery, sometimes a cesarean section. After birth the baby may be hypoglycemic from its own high insulin.

16Ch. 10a10a.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Is gestational diabetes more like type 1 or type 2?

Answer: c

The book's Stop and Think. Like type 2 it is insulin resistance, not beta-cell destruction; risk factors overlap (a parent or sibling with type 2, overweight, a high-prevalence group); and treatment is diet and exercise first, insulin only if needed. The mother's later risk is of type 2.

1Ch. 10ashort answer10a.2
  • textbook
  • lecture

Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus: cause, share of cases, whether insulin is required, and whether it can be prevented.

Model answer

Type 1 — autoimmune destruction of the pancreas's beta cells, so little or no insulin is made; about 5% of cases (5–10% on the deck); usually begins before 25; insulin is always required (injection or pump); cannot be prevented or cured, though strict glucose control delays complications; ketoacidosis much more common. Type 2 — insulin resistance: cells fail to respond adequately to insulin (not enough GLUT transporters placed), and secretion may fall over time; 90–95% of cases; tied to obesity, inactivity, age and family history; insulin may or may not be needed (about 40% do); can be prevented or delayed by weight loss and exercise.

Marks for: production failure vs response failure; the prevalence split; insulin need; preventability. One risk factor or one treatment difference each makes the answer complete.

2Ch. 10ashort answer10a.3
  • textbook
  • lecture

Explain the cause of gestational diabetes and why it can make the baby unusually large.

Model answer

Hormones from the placenta make the mother's cells resistant to insulin; when her pancreas cannot make enough extra insulin to overcome it, she develops diabetes, usually in the second half of pregnancy, and it usually resolves after delivery. Her high blood glucose crosses the placenta, but her insulin does not. From about three months of gestation the fetal pancreas responds by making excess insulin, which moves the glucose into fetal cells and promotes excessive growth — a large baby (macrosomia, over 9 lb), a difficult delivery, sometimes a cesarean, and possible hypoglycemia in the newborn.

Marks for: placental hormones → insulin resistance; glucose crosses, insulin doesn't; the fetal pancreas's own insulin as the growth driver.
