Lab 9 — Nervous System & Nervous Tissue

Week 10 · study page · 38 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 35 flashcards

1Lab 9Neuron structure and function
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A signal arrives at a multipolar motor neuron from another cell. In which order does it pass through the neuron's parts?

Answer: d

Dendrites receive; the cell body holds the nucleus; the single axon carries the action potential away; the axon terminals branch at the distal end. Option b is the same chain run backwards — the commonest slip, because the terminals are where the next synapse is, not where this neuron's input comes in. Options a and c put the axon or cell body first, but the axon only ever carries the signal away from the cell body.

2Lab 9Neuron structure and function
  • lab manual

A sensory neuron carries touch from the skin of the finger to the cord. Which shape is it?

Answer: c

The lab makes sensory neurons pseudounipolar: a peripheral axon runs to the cell body, and a central axon runs on into the CNS. Multipolar is the shape of interneurons (CNS only) and motor neurons (options a and d); a motor neuron's cell body is in the cord, but that is not a sensory neuron. Bipolar (option b) is the 1-dendrite, 1-axon shape.

3Lab 9Neuron structure and function
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A cut axon in the arm regrows; a cut axon in the spinal cord does not. Which difference in myelin explains it?

Answer: a

A Schwann cell (PNS) wraps its membrane around one axon in many layers and leaves a neurolemma, which gives a better chance at repair. An oligodendrocyte (CNS) wraps extensions around multiple axons from different cells, leaves no neurolemma, and damaged CNS axons do not generally regenerate. Options b and c swap the two cells between CNS and PNS. Astrocytes support; they do not myelinate (option d).

4Lab 9Neuron structure and function
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture

Why does an action potential travel faster along a myelinated axon than along an unmyelinated one?

Answer: b

The lab: nodes of Ranvier — the gaps between myelinated areas — are the only sites with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so instead of firing every gate along the axon the AP jumps node to node: saltatory conduction. Myelin is lipid insulation, not a conductor (option a), and it removes channels from the covered stretch rather than adding them (option c). Whalen adds that nothing physically jumps — the signal is regenerated at each bare node — but "jumps" is the lab's and the book's word.

5Lab 9Neuron structure and function
  • lab manual

Rank three axons from fastest to slowest: a thin myelinated one, a very large unmyelinated one, a thin unmyelinated one.

Answer: d

Large axons beat small ones, but myelinated axons beat even the largest. So myelin wins outright, then diameter decides between the two bare axons. Option a is the tempting answer if you weigh size above myelin. Options c and b each rank a thin unmyelinated axon above the large one, which breaks the size rule.

6Lab 9Neuron structure and function
  • lab manual

Which pairing of a glial cell with its job is right?

Answer: a

The lab's glia table: ependymal cells make CSF; microglia are immune cells that phagocytose; oligodendrocytes (CNS) and Schwann cells (PNS) myelinate; astrocytes (CNS) and satellite cells (PNS) support. Every distractor pairs a real glial cell with another cell's job.

7Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

What mainly holds the inside of a resting neuron at about −70 mV?

Answer: c

There are many more K⁺ leak channels than Na⁺, and K⁺ leaving is what holds the inside negative. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, ATP) builds the gradients but moves no Cl⁻ (option d). Na⁺ leaking in would make the inside more positive (option a), and voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are closed below threshold (option b). Skeletal muscle rests at −85 mV because it has more K⁺ leak still.

8Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Each cycle of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump does what, at what cost?

Answer: b

3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, one ATP — which leaves Na⁺ high outside, K⁺ high inside and the outside more positive. It costs ATP because it pushes both ions against their gradients. Whalen himself swapped the ions twice in the 10/07 recap and corrected himself both times — option a is his slip; option d swaps the counts.

9Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Summed EPSPs bring a resting neuron to −55 mV. What happens next?

Answer: d

−55 mV is threshold — a figure from Whalen's 10/05 lecture only; the lab gives no value and Figure 7.5 draws the line unlabelled. At threshold all voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in the region open and Na⁺ floods in. The textbook says "more" channels open; the lab and the deck say "all" — answer "all" here. Option a describes a graded potential, which is what happens below threshold. +30 mV is the peak, not the threshold (option b).

10Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

On the action-potential curve, what stops the rise at +30 mV?

Answer: c

At +30 mV the Na⁺ channels inactivate, stopping the rise; by then the voltage-gated K⁺ channels are fully open and K⁺ moves out — repolarization. The pump acts only at the end, bringing the membrane back to rest after hyperpolarization (option a). Leak channels never close (option b), and Cl⁻ is not part of the action potential (option d).

11Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Why does the curve dip below −70 mV before returning to rest?

Answer: a

K⁺ channels are slow to close, so the membrane falls below RMP — hyperpolarization (phase 5). Then the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and K⁺ leak channels bring it back (phase 6). Na⁺ coming in would push the membrane up, not down (option c). The pump restores rest rather than causing the dip (option b).

12Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

A second, stronger stimulus arrives just after the Na⁺ channels have reset but while K⁺ is still leaving. On the lab's account, what happens?

Answer: b

That is the relative refractory period: the Na⁺ channels have reset, so an AP is possible but needs a stronger stimulus, because K⁺ is still leaving. It ends when all K⁺ channels close and the membrane is back at RMP. Option a is the absolute period, while Na⁺ channels are open and then inactivated. Whalen splits the period the same way ("possible but highly unlikely"); the textbook gives one period in which the neuron "cannot be stimulated" — that single period is his absolute one. APs never summate (option c).

13Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

A light touch and a firm press both trigger action potentials in the same sensory neuron. How does the firm press differ?

Answer: d

All-or-nothing: APs cannot summate, so a stronger stimulus gives more APs per second, not a bigger one. Every AP peaks at the same +30 mV (option a) and runs the same course (option c). Summation (option b) belongs to graded potentials, which add up before threshold.

14Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

A neurotransmitter opens channels that let Cl⁻ into a neuron. What is the result?

Answer: c

Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ are both concentrated outside. Ca²⁺ in makes the inside more positive; Cl⁻ in makes it more negative. A hyperpolarizing graded potential is an IPSP — it moves the cell away from threshold and makes an AP less likely. Option a is what Na⁺ (or Ca²⁺) entry does. Option d gets the gradient backwards. EPSP/IPSP are Whalen's terms; the lab uses them too.

15Lab 9Action potential graph
  • lab manual
detail

Receptors that sense stretch in blood-vessel walls for blood pressure use which kind of gated channel?

Answer: a

Gated channels are closed until a stimulus opens them; the three keys are chemicals, voltage changes and mechanical changes. Mechanically gated channels open on stretch or vibration and are used by sensory neurons — the lab's two examples are touch in the skin and stretch in blood vessels for blood pressure. Ligand-gated is the synapse's key; voltage-gated runs the AP. Leak channels are not gated at all (option d).

16Lab 9PNS
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

A patient's left dorsal roots at one level are cut. What would you expect at that level?

Answer: d

Dorsal = sensory in, with its cell bodies outside the cord in the dorsal-root ganglion; ventral = motor out, cell bodies inside the cord. Whalen said "sensory in the back, motor out the front" four times. Option b swaps the roots. Option c confuses the roots with the spinal nerve they join to form, which is mixed. The lateral horn, which holds ANS cell bodies, sits inside the cord and is not part of a dorsal root (option a).

17Lab 9PNS
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Which statement about the nerves of the PNS is right?

Answer: b

31 pairs of spinal nerves, all carrying both sensory and motor fibers. 12 pairs of cranial nerves — some sensory only, some motor only, some both. Options a and c swap the two rules; option d swaps the counts. Whalen: "I want you to know that."

18Lab 9PNS
  • lab manual

A cluster of neuron cell bodies sits outside the brain and cord. What is it called, and what would the same thing be called inside the CNS?

Answer: c

The lab's naming table: cell bodies are a nucleus in the CNS and a ganglion in the PNS; axons are a tract in the CNS and a nerve in the PNS. Option b reverses the cell-body pair. Options a and d name axon bundles, not cell bodies.

19Lab 9PNS
  • lab manual
detail

Which division of the PNS keeps working within the digestive tract even without input from the brain and cord?

Answer: a

The enteric branch is nervous tissue within the organs of the digestive tract, and it operates independently of the brain and cord. The sympathetic division is part of the ANS and starts in the cord (option d). Somatic motor drives skeletal muscle (option b); visceral sensory carries information to the CNS (option c).

20Lab 9Somatic
  • lab manual
detail

On a model, one spinal nerve carries both somatic and autonomic fibers. What does the lab say tells the two apart?

Answer: d

Somatic structures are the spinal nerves, carrying both motor and sensory fibers, plus the sensory ganglia — posterior root ganglia and cranial nerve ganglia. Autonomic structures run in those same nerves but add the sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia. The nerve is shared; the ganglia tell them apart — which rules out option a. Options c and b are not in any course source.

21Lab 9ANS
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Why does the sympathetic division tend to fire as a unit while the parasympathetic acts organ by organ?

Answer: b

Sympathetic preganglionic fibers run to the chain ganglia on either side of the vertebral column (or to collateral ganglia in the abdomen); the chain links the pathways, so the division fires as a unit — what an emergency needs. Option a is the parasympathetic arrangement: terminal ganglia near or within each organ, so its effects are local. Option c is also parasympathetic. Option d is wrong for the sympathetic, whose postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine.

22Lab 9ANS
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Where do parasympathetic preganglionic neurons originate?

Answer: c

Parasympathetic = craniosacral: brain-stem nuclei (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X) and the lateral horn of the sacral cord (S2–S4). Option a is the sympathetic (thoracolumbar) origin. Whalen's deck and lecture once said "cervical and sacral"; the chapter, Figure 8.10, the animation and his own word craniosacral all say cranial — write cranial. Ventral horns hold somatic motor neurons; dorsal-root ganglia hold sensory cell bodies.

23Lab 9ANS
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which pair of postganglionic transmitters is right?

Answer: d

Sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine; parasympathetic ones release acetylcholine. Whalen adds that every preganglionic neuron, in both divisions, releases ACh — the parasympathetic "never makes that switch" — and called it "an A question right there." Option a swaps them; options c and b each give one division's transmitter to both.

In lecture: "That's an A question right there." — postganglionic transmitters, Wed 10/14

24Lab 9ANS
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Which two targets receive sympathetic input with no parasympathetic partner?

Answer: a

The adrenal gland releases epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood, which back up and prolong the nerve signal; the kidney responds with salt and water retention. Neither has a parasympathetic partner. The other organs get both divisions, with antagonistic effects — most, but not all, organs get both.

25Lab 9ANS
  • lab manual

After a large lunch, which division dominates and what does it do?

Answer: b

Parasympathetic = rest-and-digest: homeostasis during relaxation, energy stores replenished — the division activated just after a meal. Its terminal ganglia make its effects local, so each organ returns to rest at its own pace. Options a and c describe the sympathetic division, which slows digestion. Option d gives the parasympathetic the sympathetic's chain.

26Lab 9CNS
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Going inward from the skull, which order of protective layers is right?

Answer: d

Dura mater (tough) — thickest, just under the bone. Arachnoid (spider) — attached to the dura, sending extensions down to the pia. Pia mater (tender) — thin, directly on the CNS. The arachnoid's extensions create the subarachnoid space, filled with CSF. Option a is the stack upside down; c and d each swap a neighbouring pair.

27Lab 9CNS
  • lab manual

Where is cerebrospinal fluid made, and where is it reabsorbed?

Answer: c

CSF is made by ependymal cells in the choroid plexus of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles, and reabsorbed at the arachnoid granulations. It fills the ventricles, the central canal and the subarachnoid space, and it nourishes, removes waste, cushions and supports. Option a runs the two ends backwards; astrocytes and microglia make no CSF.

28Lab 9CNS
  • lab manual

Which substance crosses the blood–brain barrier most easily?

Answer: b

The barrier is endothelial cells joined by tight junctions, so everything must cross through the cells. Small and lipid-soluble substances pass; large or polar ones need a transport protein. It also protects the brain from the body's own immune cells (option d), pathogens and toxins — and it limits drug transport.

29Lab 9Brain
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the dissected brain, which structure relays every sense except smell to the cortex?

Answer: a

The thalamus is the gateway to the cortex for all sensory input except smell. The hypothalamus runs homeostasis — heart rate, BP, temperature, sleep/wake — and is the ANS control centre. The epithalamus handles circadian rhythm, and the pineal gland is an endocrine structure the dissection has you pin. The first three make up the diencephalon.

30Lab 9Brain
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A stroke damages the medulla. Which functions are most at risk?

Answer: d

Medulla — heart rate, breathing. Midbrain — vision and hearing reflexes (option a). Cerebellum — coordination, correcting motor error, balance (option c). Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the left cerebral cortex handle speech (option b). The pons is the connection to the cerebellum, and all axons to and from the cortex pass through pons and medulla, many crossing over there.

31Lab 9Brain
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A patient understands speech well but cannot produce fluent speech. Which area, on which side, is damaged?

Answer: c

Broca's area — speech production; Wernicke's area — understanding. Both are lateralized LEFT. Option a would leave production intact and impair understanding. Options b and d put the areas on the wrong side.

32Lab 9Brain
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the dissected brain, what connects the two cerebral hemispheres across the midline?

Answer: b

The longitudinal fissure splits the hemispheres; the corpus callosum connects them. The fissure (option a) is the gap, not the bridge. The pons bridges to the cerebellum, not between hemispheres. A sulcus is a groove on the surface.

33Lab 9Spinal cord structure
  • lab manual
detail

Under the microscope, a cord cross-section shows a lateral horn. What does that tell you, and what does the horn hold?

Answer: a

The lab's cord: dorsal (posterior) horn — sensory axons enter; ventral (anterior) horn — motor neuron cell bodies; lateral horn — thoracic only, ANS cell bodies. Tracts (option d) are white matter, outside the gray butterfly, grouped as columns. Sensory cell bodies sit outside the cord in the dorsal-root ganglion (option b).

34Lab 9Spinal cord structure
  • lab manual
  • textbook

How does the spinal cord's arrangement differ from the brain's?

Answer: d

The cord is inside-out compared with the brain. Its white matter is OUTSIDE — tracts grouped as columns, ascending = sensory up, descending = motor down — and its gray matter is INSIDE, butterfly-shaped around the central canal. The cerebrum is gray outside (cortex), white inside (tracts) — which is option b and option a.

35Lab 9reflex function/ components
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which sequence of reflex-arc components is right?

Answer: b

1 receptor detects the stimulus → 2 sensory (afferent) neuron carries the AP to the CNS → 3 integration, direct onto a motor neuron or via an interneuron → 4 motor (efferent) neuron carries the AP out → 5 effector, muscle or gland, responds. Whalen: the arc is on Exam 3, and the interneuron "may or may not" be there. Option d is the arc backwards.

In lecture: "That will probably be on an upcoming exam, three, that I've already looked at." — the reflex arc, Wed 10/14

36Lab 9reflex function/ components
  • lab manual

In the patellar reflex, what is the stimulus?

Answer: c

The hammer hits the patellar ligament, which stretches the quadriceps muscle spindles — that stretch is the stimulus. One sensory neuron comes in, then two synapses: one direct to a motor neuron, so the quadriceps contracts and the lower leg kicks up; one to an inhibitory neuron, so the hamstrings are inhibited (option b is backwards). A reflex does not require perception — no pain is involved (option d).

37Lab 9reflex function/ components
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

In the patellar reflex, why does the sensory neuron also synapse on an inhibitory neuron?

Answer: d

The inhibitory neuron inhibits the hamstrings, so the antagonist cannot fight the movement. Muscles work in antagonistic pairs — Whalen: excitatory says contract, inhibitory says don't, and "then and only then across a joint can I cause a bending." The signal does still reach the brain afterward (option c); the reflex simply does not wait for it.

38Lab 9reflex function/ components
  • lab manual
  • lecture

You pull your hand off a hot pan before you feel the heat. Which statement explains it?

Answer: a

A reflex is a pre-set, protective pathway — same response every time, very fast, and it does not require perception: the response happens before you feel it. A spinal reflex integrates in the cord; a cranial reflex integrates in the brain. Whalen: "Your brain wasn't involved in that decision. Your spinal cord made that decision." Pulling the hand uses skeletal muscle, so it is not autonomic (option d).

1Lab 9short answerAction potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Draw the action potential graph. Label the axes and the four voltages, number the six phases, and explain what each ion channel is doing in each phase. Mark the two refractory periods.

Model answer

Axes: Y = membrane potential in mV, X = time. Marks at +30, 0, −55 (threshold) and −70 (rest). Phase 1 — rest, −70 mV: only leak channels; there are far more K⁺ leak than Na⁺, so K⁺ leaving holds the inside negative; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, ATP) keeps Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside. Phase 2 — to threshold: a stimulus opens gated channels (ligand, voltage or mechanical); graded potentials (EPSPs) summate up to −55 mV. Phase 3 — depolarization: at threshold all voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in the region open, Na⁺ floods in and the membrane rises to +30 mV. Phase 4 — repolarization: the Na⁺ channels inactivate; voltage-gated K⁺ channels are fully open and K⁺ moves out, back toward rest. Phase 5 — hyperpolarization: the K⁺ channels are slow to close, so the membrane dips below −70. Phase 6 — back to RMP: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and leak channels restore rest. Refractory periods: absolute over the rise and early fall — Na⁺ channels open then inactivated, no AP at any strength; relative after the Na⁺ channels reset — an AP is possible with a stronger stimulus, ending when all K⁺ channels close and the membrane is back at RMP. All-or-nothing: APs do not summate; a stronger stimulus gives more APs per second.

Marks for the axes and four voltages (−55 mV is Whalen's lecture figure — the lab and Figure 7.5 give no number), the six phases in order each with its ion and its direction (up = Na⁺ in, down = K⁺ out — the question Whalen asked at every step), hyperpolarization explained by slow K⁺ channels, and both refractory periods. The textbook gives one period; the lab and lecture give two — name both here.

2Lab 9short answerreflex function/ components
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Diagram the generic reflex arc as five components, then the patellar reflex. Explain what makes a reflex a reflex.

Model answer

A reflex is a pre-set, protective pathway: the same response every time, very fast, and it does not require perception — the response happens before you feel it. A spinal reflex integrates in the cord, a cranial reflex in the brain. The five components: 1 receptor detects the stimulus → 2 sensory (afferent) neuron carries the AP to the CNS → 3 integration, either directly onto a motor neuron or through an interneuron → 4 motor (efferent) neuron carries the AP out → 5 effector, a muscle or gland, responds. Patellar reflex: the hammer strikes the patellar ligament and stretches the quadriceps muscle spindles — the stimulus. One sensory neuron enters the cord and makes two synapses: one directly onto a motor neuron to the quadriceps, which contracts and kicks the lower leg up; one onto an inhibitory neuron that inhibits the hamstrings, so the antagonist cannot fight the movement. The patellar reflex is therefore the direct version of step 3 for the quadriceps; the withdrawal reflex in Figure 8.8 runs through an interneuron.

Whalen flagged the arc as on Exam 3. Marks for the five components in order with afferent/efferent named, that the interneuron can be skipped, the stimulus being stretch of the spindles (not the hammer), and the inhibitory synapse to the hamstrings with its reason.

In lecture: "That will probably be on an upcoming exam, three, that I've already looked at." — the reflex arc, Wed 10/14

3Lab 9short answerNeuron structure and function
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Draw and label a multipolar neuron with a myelinated axon. Explain myelin, compare the two myelinating cells, and say why myelin speeds conduction.

Model answer

Parts: dendrites receive; the cell body holds the nucleus; one axon carries the AP away; axon terminals branch at the distal end. Shapes: bipolar (1 dendrite, 1 axon); pseudounipolar (sensory — peripheral axon to the cell body, central axon to the CNS); multipolar (interneurons, CNS only, and motor neurons). Myelin is lipid insulation formed around axons. Schwann cell (PNS): wraps its membrane around one axon in many layers, leaving a neurolemma — a better chance at repair. Oligodendrocyte (CNS): wraps extensions around multiple axons from different cells, no neurolemma — damaged CNS axons do not generally regenerate. Nodes of Ranvier, the gaps between myelinated segments, are the only sites with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so instead of firing every gate the AP jumps node to node — saltatory conduction. Large axons beat small ones, but myelinated axons beat even the largest. Myelin is found in vertebrates only.

Marks for the labelled drawing (dendrite, cell body, nucleus, axon, terminals, myelin, node), the Schwann/oligodendrocyte contrast with the neurolemma and its consequence for repair, and saltatory conduction explained by where the Na⁺ channels are. Whalen accepts "jumps" as the book's word but stresses the signal is regenerated at each node.

4Lab 9short answerANS
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Compare the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the ANS: origin, ganglia, transmitter, behaviour and effects. Include the two-neuron pathway.

Model answer

The ANS is the visceral motor division of the PNS — involuntary control of organs, glands, smooth and cardiac muscle. Both divisions maintain homeostasis and both use a 2-neuron pathway: preganglionic (CNS → ganglion), then postganglionic (ganglion → effector). Most, but not all, organs get both, and where both arrive the effects are antagonistic. Sympathetic — fight-or-flight: homeostasis during stress, maintaining delivery of oxygen and glucose; origin thoracolumbar (lateral horn of the thoracic and lumbar cord); preganglionic fibers go to the chain ganglia beside the vertebral column or collateral ganglia in the abdomen, and the chain links the pathways so the division fires as a unit; postganglionic transmitter norepinephrine; ↑ breathing rate, heart rate and BP, ↓ digestion; the adrenal gland adds epinephrine and norepinephrine to the blood and the kidney retains salt and water — neither has a parasympathetic partner. Parasympathetic — rest-and-digest: homeostasis during relaxation, replenishing energy stores, active just after a meal; origin craniosacral (brain-stem nuclei of cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral S2–S4); terminal ganglia near or within each organ, short postganglionic axons, so effects are local, organ by organ; postganglionic transmitter acetylcholine.

Marks for the five rows of the lab's table (nickname, origin, ganglia, behaviour, transmitter), the two-neuron pathway, and antagonism. Write cranial, not cervical — Whalen's deck slipped once. His lecture adds that every preganglionic neuron releases ACh and that the vagus carries ~75% of parasympathetic outflow.

5Lab 9short answerSpinal cord structure
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Draw a cross-section of the spinal cord with its roots. Label the gray and white matter, the horns, columns and roots, and explain the cord's two jobs.

Model answer

Gray matter is INSIDE, butterfly-shaped, around the central canal (CSF); white matter is OUTSIDE — the opposite of the brain. Horns (gray): dorsal (posterior) — sensory axons enter; ventral (anterior) — motor neuron cell bodies; lateral — thoracic only, ANS cell bodies. Columns (white): posterior, lateral and anterior, made of tracts — ascending carry sensory information up to the brain, descending carry motor commands down. Roots: the dorsal root carries sensory fibers in, with its cell bodies outside the cord in the dorsal-root ganglion; the ventral root carries motor fibers out, with cell bodies inside the cord; the two join into one mixed spinal nerve (31 pairs). Two jobs: conduct — a conduit for APs to and from the brain, receiving from the sensory PNS and transmitting to the motor PNS; and integrate — the integration centre for all spinal reflexes, through its synapses with other neurons.

Marks for the inside-out arrangement, three horns with their contents (lateral = thoracic only), ascending vs descending, dorsal in / ventral out with the ganglion placed outside the cord, and both jobs. This is the slide on the lab-exam microscope (LM × 40).

6Lab 9short answerBrain
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Name the four regions of the brain, and give the job of each structure you would point to on a dissected brain: cerebrum, corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, medulla, cerebellum. Then list the four layers that protect the CNS.

Model answer

Four regions: cerebrum · diencephalon · brain stem · cerebellum. Cerebrum — gray cortex outside, white tracts inside; gyri (ridges), sulci (grooves), fissures (deep); four lobes named for the skull bones over them; the longitudinal fissure splits the hemispheres and the corpus callosum connects them; Broca's (speech production) and Wernicke's (understanding) areas are on the left. Diencephalon: thalamus — gateway to the cortex for all sensory input except smell; hypothalamus — homeostasis (heart rate, BP, temperature, sleep/wake), control centre of the ANS, an endocrine structure. Brain stem: midbrain — vision and hearing reflexes; pons — the connection to the cerebellum; medulla — heart rate and breathing; all axons to and from the cortex pass through pons and medulla, many crossing over there. Cerebellum — coordination, correcting motor error, and balance from vestibular, visual and proprioceptor input. Protection, outside in: bone → meninges (dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater) → CSF in the subarachnoid space → blood–brain barrier.

The Exam 3 lab practical uses a dissected brain, so marks go for one correct function per structure and the four regions by name. The protection stack is the lab's largest single CNS section.

1Lab 9flashcardNeuron structure and function
  • lab manual

Main function of nervous tissue, and its two cell types

Back

Communication, by transmitting action potentials to and from the CNS. Neurons generate APs; neuroglia support them.

2Lab 9flashcardNeuron structure and function
  • lab manual

The three neuron shapes and who has them

Back

Bipolar — 1 dendrite, 1 axon. Pseudounipolar — sensory neurons. Multipolar — interneurons (CNS only) and motor neurons.

3Lab 9flashcardNeuron structure and function
  • lab manual
detail

Four things neuroglia do

Back

Maintain the extracellular fluid around neurons · insulate them · promote growth and development · phagocytose debris and pathogens.

4Lab 9flashcardNeuron structure and function
  • lab manual

The glia table — CNS and PNS

Back

Support: astrocyte / satellite cell. Myelination: oligodendrocyte / Schwann cell. Immune: microglia (CNS). Makes CSF: ependymal cell (CNS).

5Lab 9flashcardNeuron structure and function
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Node of Ranvier

Back

The gap between myelinated segments — the only site with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so the AP jumps node to node: saltatory conduction.

6Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Resting membrane potential

Back

The charge difference across the membrane at rest — about −70 mV in a neuron, inside negative, localized right at the membrane. Skeletal muscle: −85 mV.

7Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lecture

Threshold

Back

−55 mV — where all voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open. A lecture figure: the lab and textbook never state it.

8Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lab manual

The three keys that open gated channels

Back

Chemicals (ligand-gated) · voltage changes (voltage-gated) · mechanical changes (mechanically gated — stretch or vibration).

9Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Graded potential

Back

A local, reversible change whose size varies with the number of gates opened. Depolarizing = EPSP; hyperpolarizing = IPSP.

10Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Summation (at the neuron)

Back

The additive effect of several graded potentials. Net positive → closer to threshold, AP more likely; net negative → further away.

11Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lab manual
detail

Which cells are excitable?

Back

Muscle cells, neurons and cardiac pacemaker cells — the only cells that fire action potentials.

12Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Peak of the action potential

Back

+30 mV, where the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels inactivate.

13Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Absolute vs relative refractory period

Back

Absolute — Na⁺ channels open then inactivated; no AP at any strength. Relative — Na⁺ channels reset; an AP is possible with a stronger stimulus, while K⁺ is still leaving.

14Lab 9flashcardAction potential graph
  • lab manual
  • lecture

All-or-nothing

Back

APs cannot summate and are the same size every time. A stronger stimulus gives more APs per second, not a bigger one.

15Lab 9flashcardPNS
  • lab manual

Afferent vs efferent

Back

Afferent = sensory, toward the CNS. Efferent = motor, away from it. Each splits into somatic and visceral.

16Lab 9flashcardPNS
  • lab manual
detail

The one part of the PNS that sits inside the CNS

Back

Motor neuron cell bodies — the PNS is all nervous tissue outside the CNS, except these.

17Lab 9flashcardPNS
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Spinal and cranial nerve counts

Back

31 pairs of spinal nerves, all mixed. 12 pairs of cranial nerves — some sensory, some motor, some both.

18Lab 9flashcardPNS
  • lab manual

Nucleus, ganglion, tract, nerve

Back

Cell bodies: nucleus in the CNS, ganglion in the PNS. Axons: tract in the CNS, nerve in the PNS.

19Lab 9flashcardSomatic
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Somatic sensory vs somatic motor

Back

Somatic sensory — conscious perception, e.g. touch. Somatic motor — voluntary movement of skeletal muscle.

20Lab 9flashcardSomatic
  • lab manual
detail

The two sensory ganglia of the somatic system

Back

Posterior (dorsal) root ganglia and cranial nerve ganglia.

21Lab 9flashcardANS
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Preganglionic vs postganglionic neuron

Back

Preganglionic — CNS to the ganglion. Postganglionic — ganglion to the effector. Every ANS pathway is these two.

22Lab 9flashcardANS
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Thoracolumbar vs craniosacral

Back

Thoracolumbar = sympathetic (lateral horn, T and L cord). Craniosacral = parasympathetic (CN III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4).

23Lab 9flashcardANS
  • lab manual
detail

Chain, collateral and terminal ganglia

Back

Chain — beside the vertebral column (sympathetic). Collateral (prevertebral) — anterior to it, in the abdomen (sympathetic). Terminal — near or within the organ (parasympathetic).

24Lab 9flashcardANS
  • lecture
detail

Vagus nerve's share of parasympathetic outflow

Back

About 75% — cranial nerve X. A lecture-only number.

25Lab 9flashcardCNS
  • lab manual

The CNS's role

Back

The integration centre: it processes incoming sensory information and creates a response. Brain in the cranial cavity, cord in the vertebral cavity.

26Lab 9flashcardCNS
  • lab manual

The four layers protecting the CNS

Back

Bone → meninges → CSF → blood–brain barrier.

27Lab 9flashcardCNS
  • lab manual
detail

Dura, arachnoid, pia — meanings

Back

Dura = tough (thickest, under the bone). Arachnoid = spider (extensions down to the pia). Pia = tender (thin, on the CNS).

28Lab 9flashcardCNS
  • lab manual

What CSF does

Back

Nourishes, removes waste, cushions and supports — shock absorption. Fills the ventricles, central canal and subarachnoid space.

29Lab 9flashcardCNS
  • lab manual

The blood–brain barrier is built from…

Back

Endothelial cells and the tight junctions between them — everything must cross through the cells.

30Lab 9flashcardBrain
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Four regions of the brain

Back

Cerebrum · diencephalon · brain stem · cerebellum.

31Lab 9flashcardBrain
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Gyrus, sulcus, fissure

Back

Gyrus — a ridge. Sulcus — a groove. Fissure — a deep groove (the longitudinal fissure splits the hemispheres).

32Lab 9flashcardBrain
  • lab manual
detail

Hypothalamus and pineal gland — what they share

Back

Both are endocrine structures. The hypothalamus is also the control centre of the ANS.

33Lab 9flashcardSpinal cord structure
  • lab manual

The three horns of the cord

Back

Dorsal — sensory axons enter. Ventral — motor cell bodies. Lateral — thoracic only, ANS cell bodies.

34Lab 9flashcardSpinal cord structure
  • lab manual

Ascending vs descending tracts

Back

Ascending — sensory, up to the brain. Descending — motor, down from it. Both run in the white-matter columns.

35Lab 9flashcardreflex function/ components
  • lab manual

Spinal vs cranial reflex

Back

Spinal — integrated in the cord. Cranial — integrated in the brain.

Lab 10 — Senses

Week 11 · study page · 30 multiple choice · 5 short answer · 29 flashcards

1Lab 10General senses
  • lab manual

A rod releases neurotransmitter onto a bipolar cell rather than firing itself. Which of the lab's three receptor cell types is it?

Answer: c

Specialized receptor cell — a separate cell that passes the signal on: rod → neurotransmitter → bipolar cell → optic nerve neurons. Free nerve endings are bare dendrites in tissue; encapsulated ones have a connective-tissue capsule that enhances sensitivity. Most general senses use a modified axon terminal of the sensory neuron itself (d).

2Lab 10Smell (olfaction)
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

Every special sense except one uses a separate receptor cell. Which one detects its stimulus on the sensory neuron's own dendrites?

Answer: b

Smell. Odorants bind receptors on the olfactory neurons' own dendrites — the lab calls it unique. Taste cells are not neurons (c); rods and cones (a) and hair cells (d) are separate receptor cells that signal a neuron.

3Lab 10General senses
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Reading Braille depends on light touch with very fine spatial resolution. Which receptor, in which skin layer, provides it?

Answer: a

Merkel cells sit in the stratum basale and give light touch with fine spatial resolution — hands, feet, Braille. Meissner's corpuscles are light touch too, but in the dermal papillae and, in the lab's wording, with less detail than Merkel (the textbook stresses instead that Meissner's tell you where you were touched). Pacinian and Ruffini are deep.

4Lab 10General senses
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

On the skin model you find a deep receptor that looks like an onion in section. What is it?

Answer: d

Pacinian (lamellated) corpuscle — in the deep dermis, with a layered capsule, "an onion in section". The chapter makes it the strong-pressure and vibration receptor. Meissner's sit high in the dermal papillae; Ruffini are deep but not layered.

5Lab 10General senses
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

According to the lab, Ruffini endings in the deep dermis and hypodermis respond to what, and serve which sense?

Answer: b

The lab: Ruffini — stretch → proprioception, and it lists them as proprioceptors with muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs. The textbook describes them as continuous-pressure receptors — not a contradiction so much as a different emphasis, but on the lab exam give stretch. Vibration (a) is Pacinian; light touch (d) is Merkel and Meissner's.

6Lab 10General senses
  • lab manual
detail

A receptor in the hypothalamus monitors the solute concentration of the blood. What is it, in the lab's table?

Answer: d

Osmoreceptor — a kind of chemoreceptor detecting solute concentration; the lab's example is the hypothalamus. A baroreceptor (a) is a specialized mechanoreceptor sensing stretch in vessel and heart walls — the carotid sinus and right atrium.

7Lab 10General senses
  • lab manual

In the lab's terms, what is the difference between transduction and transmission?

Answer: a

Transduction — stimulus → action potential, at the receptor: ion channels open and the membrane potential changes. The AP then travels along the sensory neuron — transmission — and the neurons and synapses involved are the transmission pathway. Option b is the exact swap; every sense does both (c).

8Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the eye model, which tunic contains the iris, the ciliary body and the choroid?

Answer: c

Vascular (middle) tunic — iris, ciliary body, choroid. Fibrous (outer) — sclera and cornea. Nervous (inner) — retina. There is no "pigmented tunic"; pigmented epithelium is the outermost layer of the retina. The tunic names are the lab's — the textbook just says outer, middle and inner layers.

9Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The ciliary muscle is labelled on the eye model. What does it control?

Answer: b

Ciliary muscle → lens shape → near and far focus. Pupil size (a) is the iris, with its two smooth muscles. Moving the eyeball (d) is the external muscles anchored to the sclera.

10Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Reading the retina from the inside of the eye outward, which order is correct?

Answer: d

Inner → outer: ganglion → bipolar → photoreceptors → pigmented epithelium. So light crosses the ganglion and bipolar layers first — the lab's figure draws the light arrows coming from the bottom. Three cell layers, two synaptic layers between them. Option a is the order read from the back.

11Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual

Which sequence is the path of light through the eye?

Answer: a

Cornea → aqueous humor (anterior cavity) → pupil → posterior chamber → lens → vitreous humor → retina. Aqueous is in front of the lens, vitreous behind it — every wrong option misplaces one humor or puts the lens before the pupil.

12Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On the eye model, where do the ganglion axons leave as the optic nerve and the blood vessels enter and leave?

Answer: c

Optic disc — ganglion axons exit as the optic nerve, vessels enter and leave, and there are no photoreceptors, so nothing reaches the cortex from it: the blind spot. The macula sits opposite the cornea and its fovea is the sharpest point — the opposite of blind.

13Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In the blind-spot test you cover your left eye, fix your right eye on the cross and move closer. Why does the circle vanish?

Answer: b

At one distance the circle's image lands on the optic disc, where there are no photoreceptors, so it disappears. The fovea (a) is where vision is sharpest, not absent. The circle is seen by the right eye alone throughout, so option d does not explain the vanishing.

14Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of these is a job of the vitreous humor, according to the lab?

Answer: d

Vitreous humor is a gel: it passes light, shapes the eye and holds the retina back against the wall. Nourishing the cornea and lens and removing waste (a) is the aqueous humor; focusing (b) is the lens; stopping scatter (c) is the choroid.

15Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • textbook

You look from your lab notebook to a poster across the room. What does the lab say happens?

Answer: a

Far: parallel rays → ciliary muscle relaxes → lens flatter. Near: steep angle → lens more convex (d — the notebook you just looked away from). Options b and c mix one half of each.

16Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Light hits a photoreceptor. In the lab's sequence, what happens next?

Answer: b

Pigment changes shape → cascade → hyperpolarization → the inhibitory neurotransmitter stops → the bipolar cells, no longer inhibited, fire → ganglion AP → visual cortex, occipital lobe. Option d keeps the hyperpolarization but reverses its effect. The photoreceptor never sends its own AP down the optic nerve (c) — the ganglion cells do.

17Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Under the microscope, a photoreceptor has a long, columnar outer segment packed with discs. What is it, and what pigment is in the discs?

Answer: d

Rods — long, columnar outer segment, rhodopsin discs, low light, no colour. Cones — short, tapered outer segment of membrane folds, detecting specific wavelengths. Both have an inner segment (nucleus, organelles) and an outer segment carrying opsin. Melanin is the choroid's pigment.

18Lab 10Eye
  • lab manual
detail

The cow-eye dissection shows a layer at the back of the eye that the human eye model lacks. What is it, and why the difference?

Answer: a

The tapetum lucidum — many animals have one because it improves night vision, but humans do not have this structure. The human eye's choroid does the opposite job: its pigment absorbs light to stop scatter. The kind of observation a lab quiz asks.

19Lab 10Ear
  • lab manual
detail

On the ear model, which structures are not encased in the petrous temporal bone?

Answer: d

The lab: the middle ear is encased in the petrous temporal bone, except the tympanic membrane, the oval window, the round window and the Eustachian tube — its openings. The ossicles (a, c) sit inside the encased cavity, and the inner ear (a, b, c) is buried in the same bone.

20Lab 10Ear
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

The ear model shows the malleus fixed to one structure and the stapes against another. Which two?

Answer: c

The malleus is fixed to the tympanic membrane and the incus, so the membrane moves malleus → incus → stapes, amplifying the vibration. The stapes sits against the oval window — the membrane over the opening to the fluid-filled cochlea. The round window (b, d) is where the wave exits. Option a is the exact swap.

21Lab 10Ear
  • lab manual
  • lecture

The stapes moves the oval window. What happens next in the cochlea, in the lab's words?

Answer: a

Wave in the scala vestibuli → perilymph moves → the basilar membrane (floor of the cochlear duct) undulates → hair cells pushed up into the tectorial membrane → they bend → neurotransmitter → sensory neurons fire. The wave exits at the round window, which bulges out (d). The scala vestibuli comes first — Whalen's "be specific" question.

22Lab 10Ear
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

On a cross-section of the cochlea, where is the organ of Corti?

Answer: b

The lab's cross-section: the organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane, adjacent to the scala tympani, with the tectorial membrane above it. Option a puts it on the membrane it bends against. Lab name organ of Corti = textbook spiral organ.

23Lab 10Ear
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

A 20,000 Hz tone and a 20 Hz tone are played. Where on the uncoiled cochlea does each register?

Answer: c

High → base (20,000 Hz); mid ~1,500 Hz; low → apex (20 Hz) — one region per frequency. The basilar membrane is thick and narrow at the base, near the middle ear, and thin and wide at the apex; that variation is what lets frequencies be told apart. Option a is the classic reversal.

24Lab 10Ear
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Which pairing of primary cortex and lobe does the lab give?

Answer: b

The lab's four: visual — occipital · auditory — temporal · olfactory — temporal · gustatory — parietal. The chapter names none of these lobes, so this is a lab-exam fact. Whalen's lecture adds that the cochlear signal passes the inferior colliculi of the midbrain on the way.

25Lab 10Vestibular sensation
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

You turn your head to the left. On the lab's figure, which way does the cupula bend, and why?

Answer: b

The canal swings with the head, but the fluid lags and moves opposite, so the cupula bends in the direction opposite the rotation. The bend direction sets whether neurotransmitter release goes up or down, signalled along the vestibular nerve (CN VIII). Otoliths (c) are in the vestibule, not the canals.

26Lab 10Vestibular sensation
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Where are the maculae of the vestibule?

Answer: c

The macula — gel with hair cells at its base and otoliths on top — is on the floor of the utricle (horizontal when upright) and the sides of the saccule. Option b swaps them. The ampulla (a) holds the cupula, not a macula.

27Lab 10Vestibular sensation
  • lab manual
  • lecture

A car accelerates forward from a stop. How do the maculae detect it?

Answer: d

Inertia differs between the stereocilia and the heavier otolithic membrane, so a shearing force bends the stereocilia in the direction of acceleration. The utricle's fluid does not move the hair cells (a) — the otoliths' weight does. The cupula (b) is the canals, which sense rotation.

28Lab 10Taste (gustation)
  • lab manual
detail

Which cranial nerves carry taste from the tongue and pharynx?

Answer: c

CN VII, IX and X carry taste to the primary gustatory cortex in the parietal lobe. CN I is smell, II is vision, VIII is hearing and balance (a); III, IV and VI move the eye (d).

29Lab 10Taste (gustation)
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

Of the five taste cells, which does the lab call the most sensitive, and what does it guard against?

Answer: b

Bitter — alkaloids — the most sensitive, guarding against spoilage and toxins (Whalen: many natural poisons are alkaloids). Sour is H⁺, salty K⁺ and Na⁺, umami amino acids — savory.

30Lab 10Smell (olfaction)
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Following the lab, trace an olfactory signal after the neuron reaches threshold.

Answer: a

AP along the olfactory neuron → through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid → synapse in the olfactory bulb → primary olfactory cortex, temporal lobe. Whalen adds that the route runs past the limbic system, which is why smell calls up memory. The parietal lobe (c) is taste.

1Lab 10short answerEye
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Name the three tunics of the eye, the structures in each, and the job of each structure.

Model answer

Fibrous (outer): sclera — the white; protects and shapes the eye · cornea — clear front; its curve refracts light. Vascular (middle): iris — two smooth muscles set the pupil's size and so the light let in · ciliary body / ciliary muscle — changes the lens's shape for near and far · choroid — vessels plus pigment that absorbs light and stops scatter. Nervous (inner): retina — three cell layers (ganglion, bipolar, photoreceptors) and two synaptic layers; its macula has the fovea, only cones, sharpest detail; the optic disc has no photoreceptors (blind spot) and is where the ganglion axons leave as the optic nerve.

The eye model is on the lab exam. A mark per tunic placed correctly, and one per structure with its job. The tunic names are the lab's; the textbook says outer, middle and inner layer.

2Lab 10short answerEar
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Label the ear from outside to inside and give the job of each part: outer, middle and inner ear.

Model answer

Outer: pinna (auricle) — a satellite dish funnelling sound · external auditory canal · tympanic membrane — vibrates; the outer/middle boundary. Middle (in the petrous temporal bone): malleus → incus → stapes — amplify the vibration (about 22×) · oval window — the stapes sits on it; it starts the fluid wave · round window — where the wave exits · Eustachian (auditory) tube — to the pharynx; equalizes pressure. Inner: cochlea — hearing; scala vestibuli (wave first) and scala tympani filled with perilymph, the cochlear duct between them, its floor the basilar membrane carrying the organ of Corti whose hair cells bend against the tectorial membrane → cochlear branch of CN VIII → auditory cortex, temporal lobe · vestibule and semicircular canals — equilibrium.

"Label the parts of the ear and describe the role of each part" is one of the Ch. 9 objectives he read out, and the ear model is on the exam. Order matters, and so do the paired names (pinna/auricle, organ of Corti/spiral organ, Eustachian/auditory tube).

3Lab 10short answerVestibular sensation
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Explain how the vestibular apparatus detects rotation and how it detects head tilt and linear acceleration.

Model answer

Rotation — semicircular canals. Three fluid-filled canals in different planes, each with an ampulla holding a gel cupula with hair cells at its base. When the head turns, the canal swings with it but the fluid lags and moves the opposite way, bending the cupula and the stereocilia; the bend direction raises or lowers neurotransmitter release onto the vestibular nerve (CN VIII). Canals pair up across the head to give direction; all six give 3-D movement — dynamic equilibrium. Tilt and linear acceleration — the vestibule (utricle and saccule). Their maculae — floor of the utricle, sides of the saccule — have hair cells in a gel topped with otoliths. The fluid does not move the hair cells; when the head tilts, the otoliths' weight pulls the gel with gravity and bends them. In linear acceleration the heavier otolithic membrane lags, and the shearing force bends the stereocilia in the direction of acceleration.

Marks for: canals vs vestibule, cupula vs otoliths, fluid lag vs gravity/inertia, and CN VIII. Whalen's "test question" is the canal = dynamic, vestibule = static split.

In lecture: "Vestibule responsible for static equilibrium… Semicircular canals, dynamic equilibrium, test question." — Wed 10/21

4Lab 10short answerGeneral senses
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Name the three receptor cell types and the four touch receptors of the skin, giving where each touch receptor is and what it senses.

Model answer

Receptor cell types: free nerve endings (dendrites embedded in tissue) · encapsulated nerve endings (a connective-tissue capsule enhances sensitivity) · specialized receptor cells (a separate cell, e.g. a rod releasing onto a bipolar cell). Touch receptors — all mechanoreceptors: Merkel cell — stratum basale; light touch, fine spatial resolution (Braille) · Meissner's corpuscle — dermal papillae, encapsulated; light touch, less detail · Pacinian corpuscle — deep dermis, layered (lamellated) capsule like an onion · Ruffini corpuscle — deep dermis and hypodermis; stretch, for proprioception. Free nerve endings round hair follicles sense hair movement, and others act as nociceptors (pain) and thermoreceptors.

The skin model block of the lab. A mark per type and per receptor with its depth and stimulus. For Ruffini, the textbook says continuous pressure; the lab says stretch.

5Lab 10short answerTaste (gustation)
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Describe a taste bud and trace a taste from food to the brain.

Model answer

Taste buds sit on certain papillae — the four types are circumvallate, fungiform, filiform and foliate. A bud is taste (gustatory) cells, supporting cells and basal cells; the basal cells divide to replace the taste cells. Food chemicals must dissolve in saliva, enter the taste pore and bind the taste hairs of a taste cell; each of the five taste cells answers one class of chemical — sweet (mono- and disaccharides), salty (K⁺, Na⁺), sour (H⁺), bitter (alkaloids, the most sensitive), umami (amino acids). The taste cell signals a sensory neuron, and CN VII, IX and X carry the message to the primary gustatory cortex in the parietal lobe.

"The mechanisms of taste and smell" is a Ch. 9 objective he read out. Marks: the three cell types, dissolving in saliva, the five tastes with their chemicals, three nerves, parietal lobe.

1Lab 10flashcardGeneral senses
  • lab manual

General senses (lab definition)

Back

All senses except the special senses — somatic plus visceral.

2Lab 10flashcardGeneral senses
  • lab manual

The three receptor cell types

Back

Free nerve ending · encapsulated nerve ending · specialized receptor cell.

3Lab 10flashcardGeneral senses
  • lab manual

Transduction vs transmission

Back

Transduction — stimulus → AP at the receptor. Transmission — the AP travelling along the sensory neuron.

4Lab 10flashcardGeneral senses
  • lab manual
detail

Merkel cell

Back

Stratum basale; light touch with fine spatial resolution — Braille.
