Lab 11 — Endocrine System

Week 12 · study page · 33 multiple choice · 6 short answer · 33 flashcards

1Lab 11HT/ Post pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

A mark-all-that-apply item asks which hormones the posterior pituitary makes. What is the right answer?

Answer: c

Posterior-pituitary hormones are made by hypothalamic neurosecretory neurons, stored in their axon terminals in the posterior pituitary, and released into the blood through the capillary plexus. Whalen: "None of them were made there" — he called this out as the trap. The posterior lobe releases ADH and OT (option a is right about release, wrong about making). Prolactin is an anterior-pituitary hormone.

In lecture: "Don't fall for a question that says, which of the following hormones are made in the posterior pituitary? Mark all that apply. Because none of them were made there." — Wed 10/28

2Lab 11HT/ Post pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

On the lab's posterior-pituitary figure, which hypothalamic nucleus sends oxytocin down the infundibulum?

Answer: a

The lab pairs paraventricular → oxytocin and supraoptic → ADH. Whalen's lecture said the supraoptic nucleus is "home to the production and secretion of oxytocin" and did not say what the paraventricular makes; the textbook names neither. The course rule ranks lecture above lab, so this is a live conflict — on the lab exam give the lab's pairing, and know the lecture said supraoptic. Options c and d appear in no course source for this lab.

3Lab 11HT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture

A releasing hormone leaves the hypothalamus bound for the anterior pituitary. What route does it take?

Answer: d

The hypophyseal portal system: a hypothalamic capillary bed, a vein, then an anterior-pituitary capillary bed. Through it the hypothalamus releases hormones that stimulate or inhibit anterior-pituitary release. Option a is how the posterior lobe gets ADH and OT. Option c is the route the portal system exists to avoid, and there is no synapse onto the anterior-pituitary cells (option b) — the link is the portal blood supply.

4Lab 11HT/ Post pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

During labour, contractions push the fetus against the cervix. What does the resulting stretch cause, and what ends the loop?

Answer: b

Oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions; they push the fetus against the cervix, stretching and dilating it, which releases more OT — until the fetus is delivered. That is positive feedback: the result amplifies the process until an outside event ends it. Option a describes negative feedback. ADH and prolactin are not part of this loop.

5Lab 11HT/ Post pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture

A newborn suckles and milk flows from the breast within seconds. Which hormone produced the milk and which ejected it?

Answer: d

Prolactin stimulates milk production; oxytocin contracts the milk ducts and releases the milk. Whalen stopped the class twice to correct this: "let-down and ejection" is oxytocin. Option a is the exact swap he corrected. In the lab, suckling releases OT, OT contracts the ducts, and the infant suckles more — positive feedback until it stops.

6Lab 11HT/ Post pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture

A runner is dehydrated and her blood osmolarity is high. How does ADH respond, and what does it do?

Answer: b

High blood osmolarity (or low blood volume/pressure via RAAS) releases ADH. ADH inserts aquaporins in the DCT and collecting-duct cells — more channels, more water reabsorbed. Its second target is vascular smooth muscle, which it contracts, raising BP. Option c is aldosterone's job, and it moves Na⁺ the other way — reabsorbing it. Options a and d have the direction wrong.

7Lab 11HT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

According to the lab, how many hormones does the anterior pituitary release?

Answer: c

The lab says seven: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, PRL and MSH. Whalen's deck and his "7 main hormones" line agree. The textbook (§10.2, its summary and Figure 10.6) says six and never mentions MSH — option b is the textbook answer. Give seven on the lab exam. ADH and OT are posterior-pituitary hormones (option d).

8Lab 11HT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Which chain for growth hormone is right?

Answer: a

GHRH from the hypothalamus stimulates somatotrophs to release GH. GH directly speeds protein synthesis in muscle and bone, and activates IGF-1, which indirectly supports it. Thyrotrophs make TSH (option b). Options c and d reverse links in the chain — the releasing hormone always comes from the hypothalamus.

9Lab 11HT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
detail

Which pairing of anterior-pituitary cell with its hormone is right?

Answer: d

The lab: thyrotrophs → TSH; corticotrophs → ACTH and also MSH (stimulated by UV light); gonadotrophs → FSH and LH; lactotrophs → PRL; somatotrophs → GH. Corticotrophs making MSH is the lab's own statement — easy to miss because MSH has its own section. Each distractor gives a real cell type another cell's hormone.

10Lab 11HT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

What stimulates melanocyte-stimulating hormone, according to the lab?

Answer: c

UV light stimulates corticotrophs to secrete MSH; MSH stimulates melanin production, and it rises in pregnancy. Cold triggers TRH, stress triggers CRH, and suckling triggers oxytocin. Whalen added that MSH's role in humans is unclear — "We don't even know" — and that it stimulates libido and hunger.

11Lab 11Sex hormones
  • lab manual
  • lecture

In a male, which pairing of gonadotropin and target is right?

Answer: b

LH stimulates Leydig cells to make testosterone; FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to support sperm production. Option a is the classic swap. Whalen's version is the same: LH tells the interstitial (Leydig) cells between the seminiferous tubules to make testosterone.

12Lab 11Sex hormones
  • lab manual
detail

FSH levels climb in a man. Which hormone feeds back to inhibit FSH directly at the anterior pituitary?

Answer: d

FSH raises inhibin, which directly inhibits anterior-pituitary FSH. Testosterone also feeds back, but it inhibits the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary generally — the lab gives the FSH-specific brake to inhibin. Prolactin and oxytocin are not in the gonadal loop.

13Lab 11Sex hormones
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Late in the cycle estrogen reaches a high level. What happens, and what kind of feedback is it?

Answer: a

High late-cycle estrogen flips to positive feedback — the LH surge triggers ovulation. The leftover follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which makes progesterone to maintain the endometrium; when progesterone falls, the lining sheds (option d has it backwards). Otherwise high testosterone, estrogen or progesterone inhibit the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary — negative feedback, option b's shape.

14Lab 11Adrenal gland
  • lab manual
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

Working from the capsule inward, which order of adrenal zones and products is right?

Answer: c

Glomerulosa (outer) — mineralocorticoids, aldosterone. Fasciculata — glucocorticoids, cortisol. Reticularis (deepest) — androgens, plus some glucocorticoids. Medulla — epinephrine and norepinephrine. Whalen said this zone list is on the test. Option d swaps the hormones — he made that slip himself once in lecture, then corrected it. Option b runs the cortex inside out.

In lecture: Asked "Are you gonna test us on this?" about the three adrenal-cortex zones, he said "Yeah." — Wed 10/28

15Lab 11Adrenal gland
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

According to the lab, which two stimuli act directly on the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone?

Answer: d

The lab: low Na⁺, BP or blood volume stimulate aldosterone indirectly; high K⁺ and ACTH stimulate it directly. Option a lists the indirect ones (they act through RAAS). The textbook disagrees on ACTH — it has ACTH controlling the glucocorticoids and says mineralocorticoids are released "independent of the hypothalamus" (§10.5). Use the lab's version on the lab exam.

16Lab 11Adrenal gland
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Aldosterone acts on the DCT and collecting duct. What does it change?

Answer: b

Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting ducts reabsorb Na⁺ (water follows, restoring volume, BP and Na⁺) and secrete K⁺ and H⁺ into the urine. Whalen: "I'll give up some potassium if I can get more sodium." Option a swaps the ions. Option c is ADH. Option d is the calcium hormones' territory.

17Lab 11Adrenal gland
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A patient on long-term cortisol has high blood glucose and catches infections easily. Which pair of cortisol actions explains both?

Answer: c

Cortisol raises blood glucose — it stimulates liver glycogen breakdown, and muscle protein and fat breakdown that feeds liver gluconeogenesis — and it suppresses inflammation and immunity. Options b and d have glucose going the wrong way; option a has inflammation going the wrong way and a mechanism the lab does not give.

18Lab 11Adrenal gland
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Why does epinephrine from the adrenal medulla prolong a fight-or-flight response that sympathetic neurons start?

Answer: a

Sympathetic preganglionic neurons stimulate the chromaffin (neuroendocrine) cells to release epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood. They have the same fight-or-flight actions as sympathetic neurons, but blood-borne they reach more targets and last longer. Epinephrine is water soluble and works through cAMP (option b). Option c gets it backwards: going by blood is what makes the effect wider and longer, not faster. Option d is in no course source.

19Lab 11Thyroid hormone
  • lab manual
  • lecture

A person moves into a cold climate. Put the thyroid response in order.

Answer: d

Cold or low T3/T4 stimulates the hypothalamus to release TRH; TRH stimulates the anterior pituitary (thyrotrophs) to release TSH; TSH stimulates thyroid growth and T3/T4 release. High T3/T4 inhibit the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. "Where does TRH come from?" took Whalen's class four tries — every releasing hormone comes from the hypothalamus (options a and c). Option b is the feedback arrow, not the sequence.

20Lab 11Thyroid hormone
  • lab manual
  • lecture

A diet lacks iodine, so T3/T4 stay low. What happens to TSH, and why?

Answer: b

In the 3-tier loop, high T3/T4 inhibit the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. With T3/T4 low, that brake never comes, so TRH and TSH keep rising — Whalen's simple goiter: the thyroid is stimulated without end and enlarges. Option d gets the direction of feedback backwards: T3/T4 inhibit TSH.

21Lab 11Thyroid hormone
  • lab manual
detail

Which statement comparing T3 and T4 is right?

Answer: d

T3 is the most active, with a short half-life; T4 has the longer half-life and is converted to T3. Option c reverses the conversion. T3/T4 are amines but lipid soluble — the lab lists them with the lipid-soluble hormones (option b).

22Lab 11Thyroid hormone
  • lab manual
detail

What is the calorigenic effect?

Answer: a

T3/T4 raise basal metabolic rate and body temperature — the calorigenic effect. Heat is the by-product of the raised metabolism; T3/T4 also promote growth and development and boost sympathetic effects. The distractors are real hormone actions, but not this one.

23Lab 11Calcium regulation
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Blood calcium rises above normal. Which cells respond, and what does their hormone do to bone?

Answer: c

High Ca²⁺ (hypercalcemia) stimulates parafollicular (C) cells to release calcitonin, which lowers Ca²⁺: it inhibits osteoclasts, indirectly stimulates osteoblasts (bone deposition), and inhibits kidney Ca²⁺ reabsorption. Option a is the low-calcium response. Follicular cells make T3/T4, not calcitonin (option b). Whalen: "Calcitonin, not calcitriol."

24Lab 11Calcium regulation
  • lab manual
  • lecture

PTH raises blood calcium by acting on three targets. Which list is right?

Answer: b

Low Ca²⁺ stimulates chief cells to release PTH. PTH stimulates osteoclasts (bone resorption releases Ca²⁺), increases kidney Ca²⁺ reabsorption, and activates vitamin D3 (calcitriol), which stimulates intestinal Ca²⁺ and phosphate absorption. Option a mixes in calcitonin's bone action; option c is calcitonin's bone action outright. PTH and calcitonin together hold Ca²⁺ at homeostasis — the seesaw.

25Lab 11Calcium regulation
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

On the lab exam, how is the parathyroid described?

Answer: d

The lab: 3–5 separate nodules embedded in the posterior thyroid. Whalen's lecture ("these four"), his deck and the textbook say four — and the lecture outranks the lab, so expect four on the lecture exam and 3–5 on the lab portion. Option a has the right lecture number but the wrong side. The isthmus joins the thyroid's two lobes (option c).

26Lab 11Glucose regulation
  • lab manual
  • textbook
  • lecture
detail

According to the lab, at what range does negative feedback hold blood glucose?

Answer: c

The lab sets glucose homeostasis at 70–110 mg/dL. The textbook (Ch. 10a) gives 70–150 mg/dL across a day and calls a fasting value under 100 normal — option b is the textbook answer. Give 70–110 on the lab exam. 35–40 mg/dL is where Whalen said you lose consciousness.

27Lab 11Glucose regulation
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Two hours after a meal blood glucose is falling below normal. Which response restores it?

Answer: a

Low glucose stimulates alpha cells to release glucagon: the liver breaks down glycogen (glycogenolysis) and makes new glucose (gluconeogenesis), and glucose rises. High glucose stimulates beta cells to release insulin: cells take up glucose, liver and muscle store glycogen, adipose stores fat (option b — the opposite case). Options c and d swap the cells.

28Lab 11Glucose regulation
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Why is the pancreas called both exocrine and endocrine?

Answer: b

Acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes to the duodenum (exocrine — through a duct); the islets secrete insulin (beta cells) and glucagon (alpha cells) into the blood (endocrine). Whalen's one-line rule: ducts versus blood. Option a swaps the two tissues; alpha and beta cells both make hormones (option c).

29Lab 11Water & Electrolyte Balance
  • lab manual

Blood pressure falls after a haemorrhage. Which sequence of the RAAS is right?

Answer: d

Low BP or blood volume stimulates the kidney to release renin; renin and lung ACE turn angiotensinogen into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II then raises BP: vasoconstriction, thirst, Na⁺ and water reabsorption, and release of aldosterone and ADH. Option b swaps the kidney and lung. Angiotensinogen is the starting material, not the product (option c).

30Lab 11Water & Electrolyte Balance
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Which hormone does the opposite of the RAAS, and what triggers it?

Answer: a

ANP is the opposite: a stretched right atrium (high volume) releases it, and it cuts Na⁺ reabsorption and inhibits renin — more water lost, lower blood volume. ADH and aldosterone raise volume (options b and c). Renin is released by low pressure (option d).

31Lab 11Water soluble vs lipid soluble Hormones
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Cortisol reaches a target cell. Where is its receptor, and what is the result?

Answer: c

Cortisol is lipid soluble — made from cholesterol — so it crosses the membrane, binds a receptor inside, and switches on genes, making new proteins: slower and longer-lasting. Whalen: "Lipid-soluble hormones always result in production of brand new protein", and the receptor is "always — inside the cell." Option a is the water-soluble route. cAMP belongs to surface receptors only (option d).

32Lab 11Water soluble vs lipid soluble Hormones
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

Which hormone does the lab class as water soluble, acting through a second messenger?

Answer: b

Water-soluble (protein, peptide) hormones can't cross the membrane: they bind a surface receptor (first messenger) that activates a second messenger (cAMP), which activates existing enzymes — fast and short-lived. The lab's list: pituitary hormones, PTH, calcitonin, ANP, epinephrine. Aldosterone, cortisol, the sex steroids and T3/T4 are lipid soluble. T3/T4 is the trap — an amine, but lipid soluble.

33Lab 11Negative and positive feedback
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Which pairing of feedback type with example is right?

Answer: d

Negative feedback — the result shuts the process off and holds homeostasis; it controls most hormones (high T3/T4 or cortisol inhibiting the hypothalamus and pituitary; insulin lowering glucose so insulin stops). Positive feedback — the result amplifies the process until an outside event ends it (oxytocin in childbirth; high estrogen causing the LH surge). Options a, b and c each attach a real example to the wrong type.

1Lab 11short answerThyroid hormone
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Diagram the 3-tier negative-feedback loop for thyroid hormone, from stimulus to shut-off. Name the cells and say what T3/T4 do.

Model answer

Stimulus: cold, or low T3/T4. Tier 1: the hypothalamus releases TRH into the hypophyseal portal system. Tier 2: TRH stimulates the thyrotrophs of the anterior pituitary to release TSH. Tier 3: TSH stimulates the thyroid — its growth and T3/T4 release. The follicular cells line the follicles and make colloid, an iodine-rich protein fluid that becomes T3 and T4 — the body's main use of iodine. T3 is the most active, with a short half-life; T4 has a longer half-life and is converted to T3. They are amines but lipid soluble. Effects: T3/T4 raise basal metabolic rate and body temperature (the calorigenic effect, heat being the by-product), promote growth and development, and boost sympathetic effects. Shut-off: high T3/T4 inhibit both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary — two (–) lines back. If T3/T4 can't be made (no iodine), the brake never arrives, TSH keeps stimulating, and the thyroid enlarges — simple goiter.

Marks for the three tiers in order with TRH from the hypothalamus (the step Whalen's class missed four times), TSH from the anterior pituitary, T3/T4 from follicular cells, both inhibitory lines, and at least two effects. The goiter consequence shows you understand what the feedback is for.

2Lab 11short answerWater & Electrolyte Balance
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Diagram the RAAS chain, then explain how ADH, aldosterone and ANP each change blood volume.

Model answer

RAAS: low blood pressure or blood volume stimulates the kidney to release renin; renin and lung ACE turn angiotensinogen into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II raises BP four ways: vasoconstriction, thirst, Na⁺ and water reabsorption, and release of aldosterone and ADH. ADH: released by high osmolarity (or low volume via RAAS); made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary; it inserts aquaporins in the DCT and collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed — concentrated urine, higher blood volume — and it also contracts vascular smooth muscle. Aldosterone: from the zona glomerulosa; makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb Na⁺ (water follows if ADH is present) and secrete K⁺ and H⁺, raising volume and BP. ANP — the opposite: a stretched right atrium (high volume) releases ANP; it cuts Na⁺ reabsorption and inhibits renin, so more water is lost and blood volume falls.

Marks for the chain in order (low BP → kidney renin → ACE in the lung → angiotensin II), at least three of angiotensin II's actions, ADH = water via aquaporins, aldosterone = Na⁺ in, K⁺/H⁺ out, and ANP as the antagonist with its trigger. Whalen: blood volume and blood pressure always move together.

3Lab 11short answerCalcium regulation
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Explain how calcitonin and PTH hold blood calcium steady. Name the cells, the stimulus and each hormone's targets.

Model answer

High Ca²⁺ (hypercalcemia) stimulates the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid to release the protein calcitonin, which lowers Ca²⁺: it inhibits osteoclasts, indirectly stimulates osteoblasts (bone deposition), and inhibits Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the kidney (DCT and collecting duct). When Ca²⁺ is normal again, the C cells stop being stimulated and calcitonin falls. Low Ca²⁺ (hypocalcemia) stimulates the chief cells of the parathyroid glands — 3–5 nodules in the posterior thyroid per the lab (four per the lecture and textbook) — to release the peptide PTH, which raises Ca²⁺: it stimulates osteoclasts (bone resorption releases Ca²⁺), increases kidney Ca²⁺ reabsorption, and activates vitamin D3 (calcitriol), which increases intestinal absorption of Ca²⁺ and phosphate. When Ca²⁺ is normal, PTH falls. The two are antagonistic — a seesaw — and together hold calcium at homeostasis.

Marks for both cell types, both stimuli, the osteoclast lever going opposite ways, the kidney going opposite ways, and calcitriol for PTH ("calcitonin, not calcitriol"). The parathyroid count is a live lab-vs-lecture conflict; giving the lab's 3–5 here and naming the four is safe on the lab paper.

4Lab 11short answerGlucose regulation
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Diagram blood-glucose regulation by the pancreas, starting from homeostasis. Include the cells, hormones and the liver's actions.

Model answer

The pancreas is exocrine and endocrine: acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes to the duodenum; the islets secrete hormones. Negative feedback holds glucose at 70–110 mg/dL (the lab's range; the textbook gives 70–150 across a day). High glucose (after a meal) stimulates beta cells to release insulin: cells take up glucose, the liver and muscle store it as glycogen, and adipose stores fat — glucose falls, and with it the stimulus for insulin. Low glucose stimulates alpha cells to release glucagon: the liver breaks down glycogen (glycogenolysis) and makes new glucose (gluconeogenesis) — glucose rises. Insulin and glucagon are antagonistic.

Marks for the set-point with its number, the right cell for each hormone (beta = insulin, alpha = glucagon), at least two insulin effects, both liver actions for glucagon, and closing the loop. Whalen's negative-feedback example is exactly this one.

5Lab 11short answerHT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

Compare the hypothalamus's control of the posterior and the anterior pituitary. Name the two posterior hormones and their actions, and list the seven anterior hormones with the hypothalamic hormone that controls each.

Model answer

Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) — neural link. Hypothalamic neurosecretory neurons make the hormones; their axons run down the infundibulum, store them in axon terminals in the posterior lobe, and release them into the capillary plexus. The lab puts oxytocin in the paraventricular nucleus and ADH in the supraoptic (the lecture said supraoptic for OT). Oxytocin: uterine contractions in childbirth and milk ejection on suckling — both positive feedback — and uterine involution after birth. ADH: released by high osmolarity; aquaporins in the DCT and collecting duct, more water reabsorbed; contracts vascular smooth muscle. Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) — blood link. The hypophyseal portal system (hypothalamic capillary bed → vein → anterior capillary bed) carries releasing and inhibiting hormones. GHRH → somatotrophs → GH (growth; activates IGF-1) · TRH → thyrotrophs → TSH (thyroid) · CRH → corticotrophs → ACTH (adrenal cortex: cortisol, aldosterone) · GnRH → gonadotrophs → FSH and LH (gonads) · prolactin-releasing hormone → lactotrophs → PRL (milk production) · UV light → corticotrophs → MSH (melanin). Seven anterior hormones per the lab and lecture; the textbook counts six, without MSH.

Marks for neural vs portal connection, made in the hypothalamus, not the posterior lobe, both posterior hormones with an action each, and the seven releasing-hormone → cell → hormone chains. Name both conflicts (OT nucleus, six vs seven) rather than picking silently.

6Lab 11short answerAdrenal gland
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Describe the adrenal gland: its regions and hormones, the CRH → ACTH → cortisol cascade with its feedback, and how the medulla is stimulated.

Model answer

Triangular, atop each kidney: an outer cortex and inner medulla inside a connective tissue capsule. Cortex, outside in: zona glomerulosa — mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); zona fasciculata — glucocorticoids (cortisol); zona reticularis — androgens, and some glucocorticoids. Aldosterone (lipid soluble, from cholesterol) makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb Na⁺ and secrete K⁺ and H⁺; high K⁺ and ACTH stimulate it directly, low Na⁺/BP/volume indirectly. Cortisol raises blood glucose (liver glycogen breakdown; muscle protein and fat breakdown feeding gluconeogenesis) and suppresses inflammation and immunity. Cascade: stress stimulates the hypothalamus to release CRH; CRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release ACTH; ACTH stimulates the cortex to release cortisol (and, per the lab, aldosterone). High cortisol inhibits the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. Medulla: in stress or exercise, sympathetic preganglionic neurons stimulate chromaffin cells to release epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood — the same fight-or-flight actions as sympathetic nerves (↑ heart rate, BP, glucose), but reaching more targets and lasting longer.

Marks for the three zones in order with their products (Whalen: "Yeah", it's on the test), the cascade with its negative-feedback line, cortisol's two main effects, and the medulla's nerve (not hormone) trigger. ACTH → aldosterone is the lab's claim; the textbook says mineralocorticoids are independent of the hypothalamus.

In lecture: Asked "Are you gonna test us on this?" about the three adrenal-cortex zones, he said "Yeah." — Wed 10/28

  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

Paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei (lab)

Back

Paraventricular → oxytocin. Supraoptic → ADH. The lecture put oxytocin in the supraoptic — a live conflict.

4Lab 11flashcardHT/ Post pituitary
  • lab manual
detail

Uterine involution

Back

Post-partum contraction of the uterus, driven by the oxytocin that suckling releases.

5Lab 11flashcardHT/ Post pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture

ADH — stimulus and two targets

Back

High blood osmolarity (or low volume/BP via RAAS). Targets: DCT + collecting duct (inserts aquaporins) and vascular smooth muscle (contracts it).

6Lab 11flashcardHT/ Post pituitary
  • lecture

Alcohol and ADH

Back

Alcohol inhibits ADH → more urine → dehydration.

7Lab 11flashcardHT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
  • lecture

The seven anterior-pituitary hormones (lab)

Back

GH · TSH · ACTH · FSH · LH · PRL · MSH. The textbook counts six, without MSH.

8Lab 11flashcardHT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lecture

Tropic hormone

Back

A hormone that influences another endocrine gland's secretion — TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH. FSH and LH are the gonadotropic ones.

9Lab 11flashcardHT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
detail

Somatotrophs, thyrotrophs, corticotrophs

Back

Somatotrophs → GH (by GHRH). Thyrotrophs → TSH (by TRH). Corticotrophs → ACTH (by CRH) and MSH (by UV light).

10Lab 11flashcardHT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
detail

Gonadotrophs and lactotrophs

Back

Gonadotrophs → FSH and LH (by GnRH). Lactotrophs → PRL (by prolactin-releasing hormone).

11Lab 11flashcardHT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
detail

IGF-1

Back

Activated by GH; indirectly supports protein synthesis and growth, while GH acts directly on muscle and bone.

12Lab 11flashcardHT/ Anterior Pituitary
  • lab manual
detail

GH — short-term vs long-term effects

Back

Short term: breaks down fat and glycogen for energy. Long term: amino-acid uptake, protein synthesis, cell division, tissue growth.

13Lab 11flashcardSex hormones
  • lab manual
  • lecture

FSH and LH in the female

Back

FSH — follicle and oocyte development. LH — estrogen and progesterone, and ovulation.

14Lab 11flashcardSex hormones
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

Corpus luteum

Back

The leftover follicle after ovulation; makes progesterone to maintain the endometrium. When it falls, the lining sheds.

15Lab 11flashcardSex hormones
  • lab manual
detail

Inhibin

Back

Raised by FSH; directly inhibits anterior-pituitary FSH.

16Lab 11flashcardAdrenal gland
  • lab manual

Mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, androgens

Back

Mineralo- — mineral balance (aldosterone). Gluco- — glucose metabolism (cortisol). Androgens — masculinization (dehydroepiandrosterone).

17Lab 11flashcardAdrenal gland
  • lab manual
detail

Chromaffin cells

Back

Neuroendocrine cells of the adrenal medulla; stimulated by sympathetic preganglionic neurons to release epinephrine and norepinephrine.

18Lab 11flashcardGlucose regulation
  • lab manual

Gluconeogenesis vs glycogenolysis

Back

Gluconeogenesis — making new glucose. Glycogenolysis — breaking glycogen down to glucose.

19Lab 11flashcardGlucose regulation
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Normal blood glucose (lab)

Back

70–110 mg/dL. The textbook gives 70–150 across a day, fasting under 100.

20Lab 11flashcardGlucose regulation
  • lab manual

Alpha and beta cells

Back

Islet cells of the pancreas. Alpha → glucagon (raises glucose). Beta → insulin (lowers glucose).

21Lab 11flashcardThyroid hormone
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Thyroid — location and two cell types

Back

Butterfly-shaped, anterior to the trachea, below the larynx. Follicular cells (T3/T4) and parafollicular (C) cells (calcitonin).

22Lab 11flashcardThyroid hormone
  • lab manual
  • lecture
detail

Colloid

Back

The iodine-rich protein fluid made by follicular cells inside the follicles; it becomes T3 and T4.

23Lab 11flashcardThyroid hormone
  • lab manual
detail

Calorigenic effect

Back

T3/T4 raising basal metabolic rate and body temperature.

24Lab 11flashcardCalcium regulation
  • lab manual

Hypercalcemia vs hypocalcemia

Back

Hyper — high blood Ca²⁺ → calcitonin. Hypo — low blood Ca²⁺ → PTH.

25Lab 11flashcardCalcium regulation
  • lab manual
detail

Chief cells

Back

Cells of the parathyroid that release PTH when blood Ca²⁺ is low.

26Lab 11flashcardCalcium regulation
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Calcitriol

Back

Activated vitamin D3; PTH switches it on, and it increases intestinal Ca²⁺ and phosphate absorption. "Calcitonin, not calcitriol."

27Lab 11flashcardCalcium regulation
  • lab manual

Bone resorption vs bone deposition

Back

Resorption — osteoclasts break bone down, releasing Ca²⁺ (PTH). Deposition — osteoblasts build bone (calcitonin, indirectly).

28Lab 11flashcardWater & Electrolyte Balance
  • lab manual

Angiotensin II — four actions

Back

Vasoconstriction · thirst · Na⁺ and water reabsorption · release of aldosterone and ADH. All raise BP.

29Lab 11flashcardWater & Electrolyte Balance
  • lab manual
  • lecture

ANP

Back

Atrial natriuretic peptide — from a stretched right atrium; cuts Na⁺ reabsorption and inhibits renin, lowering blood volume.

30Lab 11flashcardWater soluble vs lipid soluble Hormones
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Lipid-soluble hormones — source, receptor, effect, examples

Back

From cholesterol; receptor inside; switch on genes → new proteins; slow, long-lasting. Aldosterone, cortisol, sex steroids, T3/T4.

31Lab 11flashcardWater soluble vs lipid soluble Hormones
  • lab manual
  • lecture

First vs second messenger

Back

First messenger — the water-soluble hormone at its surface receptor. Second messenger — the molecule inside, e.g. cAMP, that activates existing enzymes.

32Lab 11flashcardNegative and positive feedback
  • lab manual
  • lecture

Negative vs positive feedback

Back

Negative — the result shuts the process off; holds homeostasis; most hormones. Positive — the result amplifies the process until an outside event ends it.

33Lab 11flashcardNegative and positive feedback
  • lab manual

The lab's two positive-feedback examples

Back

Oxytocin in childbirth (ends at delivery) and high estrogen causing the LH surge.
